日.note_tr: On'yomi にち is the standard reading for 'day' in most compounds; kun'yomi ひ refers to 'sun' or 'daytime'. The suffixes -び and -か appear in weekdays and day counters respectively.

一.note_tr: The onyomi いち is used in compounds (一番, 第一) and modern counting, while the kunyomi ひと- forms are used in native words (一人, 一つ). This is the first Kangxi radical and appears frequently in both written and spoken Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: one's whole life; lifetime; entire life

国.note_tr: On'yomi こく appears in compounds (国家, 国民), while kun'yomi くに is used when the kanji stands alone or begins a word (日本国). A foundational N5 kanji for discussing geography, history, and any international topics.

人.note_tr: The kunyomi ひと is used for the standalone word 'person,' while onyomi にん and じん appear in compounds (人気=popularity, 人生=life, 人間=humanity). In counting people, use the -り suffix: 一人 (ひとり, one person), 二人 (ふたり, two people).

年.note_tr: The onyomi ねん (nen) is typically used in compounds and with counters, such as 来年 (rainen, next year); the kunyomi とし (toshi) is used in everyday conversational expressions like 今年 (kotoshi, this year) and 毎年 (mai-toshi, every year).

examples.meaning_tr: All year round; throughout the year

大.note_tr: The kunyomi おお.きい appears in the common adjective 大きい (big, large). The onyomi だい is used in many compound words and formal contexts, like 大学 (university) and 大好き (to really like). The たい reading is less common and appears in a few fixed expressions like 大会 (tournament) and 大変 (serious/difficult).

十.note_tr: じゅう is the standard onyomi in compounds (十人 ten people, 十月 October); とお is the kunyomi for standalone use or in date expressions like 十日 (tooka, 10th day). The character resembles a cross shape (+).

二.note_tr: The に reading (onyomi) is used in most compounds and with counters (二人, 二月). The ふた reading (kunyomi) stands alone for counting objects (ふたつ). The reading ふたたび means "again" and appears in older or formal contexts.

本.note_tr: ほん (on'yomi) is the most common reading, used in everyday words, compounds, and as a counter for long thin objects. The もと (kun'yomi) reading, meaning "origin" or "root," appears less frequently in basic vocabulary. Start with words like 本 (book) and 日本 (Japan).

中.note_tr: Use onyomi ちゅう in compound words (中国, 中学) and kunyomi なか/うち in standalone or descriptive contexts (真ん中, 中身). This is one of the most fundamental kanji in Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: on the way; in the middle of
all year round; throughout the year

長.note_tr: The kunyomi なが.い is used for the adjective 'long' and related measurements. The onyomi ちょう appears in compounds meaning leader/head (校長=principal), eldest (長男=eldest son), or long-term (長期=long-term).

出.note_tr: Kunyomi (で-, だ-) is used for everyday action verbs like 出る and 出す. Onyomi (しゅつ) appears in formal nouns like 出版 (publication) and 出発 (departure). In context, 出る can mean 'to appear' or 'to show up', while 出す means 'to hand in' or 'to serve'.

examples.meaning_tr: to come out, to go out, to appear
to take out, to put out, to submit
to go out, to set out on a trip

三.note_tr: Use the onyomi reading さん when combining with other kanji (e.g., 三月 March, 三人 three people); use the kunyomi み or みっつ when the kanji stands alone for counting objects (三つ three things) or for specific dates (三日 the third day). The ぞう reading is rare in modern Japanese.

時.note_tr: Use じ (on'yomi) in compounds like 時間 (じかん), 何時 (なんじ), and 同時 (どうじ); use とき (kun'yomi) when 時 stands alone meaning 'when' or 'time' (e.g., その時, at that time). Avoid confusing with 間 (あいだ, interval), which relates to time but emphasizes duration or space between events.

examples.meaning_tr: Time; when; the point at which something happens
Time (duration); hours; a period of time
Sometimes; occasionally; from time to time
At the same time; simultaneously; concurrently

meanings_tr: To do, to carry out, to conduct, to perform
A journey, a trip, to travel
行.note_tr: The kunyomi い.く means 'to go', while the onyomi こう is used in compounds like 旅行 (travel) and 銀行 (bank). The verb form おこなう means 'to conduct' or 'to perform'.

examples.meaning_tr: to do, to carry out, to conduct

見.note_tr: The kanji 見 has three main kun'yomi: み.る (to see, deliberate action), み.える (to appear, passive or spontaneous visibility), and み.せる (to show, transitive). The on'yomi けん appears primarily in formal or compound words like 意見 (opinion) and 見物 (sightseeing). Common in anime and manga: 見る for "watching" a show, 見える for "can be seen."

examples.meaning_tr: to see, to watch, to look at
to be visible, to appear, to look like

月.note_tr: Use the kunyomi つき for 'moon' and poetic phrases like moonlight; use the onyomi げつ/がつ for 'month' in compounds like January (一月) and Monday (月曜日). Don't confuse 月 with 日 (day), they're separate kanji but often appear together in dates and times.

後.note_tr: Use うしろ for physical position (back/behind), あと/あとで for temporal meaning (later/after), and ご/こう in compounds like 午後 (afternoon) or 後悔 (regret). Often paired with 前 (before/front) for contrast.

前.note_tr: Kunyomi まえ (mae) is used for spatial or standalone words: 前 = front/before. Onyomi ぜん (zen) appears in formal compounds with temporal or abstract meanings: 前日 = day before, 前方 = ahead. Both readings are common and important to master.

生.note_tr: The onyomi reading せい appears frequently in compounds like 学生 (student) and 先生 (teacher). The kunyomi なま means "raw" in food contexts; い.きる means "to live"; う.まれる means "to be born."

五.note_tr: ご (on'yomi) is used in compounds and formal counting contexts; いつ (kun'yomi) appears mainly in calendar expressions like 五日 (the fifth day). Both readings are equally important at this level.

間.note_tr: Use かん in formal compounds (時間 'time', 空間 'space'); use あいだ in natural conversation for 'between' or 'during' (この間 'recently'); use ま for simple 'space' or 'gap' (昼間 'daytime'). The onyomi かん is far more common in compounds than けん.

examples.meaning_tr: space, gap, interval between two things
recently, the other day, a while ago
nighttime, at night, during the night

上.note_tr: うえ (native reading) is the most common for 'above/on top' in everyday speech; じょう (Sino-Japanese reading) dominates in compounds like 上手 (skillful) and 上司 (boss). The reading のぼる emphasizes climbing or ascending, especially mountains. Not to be confused with 下 (shita, down, the opposite).

examples.meaning_tr: to go up; to rise; to improve
to raise; to lift up; to give
to climb; to ascend; to go up

東.note_tr: Use ひがし (kun'yomi) for simple directional reference, as in "east wind." Use とう (on'yomi) in compounds and place names like 東京 (Tokyo). This kanji is one of the four cardinal directions and appears frequently in geography and directional contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: East and west; the two extremes

四.note_tr: The onyomi reading し is common in compounds like 四月 (April) and 四季 (four seasons). The kunyomi readings よ and よん appear in direct counts or with numerals (四つ, 四人); よっ is used before small tsubo/doubling sounds, as in 四日 (fourth day).

今.note_tr: The kunyomi いま is used for the standalone word meaning "now," while the onyomi こん appears in many common compounds like 今日 (today) and 今年 (this year). The reading きん is extremely rare and not used in modern Japanese.

金.note_tr: The onyomi reading きん appears in most compound words and formal contexts (金曜日 Friday, 金属 metal, 金色 gold color). The kunyomi reading かね means money and is used when the kanji stands alone. This kanji historically represents gold and has come to also mean currency and money in general.

九.note_tr: The on'yomi きゅう (kyuu) is used in most compounds and abstract counting contexts. The kun'yomi ここの (kokono) appears mainly in date and time counter expressions. This is a straightforward number kanji with no commonly confused counterparts.

examples.meaning_tr: The ninth day of the month

入.note_tr: The kunyomi はい.る describes entering or coming in, while い.れる means putting something in (transitive). The onyomi にゅう appears mainly in formal compound words, particularly in educational and medical contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: admission, entry (to an event or venue)

学.note_tr: The onyomi (がく) is commonly used in noun compounds like 学生 and 学校; the kunyomi (まなぶ) functions as a verb meaning 'to study' or 'to learn'. This fundamental kanji appears frequently in school-themed contexts and is especially common in anime and manga.

高.note_tr: The kunyomi form 高い (takkai) is the most frequent word beginners encounter and works as an adjective meaning "high/tall" or "expensive." The onyomi 高 (kou) appears in compounds like 高校 (high school), common in anime/manga contexts. Both readings denote elevation or cost; context determines which meaning applies.

examples.meaning_tr: To rise, to increase, to heighten

円.note_tr: The onyomi えん primarily appears in currency amounts (100円, 1000円) and formal geometric terms. Don't confuse 円 with 園 (also えん, meaning garden/park), which sounds identical but looks different.

子.note_tr: The reading こ is the most common in everyday use, appearing in words like 子ども (child), 子犬 (puppy), and 子猫 (kitten). This kanji also represents the Rat sign in the Chinese zodiac, associated with the hours 11pm–1am.

meanings_tr: To remove / come off (in verb forms)
外.note_tr: Use そと when 外 refers to the physical "outside" (e.g. 外に出る "to go outside"), but note that がい is the reading in most compound words like 外国 (foreign country) or 海外 (overseas); very useful for travel-related vocabulary. The on'yomi げ is rare and appears almost only in 外科 (surgery), so don't default to it. The kun'yomi verb forms はず.す (to remove) and はず.れる (to come off/miss) are common everyday verbs, distinct from the noun readings.

examples.meaning_tr: to come off, to be disconnected, to miss

八.note_tr: The onyomi はち is primarily used in compound words such as months (八月 August) and time expressions (八時 8 o'clock). The kunyomi や appears in simple counting, while the special reading よう appears in calendar expressions like 八日 the eighth day of the month.

六.note_tr: ろく (roku) is the standard onyomi reading used in most compound words and counting. The special reading むいか (muika) applies only to "the sixth day of the month", an important exception to memorize. Counter suffixes vary depending on what is being counted (people, objects, etc.).

examples.meaning_tr: The sixth day of the month

下.note_tr: The reading した (shita) for 'below/under' is most common; くだ- (kuda-) means 'to descend' and appears in ください (please). The onyomi か and げ mainly appear in compounds like 地下 (underground) and 上下 (up and down).

examples.meaning_tr: Up and down, top and bottom

来.note_tr: The kun'yomi reading 来る (くる) means 'to come' or 'to arrive' and is used as an independent verb. On'yomi readings (らい) typically appear in time-related compounds: 来週 (next week), 来月 (next month), 来年 (next year). These time expressions are everyday vocabulary for beginners.

examples.meaning_tr: to not come, to not arrive (negative form)

気.note_tr: The onyomi き is overwhelmingly common in everyday compounds like 気分 (mood) and 気持ち (feeling). The variant pronunciation け appears in the word 元気 (energy/health, roughly "original spirit"). The kunyomi いき is rare in modern Japanese and seldom encountered at beginner level.

examples.meaning_tr: air, atmosphere, mood in a place or situation
to be careful, to pay attention, to watch out

小.note_tr: The kunyomi ちいさい (chiisai) is the most common way to express "small" as an adjective. The onyomi しょう appears primarily in compound words and Sino-Japanese terms. Prefix forms (こ-, お-) appear in words like 小鳥 (small bird) and 小犬 (puppy).

七.note_tr: Onyomi しち is used in formal contexts, months, and official counting. Kunyomi なな is standard for everyday use. The form ななつ is used when counting objects or describing ages.

examples.meaning_tr: seven mysteries; seven wonders (popular in anime and folklore)

山.note_tr: Kunyomi やま is used for the standalone word "mountain" and many nature-related compounds. Onyomi さん is typical in proper nouns like mountain names (富士山 Mount Fuji). Both readings are equally important at N5.

meanings_tr: To speak, to talk, to tell
話.note_tr: The onyomi わ typically appears in compound words like 電話 (telephone) and 会話 (conversation). The kunyomi has two main uses: はな.す for the verb "to speak/talk", and はなし for the noun "story/tale".

examples.meaning_tr: to speak, to talk, to tell

女.note_tr: Use おんな (kunyomi) for everyday contexts like 女 (woman) and 女の子 (girl), and じょ (onyomi) for formal compounds like 女性 (woman, formal) and 女子 (female student). Frequently appears in anime and manga character descriptions.

北.note_tr: Use きた (kunyomi) for standalone "north" or natural phenomena like 北風 (north wind). Use ほく (onyomi) in geographic compounds such as 北京 (Beijing) or 北米 (North America).

meanings_tr: Horse (the seventh sign of the Chinese zodiac)
午.note_tr: The onyomi ご is essential for daily life: 午前 (AM), 午後 (PM), and 正午 (noon) appear constantly on schedules and in conversation. The kunyomi うま appears mainly in zodiac terms, such as 午年 (Year of the Horse), which cycles every twelve years.

百.note_tr: ひゃく (hyaku) is the standard reading used for counting and in most compounds. The kunyomi もも (momo) and the reading びゃく (byaku) are rarely used in modern Japanese.

書.note_tr: Kun'yomi か.く is used for the verb "to write" (書く). On'yomi しょ appears in compounds like 図書館 (library) and 読書 (reading). The -が.き variant appears in forms like 書き方 (way of writing).

先.note_tr: The onyomi (せん) is used in most time-related compounds like 先月 (last month) and 先輩 (senior). The kunyomi さき means 'ahead' or 'tip,' while ま.ず means 'first of all.' Distinguish 先 from 前 (mae/before), 前 emphasizes location in space or point in time, while 先 emphasizes sequence and order.

名.note_tr: The kun'yomi 'na' is used in 名前 (name). The on'yomi 'mei' appears in words about reputation and mastery (famous, masterpiece, expert), while the alternative 'myō' is used in formal or historical contexts like 大名 (daimyo).

川.note_tr: The kunyomi かわ is more common in everyday speech when referring to a river, while the onyomi せん typically appears in compound words like 河川 (かせん). As a simple three-stroke radical, 川 is frequently found in place names and geographic references in manga and anime.

千.note_tr: The on'yomi せん is used in most compound words and numerical contexts (e.g., 千円 = one thousand yen). The kun'yomi ち appears mainly in proper nouns like 千葉県 (Chiba Prefecture). This is a fundamental number kanji essential for learning Japanese numerals.

水.note_tr: みず is the native kun'yomi reading for the standalone noun and everyday compounds like 水色 (light blue). すい is the Chinese on'yomi reading, used in more formal or technical words like 水道 (tap water), 水泳 (swimming), and 水曜日 (Wednesday).

半.note_tr: Onyomi (はん) is used in compound words, especially in sports, time, and quantitative contexts. Kunyomi (なかば) is rarer and more literary. You'll frequently encounter this kanji in anime episode titles and sports broadcasts describing the 'first half' (前半) and 'second half' (後半).

男.note_tr: The kunyomi おとこ is the everyday word for 'man' or 'boy,' very common in anime and manga (e.g., 男の子 = 'boy'). The onyomi だん appears in formal/academic compounds like 男性 (male) and 男女 (men and women). The onyomi なん is rarely used in modern Japanese.

西.note_tr: Use the kunyomi にし for the standalone meaning "west" and in compounds like 西側 (west side). Use the onyomi せい in compounds like 西洋 (Western culture) and directional terms such as 南西 (southwest).

電.note_tr: 電 is primarily used in compounds with its onyomi reading でん, appearing in words related to electricity, power, and telecommunications. Unlike 光 (light), 電 specifically refers to electrical or power source contexts.

校.note_tr: The onyomi こう dominates modern usage, especially in school-related compounds. School settings (学校, 高校, 中学校) appear very frequently in anime and manga, essential vocabulary for beginners interested in these media.

語.note_tr: The onyomi ご appears in language names (日本語, 英語), making it one of the most frequently encountered readings. The kunyomi かたる means 'to speak' or 'to tell,' as seen in 物語 (story), where narrative develops from spoken words.

土.note_tr: The reading つち is used for the standalone word 土 (earth). The reading ど is very common in compounds like 土曜日 (Saturday) and 土星 (Saturn). The reading と is less common, appearing in 土地 (land).

木.note_tr: The on'yomi もく is used in compounds like 木曜日 (Thursday) and 木製 (wooden), while the kun'yomi き means 'tree' when standalone. The reading ぼく is rare in modern usage.

聞.note_tr: The kunyomi き.く (kiku) covers both 'to listen' and 'to ask', use context to determine the meaning. The related form き.こえる (kikoeru) means 'to be heard' or 'to sound.' The onyomi ぶん appears in 新聞 (newspaper).

食.note_tr: Use the kunyomi form 食べる (taberu) for the verb "to eat"; use the onyomi reading in compounds like 朝食 (breakfast) and 食事 (meal). Mastering both readings is essential for JLPT N5.

車.note_tr: This kanji has two main readings: the kunyomi くるま is used for the standalone word 車 (car), while the onyomi しゃ appears in many common compound words like 電車 (train) and 自動車 (automobile). This is one of the most frequently used kanji in Japanese.

何.note_tr: 何 is the most common interrogative word in Japanese. The reading alternates between なに (before vowels and soft sounds) and なん (before consonants and certain morphs), for example: 何か (なにか) 'something' versus 何ですか (なんですか) 'what is it?' and 何時 (なんじ) 'what time?'. Not to be confused with 誰 (だれ, 'who').

南.note_tr: 南 reads みなみ when used alone to mean "south." In compound words, it typically uses the onyomi reading なん (e.g., 南米 South America). This kanji is the opposite of 北 (north), useful for remembering both directional terms.

万.note_tr: 万 uses two main onyomi readings: まん emphasizes the numerical value (万円), while ばん appears in formal and celebratory compounds (万歳). The kunyomi よろず (meaning "all" or "everything") is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Versatile; all-purpose; able to do anything
If by any chance; just in case

毎.note_tr: The onyomi reading まい is most common in everyday words like 毎日 (every day) and 毎週 (every week). The kunyomi reading ごと appears in suffix patterns like ～ごとに but is less common at beginner level.

白.note_tr: The kunyomi (しろい, しろ) is used for the i-adjective form 'white' and standalone nouns. The onyomi (はく, びゃく) appears in compound words like 白紙 (blank paper) and 白鳥 (swan).

天.note_tr: This kanji is primarily read as てん (onyomi) in modern Japanese, appearing in many compound words related to weather, talent, and celestial concepts. The kunyomi reading あま appears in 天の川 (Milky Way). Other kunyomi readings are archaic and rarely used.

母.note_tr: Use the kunyomi reading はは when referring to 'mother' in literary contexts, and the onyomi reading ぼ in compound words. Do not confuse 母 (mother) with 父 (father).

火.note_tr: The kunyomi reading ひ is used when the kanji stands alone (火・ひ) or at the beginning of compounds. The onyomi reading か is standard in most compounds with other kanji, such as 火事 (かじ, fire/disaster) and 火曜日 (かようび, Tuesday). Reading varies by word context.

右.note_tr: The kunyomi みぎ (migi) is the most common everyday reading for indicating physical position or direction. The onyomi う/ゆう appear less frequently in modern conversational Japanese but surface in some compounds and formal contexts. A fundamental kanji for describing spatial location.

読.note_tr: The kunyomi よむ is used for the action "to read" with objects (e.g., 本を読む, to read a book). The onyomi どく appears in compounds like 読書 (reading; book study). Use よむ for verbs, どく for noun compounds.

友.note_tr: 友達 uses the kunyomi とも and is the most common, casual form for friend, especially prevalent in anime and manga. Formal contexts and compounds like 友人 (formal friend) and 親友 (best friend) use the onyomi ゆう.

左.note_tr: Kunyomi ひだり is standard for everyday use and most common compounds (e.g., 左手 'left hand'). Onyomi さ is less frequent but appears in words like 左右 (left and right).

休.note_tr: Use kunyomi (やす.む) for verb forms (休む = to rest) and the common noun 休み (rest/break). Use onyomi (きゅう) in compounds with other kanji, like 休日 (day off) and 連休 (consecutive days off). This kanji appears frequently in schedules and contexts about taking time away from work or school.

examples.meaning_tr: To rest, to take a day off, to be absent

父.note_tr: Use the kunyomi reading ちち for the standalone word 'father.' Use the onyomi reading ふ in compounds like 祖父 (grandfather) and 父母 (parents).

雨.note_tr: Use the kunyomi reading あめ for the standalone noun (e.g., 雨が降っています = it is raining). The onyomi reading う appears primarily in compounds like 大雨 (heavy rain). The kunyomi variant あま- is common in everyday words like 雨傘 (umbrella).

会.note_tr: The onyomi かい appears in compounds like 会社 (kaisha, company) and 会議 (kaigi, meeting), while the kunyomi 会う (au) is used for the verb "to meet" and is very common in everyday Japanese and anime dialogue.

同.note_tr: The kun-reading おな.じ is used for basic "same" statements (e.g., 同じ, 同じくらい). The on-reading どう appears in formal or abstract compounds: 同意 "agreement," 同期 "same generation/classmates," 同好会 "club/interest group." The readings are context-dependent and rarely confused with other kanji.

事.note_tr: The native reading こと (koto) is used when the kanji stands alone, meaning 'thing' or 'matter', while the Chinese reading じ (ji) primarily appears in compound words with meanings like 'fact' or 'incident'. This is a fundamental JLPT N4 kanji appearing in countless everyday vocabulary words.

自.note_tr: The じ reading dominates in compounds like 自分 (oneself) and 自由 (freedom). The し reading appears in 自然 (nature). Kunyomi みずか.ら is mainly literary; for beginners, focus on じ and し.

社.note_tr: The onyomi しゃ dominates modern usage in business contexts (会社 'company'). The kunyomi やしろ is archaic for 'shrine'; modern Japanese uses 神社 (じんじゃ) instead.

発.note_tr: The on'yomi はつ or はっ (before certain consonants) dominates in modern Japanese compounds. The kanji's core sense is "to send forth" or "to give off," which connects all its different meanings from launching a train to publishing ideas."

者.note_tr: The onyomi しゃ is used as a suffix in compound words (医者, 作者, 学者) meaning '-er' or '-person.' The kunyomi もの is used alone for 'person' or 'thing' in simpler, standalone contexts.

地.note_tr: Both ち and じ readings are common in compounds with 地, memorize the reading as part of each word rather than trying to predict it. The core meaning (earth/ground/place) remains constant across all uses.

業.note_tr: On'yomi ぎょう is by far the most common in modern compounds related to industry, professions, and work (業界, 農業, 工業). The alternate on'yomi ごう is rare. Kun'yomi わざ (meaning skill, technique, or deed) is uncommon in contemporary usage.

examples.meaning_tr: industry, field, world (e.g., anime industry, gaming industry)

方.note_tr: Read as ほう for 'direction' (方向) and abstract 'method' (方法). Read as かた in '-かた' compounds meaning 'way of doing X' (書き方, 話し方). Standalone かた means 'person' (honorific).

新.note_tr: The onyomi しん is primarily used in compound words and formal contexts (新聞, 新年, 新作), while the kunyomi あたらしい is used as a standalone i-adjective. The other kunyomi forms are less common in modern Japanese.

examples.reading: あたらしい ともだち

場.note_tr: Use kun'yomi ば for standalone words like 場所 (place); use on'yomi じょう for compounds naming buildings or facilities (劇場 theater, 工場 factory). The reading ちょう is rare in modern Japanese.

員.note_tr: The onyomi いん is the primary reading and is used as a suffix meaning 'member' or 'employee' in compound words. There is no kunyomi for this kanji. Common in workplace and organizational contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: group member, band member, team member

立.note_tr: The kunyomi readings 立つ (たつ) and 立てる (たてる) are the most common in everyday speech, meaning "to stand" and "to set up." The onyomi forms like 独立 (どくりつ, "independence") appear in compound words and more formal contexts.

開.note_tr: 開く (ひらく) is used for opening books, doors, hands, and other objects. 開ける (あける) emphasizes the active process of opening something. The onyomi かい appears mainly in compound words like 開始 (start) and 開店 (store opening). Do not confuse with 閉 (toji/hei), which means "to close" or "to shut."

手.note_tr: The kunyomi て (te) is the main reading for most words. The onyomi ず (zu) appears in the common word 上手(skilled). Be careful not to confuse the separate kanji 上 (up) with 手 (hand) in compounds.

力.note_tr: 力 is primarily read as ちから (chikara) when used alone or at the end of compound words. The onyomi readings (りょく/ryoku, りき/riki) appear mainly in multi-kanji compounds and formal contexts. Not to be confused with 強 (strong), which describes inherent strength rather than exerted power or force.

examples.meaning_tr: Magical power; Magic (often used in anime/fantasy)
A strong person; Someone with great strength

問.note_tr: The on'yomi もん dominates compound words (質問, 問題) and is what beginners encounter first. The kun'yomi と.う and と.い appear in the verb 'to ask' and noun 'question'; these are common in dialogue and storytelling.

代.note_tr: The onyomi readings (だい, たい) appear mainly in compound words like 時代 (era) and 交代 (shift). The kunyomi かわり/かわる/かえる are used more independently: かわり is a noun meaning 'substitute,' かわる means 'to change/alternate,' and かえる means 'to replace.' Pay attention to context, 代わりに (instead of) is a very common phrase in beginner texts and anime.

examples.meaning_tr: To take turns, to alternate, to change places

明.note_tr: The kun-reading あかるい (bright/clear) is used in common everyday adjectives; the onyomi めい appears in formal compound words. Use 明日 (あした) for "tomorrow"; it's an irregular reading. Note: 明 emphasizes clarity and light, while 暗 (くらい) means its opposite, "dark."

動.note_tr: Use kunyomi (うご.く/うご.かす) for simple verbs meaning 'to move'. Onyomi (どう) appears in formal compounds like 動画 (video) and 動物 (animal). Very frequent in anime, technology, and sports vocabulary.

examples.meaning_tr: to move; to be in motion
to move (something); to operate; to cause motion

meanings_tr: Large number (10^16 in Japanese numerical system)
京.note_tr: Most commonly read きょう in place names like 東京 (Tokyo) and 京都 (Kyoto). The kun'yomi みやこ is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese. The reading きん appears in words like 南京 (Nanjing).

examples.meaning_tr: Kyoto (historical capital and major city in Japan)
Going to; moving to the capital
Kyoto confections; traditional sweets from Kyoto

目.note_tr: The kunyomi 'me' (め) refers to the eye organ and appears in concrete, descriptive contexts; the onyomi 'moku' (もく) is used in formal compounds like 目標 (goal) and 目次 (table of contents). Use 'me' for direct, physical references and 'moku' in technical or abstract meanings.

通.note_tr: The onyomi reading つう appears frequently in compounds (e.g., 普通 'normal', 交通 'traffic', 通知 'notification'). The kunyomi readings とお.る (to pass through) and とお.り (street, way) are used for more direct, concrete meanings.

言.note_tr: The kunyomi い.う (iu) is used for the verb 'to say' and is extremely common in everyday speech and anime dialogue. The onyomi げん (gen) and ごん (gon) appear in formal compounds like 言語 (language) and 発言 (statement). The reading こと appears in 言葉 (word, language) and is the historical/classical form.

examples.meaning_tr: way of saying, manner of speech, expression

理.note_tr: The on'yomi り is overwhelmingly common in compounds; the kun'yomi ことわり is literary and rare in modern Japanese. This kanji appears frequently in academic and technical terms, watch for it in subjects like physics (物理), psychology (心理), and geography (地理).

体.note_tr: The reading たい (tai) appears in compounds and can mean 'form,' 'substance,' or 'system' (as in 体操、全体、液体), while the native reading からだ (karada) is used for 'body' when standalone.

田.note_tr: Use the kunyomi 'ta' (た) when 田 starts a word (田中, 田んぼ); use the onyomi 'den' (でん) after other kanji in compounds (水田, 油田). The similar kanji 畑 (hatake) also means 'field,' but refers to dry fields for vegetables, while 田 specifically indicates wet rice paddies.

主.note_tr: The onyomi しゅ is the standard reading in modern compounds. The kunyomi おも- forms adjectives like 主な (main). The archaic kunyomi ぬし and あるじ (both meaning master or lord) appear in literature and formal contexts but are rarely used in everyday speech.

題.note_tr: 題 reads only as だい (onyomi) with no common kunyomi. It frequently appears in compounds where it signifies 'topic,' 'subject,' or 'title.' In 問題 it emphasizes 'problem'; in 課題 it means 'assignment'; in 話題 it means 'conversation topic'; and in 題名 it means 'title.'

意.note_tr: 意 is primarily used in compound words rather than standing alone. It always reads as い (onyomi) and conveys the sense of mental content, what one thinks, intends, or wishes to express.

不.note_tr: 不 primarily functions as a prefix in compounds, using the on'yomi readings ふ (fu) in most words and ぶ (bu) in words like 不気味 (eerie) and 不細工 (ugly). When attached to other elements, it negates or reverses their meaning, similar to English prefixes "un-" or "non-".

examples.meaning_tr: Mysterious, wonder, strange; very common in anime and fantasy stories
Eerie, creepy, uncanny, spooky (uses ぶ reading)

作.note_tr: The most common reading is つくる (kunyomi) for the standalone verb "to make/create." The onyomi さく appears mainly in compound words such as 作品 (work) and 作家 (author). The kunyomi suffix -づくり appears in words like 手作り (handmade).

用.note_tr: The onyomi よう is common in compounds paired with other kanji (使用, 食用), while the kunyomi もちいる stands alone as a verb meaning 'to use.' Focus on onyomi for building basic vocabulary.

examples.meaning_tr: to use, to employ, to utilize

度.note_tr: The reading ど is most common in frequency expressions like 何度 (how many times) and measurements like 温度 (temperature). The kunyomi たび means 'each time' or 'occasion', appearing in phrases like 度々 (often).

強.note_tr: The kunyomi reading つよい is used as a standalone adjective; the onyomi きょう appears mainly in compounds like 最強 (strongest) and 強力 (powerful).

examples.meaning_tr: The strongest, most powerful (common in anime and games)
To become strong, to grow stronger
Powerful, mighty (used for forces, support, or technology)
To strengthen, to reinforce, to make stronger

公.note_tr: The onyomi reading こう is by far the most common in modern Japanese compounds. The alternative reading く and the kunyomi おおやけ rarely appear in everyday contexts and beginner-level materials.

examples.meaning_tr: public; open to the public; announcement

持.note_tr: も.つ is the most common reading for active verbs meaning "to hold" or "to have"; も.ち appears in noun compounds like 気持ち (feeling) and 手持ち (handheld). じ is used in formal onyomi compounds like 持参 (bringing/carrying with). This kanji frequently describes what characters carry or possess, making it especially relevant in anime and manga contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: to hold, to have, to carry
handheld, things one has on hand

野.note_tr: The onyomi や is far more common in modern Japanese than しょ. Most everyday vocabulary uses や (野球, 野菜, 野生). The kunyomi の appears in compounds like 野原 (field). This kanji works both for geographical features (plains, wilderness) and figurative contexts (field of study, domain).

以.note_tr: 以 primarily uses the on'yomi reading (い) in modern Japanese compounds. Common patterns include 以上 (more than), 以下 (less than), and 以前 (before). The kun'yomi もって appears in archaic or literary contexts and is rarely used in everyday language.

思.note_tr: The kunyomi おも.う is the standard reading for the everyday verb 'to think' (思う), especially common in anime and manga for characters' thoughts and feelings. The onyomi し appears in formal compounds like 思想 (ideology), which is more academic.

家.note_tr: Standalone with kunyomi (いえ) means 'house' or 'home.' When used as a suffix with onyomi か, it means 'expert' or '-ist' (e.g., 漫画家 manga artist, 音楽家 musician).

世.note_tr: Most compounds use the onyomi reading せ or せい (e.g., 世界 'world', 世紀 'century'). The kunyomi よ appears primarily in the classical expression 世の中 ('the world'). The reading そう is rare and found only in specialized or archaic phrases.

examples.meaning_tr: The world; society; the way things are
The public; society; people in general

多.note_tr: The kunyomi おお.い forms the i-adjective 多い (many/much), one of the most common words in anime and everyday Japanese. The onyomi た appears in many compounds, especially 多分 (probably), an essential adverb you'll hear constantly. Distinguish 多 (quantity/abundance) from 大 (size/bigness), they sound similar but mean different things.

正.note_tr: The kunyomi ただしい is the most common everyday reading for "correct." The onyomi せい and しょう primarily appear in compounds like 正義 and 正月. The reading まさに means "exactly" or "just" and adds emphasis in speech.

安.note_tr: The on'yomi あん is used in compounds (安全 'safe', 安心 'peace of mind', 安定 'stable'), while the kun'yomi やす.い stands alone as a common adjective meaning 'cheap.' The reading やす.らか is literary and less frequently used in everyday Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: peace of mind, to feel relieved or at ease

院.note_tr: This kanji functions primarily as a suffix (no kun-reading) that attaches to other kanji to form compound words denoting institutions or establishments. The on-reading いん is always used.

心.note_tr: The kunyomi こころ is used for the standalone word "heart/mind" and as the ending -ごころ in compounds expressing a feeling or state of mind (e.g. 遊び心). The onyomi しん appears in Sino-Japanese compounds like 心配 or 中心. Don't confuse 心 with the visually similar radical 忄(りっしんべん), which appears in kanji like 忙 or 快 but is not written as a standalone character.

界.note_tr: 界 uses only the onyomi reading かい and appears almost exclusively in compounds; it rarely stands alone. It means 'world' or a specific 'realm' (such as an industry or field). In anime and games, you'll frequently encounter fantasy compounds like 魔法界 ('magical world').

教.note_tr: The onyomi きょう is used in compounds like 教室 (classroom) and 宗教 (religion); kunyomi おしえる is the verb 'teach'. Context determines whether the focus is on instruction or faith/doctrine.

文.note_tr: The ぶん reading is dominant in modern Japanese, especially in compound words. もん is less common, appearing in words like 文字 (もじ - character).

元.note_tr: The onyomi げん is used in compound words (元気 energy, 元年 first year); the kunyomi もと means 'origin' or 'source' when standing alone. Distinguish from 原 (which emphasizes 'natural/raw') and 本 (which can mean 'book' or 'genuine').

examples.meaning_tr: first year (of an era or reign)

重.note_tr: Use kunyomi おも(い) as the adjective meaning 'heavy' or to express seriousness. Use onyomi じゅう in formal compound words (重要, 体重). Distinguish from 厚 (thick): 重 emphasizes weight and importance, while 厚 refers to thickness.

examples.meaning_tr: To layer; to overlap; to repeat

近.note_tr: The kun-reading ちか.い (chika.i) is used for the i-adjective 近い (near, close). The on-reading きん (kin) appears frequently in compounds like 最近 (recently), 近代 (modern age), and 近所 (neighborhood). Use ちかい when describing someone or something as near or physically close.

考.note_tr: The kunyomi かんが.える is far more common in everyday speech and appears frequently in anime and manga. The onyomi こう mainly appears in formal compounds like 思考 (thinking). When used as a verb, the kanji is followed by hiragana: 考える.

画.note_tr: In compound words, 画 is most commonly read as が (ga). The かく (kaku) reading appears in planning contexts like 計画 (plan). This kanji frequently appears in anime, manga, and media vocabulary, essential for entertainment enthusiasts.

海.note_tr: Use the kunyomi reading (うみ) for the standalone noun meaning "sea." The onyomi reading (かい) is used in most compound words. Notice compounds like 海賊 (pirate) and 海岸 (beach) both use the onyomi, this pattern is very common in Japanese.

売.note_tr: う.る (kunyomi) is the transitive verb "to sell"; う.れる means "to be sold" or "to sell well" (intransitive). The onyomi ばい appears in compounds. Do not confuse with 買 (to buy); opposite meanings.

examples.meaning_tr: to be sold; to sell well

知.note_tr: Kunyomi (し) is used in the verb 知る (to know); onyomi (ち) is used in compounds like 知識 and 知恵. Both readings appear frequently in Japanese.

道.note_tr: The kun-reading みち is used for concrete physical paths and roads (e.g., 道, 山道), while the on-reading どう appears in compounds describing abstract or cultural "ways" (e.g., 武道 martial arts, 茶道 tea ceremony). The reading いう is archaic and virtually never used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Tea ceremony, the way of tea

集.note_tr: Use kunyomi (あつ.まる/あつ.める) for everyday gather/collect actions; use on'yomi (しゅう) for compound words like 集中 (focus) and 集団 (group). The character appears in casual meetings and formal assemblies alike.

examples.meaning_tr: to gather, to meet, to assemble
to collect, to gather, to compile

別.note_tr: The onyomi べつ is used in most compounds and phrases like 別に 'not particularly' (common in anime/manga dialogue). The kunyomi わかれる is used for the verb meaning 'to separate' or 'to break up', particularly in relationship contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: to separate; to break up (from a relationship)

物.note_tr: The kun reading もの is most frequently used, especially for standalone words. The on readings ぶつ and もつ appear mainly in compounds like 動物 and 荷物.

使.note_tr: The kunyomi reading 使う (つかう) is the everyday form meaning "to use" and appears in most common verbs. The onyomi reading し appears in compound words like 使者 (messenger) and 天使 (angel). Anime and manga fans will frequently encounter 魔法使い (wizard) and 天使 (angel), both containing this kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: How to use; Method of use

品.note_tr: The onyomi ひん is used in most compound words (商品, 食品, 作品), while the kunyomi しな appears in simpler words (品物). The kanji carries both concrete meaning (physical goods) and abstract meaning (quality, refinement).

計.note_tr: The kunyomi はか.る is the active verb 'to measure,' while the onyomi けい appears in compounds like 計画 (plan) and 計算 (calculation). Both reflect the intellectual sense of computing or reckoning something.

死.note_tr: The kunyomi しぬ (shinu) is the main verb form meaning 'to die.' The onyomi し (shi) is used in formal or technical compounds like 死亡 (shibou - death) and appears in medical and news contexts.

特.note_tr: The character 特 uses its onyomi reading (とく) in compounds and emphasizes what makes something distinctive or unique. Don't confuse it with 別 (separate/different); 特 highlights special qualities, while 別 emphasizes being set apart or divided.

私.note_tr: Watashi (わたし) is the most common reading for "I/me" and works in both casual and polite contexts, while watakushi (わたくし) is more formal and respectful. The on'yomi reading (shi) primarily appears in compounds like 私立 (shiritsu, private school) and 私服 (shifuku, civilian clothes).

始.note_tr: The reading はじまる (intransitive) describes when something begins by itself (e.g., the movie starts), while はじめる (transitive) describes when someone deliberately starts something (e.g., to start reading a book). These are the most common readings for beginners.

examples.meaning_tr: to start; to begin; to commence

朝.note_tr: The kunyomi あさ is used for the everyday word "morning" (朝, and in compounds like 朝ご飯), while the onyomi ちょう appears in Sino-Japanese compounds related to dynasties, eras, or formal time-of-day terms (like 朝食, 王朝). Don't confuse 朝 (morning/dynasty) with the similar-looking 明 (bright) or 潮 (tide), which share the right-side component.

運.note_tr: The on'yomi (うん) is the most common reading and appears frequently in phrases about luck, destiny, and fortune, especially in anime and manga. The kun'yomi (はこぶ) means 'to carry' or 'to transport' and is less frequently encountered by beginners but important to recognize.

終.note_tr: Use 終わる (おわる) when something ends by itself (intransitive), and 終える (おえる) when someone finishes something (transitive); same distinction as "to end" vs "to end something". In compound words like 終電 or 最終回, the on'yomi しゅう is used. The reading つい/ついに (meaning "finally, at last") is rare for this kanji; in modern Japanese that meaning is almost always written with 遂に instead, so don't worry about memorizing it for 終.

examples.meaning_tr: final episode (e.g., the last episode of an anime)
the last train of the night
end, completion (often seen in apps/games as 'Game Over' or 'Finished')
all day long, throughout the day

meanings_tr: Counter for machines, vehicles, and appliances
台.note_tr: 台 has two common onyomi readings: だい (more frequent in everyday usage and counters like 台所 meaning kitchen) and たい (used in words like 台風 typhoon and 台湾 Taiwan). When counting machines, vehicles, or appliances, use 台 as a counter. The kunyomi readings are rarely used in modern Japanese.

広.note_tr: The kunyomi ひろい is most common in everyday adjectives and descriptions (広い = wide/spacious). The onyomi こう appears mainly in compound words like 広告 (advertisement), while other kunyomi forms express spreading or expanding (広がる, 広める).

examples.meaning_tr: to spread, to expand, to stretch out
to spread, to promote, to disseminate

住.note_tr: Use kunyomi す.む for the verb "to live in [place]." Onyomi じゅう appears in compounds such as 住所 (address) and 住宅 (housing). The suffix -ず.まい attaches to place words to indicate type of dwelling or residence.

真.note_tr: Onyomi しん is used in compound nouns like 真実 (truth), while kunyomi ま is used in common descriptive and positional terms like 真面目 (sincere), 真っ黒 (jet black), and 真ん中 (center). The reading まこと is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: jet black; pitch black; completely black

有.note_tr: The kunyomi form ある is one of the most frequently used verbs in Japanese and essential for basic sentences. The onyomi reading ゆう primarily appears in compound words like 有名 (famous) and 有料 (paid).

examples.meaning_tr: To exist, to be, to have

口.note_tr: The kunyomi reading くち is used for the literal meaning "mouth" in basic words and mouth-related actions. The onyomi reading こう is common in compounds for abstract spatial meanings like "entrance" (入口), "exit" (出口), and "population" (人口).

少.note_tr: The kunyomi readings (すこし and すくない) function as standalone adjectives or adverbs. The onyomi (しょう) appears mainly in compound words like 少年 (boy) and 少女 (girl), which are common in anime and manga. Both 少し and 少々 mean 'a little' but are used in slightly different contexts.

町.note_tr: Use the kunyomi reading (まち) when referring to the place itself as 'town' or in descriptive compounds; use the onyomi reading (ちょう) in formal or administrative terms. Not to be confused with 街 (street), which emphasizes thoroughfare rather than a town area.

料.note_tr: This kanji appears almost exclusively in compound words, always using the on'yomi りょう. Very common in food contexts (料理 = cooking, 調味料 = seasoning) and cost contexts (料金 = fee). No kun'yomi exists.

工.note_tr: The reading こう is most common in everyday compounds like 工場 (factory) and 工事 (construction). The reading く appears in 工夫 (ingenuity), while ぐ is less frequent. This kanji also functions as Radical 48, shaped like Katakana エ.

建.note_tr: The native reading た.てる (to build) is most common in everyday conversation and manga. The Sino-Japanese reading け.ん appears in formal and technical compounds like 建築 (architecture) and 建設 (construction). Other readings (こん, た.つ, だ.て) are not typically encountered at beginner level.

examples.meaning_tr: founding of a nation, establishment of a country

空.note_tr: そら is used for the physical sky, while から (empty) and 空く (to become empty) are used for vacancy concepts. The on'yomi くう predominantly appears in compounds like 空気 and 空港, which are common in anime and manga.

examples.meaning_tr: to become empty; to be free

急.note_tr: The kunyomi いそぐ is the main verb meaning "to hurry" (急ぐ). The onyomi きゅう appears in compounds like 緊急 (emergency) and adverbs like 急に (suddenly). Both readings are essential and equally common.

止.note_tr: The kunyomi と.まる (intransitive: to stop, to come to rest) and と.める (transitive: to make something stop) are most common in everyday use. The onyomi し appears in formal compounds like 禁止 (prohibition) and 中止 (cancellation). The reading や.める shifts the nuance to 'to quit' or 'to stop doing,' though 辞める is more standard for this meaning.

examples.meaning_tr: to stop; to halt; to make something stop
to stop; to come to rest; to come to a halt
to quit; to stop doing something; to give up

送.note_tr: The kunyomi おくる is used for the basic verb 'to send' and 'to escort.' The onyomi そう typically appears in compound words like 放送 (broadcast) and 送信 (transmission). Both readings are equally common in everyday Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: To send; to escort; to see someone off
Broadcast (especially used for anime and TV programs)
Transmission; send (for email, messages, or data)
To see off; to wave goodbye; to watch someone leave
Pick-up and drop-off service (common for transportation)

切.note_tr: The kunyomi reading (きる, きれ) is used for the verb 'to cut' and related forms. The onyomi reading (せつ) typically appears in compound words meaning 'important' or 'precious' (e.g., 大切, 親切).

転.note_tr: This kanji has multiple readings reflecting different contexts. Kunyomi readings (ころ.ぶ, ころ.がる) describe concrete physical actions like falling and rolling, while the onyomi reading てん appears in compound words for more abstract senses such as "transfer" (転送) or "turning point" (転機). In anime and manga, 転機 often marks a pivotal plot shift.

研.note_tr: The on'yomi けん (ken) is used in most compound words like 研究 (research). The kun'yomi と.ぐ (to.gu) appears in the verb 研ぐ (to sharpen), which is particularly useful in cooking and martial arts contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: To sharpen (e.g., a knife or sword)

足.note_tr: あし is the standard reading for the body part (leg/foot) in everyday contexts. The た- readings (たりる, たる, たす) express sufficiency, completion, or addition. The onyomi そく appears mainly in compounds like 満足 (satisfaction) and 不足 (shortage).

究.note_tr: The onyomi 'kyū' (きゅう) is found in most common words like 研究 (research) and 究極 (ultimate). The kunyomi 'kiwameru' (きわめる) means to master or investigate something completely, appearing less often for beginners but useful for understanding depth of study or mastery in game and sports contexts.

楽.note_tr: The がく reading appears in music-related compounds (音楽, 楽器); the kunyomi たの.しい and たの.しむ express 'fun' and 'to enjoy'; the らく reading conveys 'comfort' or 'ease' (気楽). Choose your reading based on the semantic context.

起.note_tr: The kanji 起 primarily uses kun'yomi: お.きる (okiru) for "wake up/get up," お.こる (okoru) for "happen," and お.こす (okosu) for "to wake someone" or "cause." The on'yomi き (ki) appears in formal compounds like 起立 (kiritsu, standing up). In anime dialogue, you'll frequently hear 「起きた！」(okita!) meaning "I'm awake!" or "(Someone) woke up!"

examples.meaning_tr: to wake up, to get up

着.note_tr: This kanji has two main kunyomi readings with distinct meanings: き.る = 'to wear' and つ.く = 'to arrive.' The onyomi ちゃく appears in formal compounds like 到着 (arrival). Don't confuse this with 付く (to attach/stick), which uses a different kanji.

店.note_tr: The kunyomi みせ is used for the standalone word meaning 'shop' or 'store'; the onyomi てん appears in compounds like 書店 (bookstore) and 喫茶店 (coffee shop). The second kunyomi たな means 'shelf' and is less common at beginner level.

meanings_tr: To fall ill, to become sick
病.note_tr: On'yomi びょう dominates medical compounds (病気, 病院), while kun'yomi やむ is the verb 'to fall ill.' This kanji appears frequently in anime and manga, especially in character descriptions.

examples.meaning_tr: To fall ill, to become sick

質.note_tr: The on-reading しつ is most common in compound words (質問, 品質, 性質). The reading しち appears in the standalone word 質 (pawn, used in games like Go and Shogi). Kunyomi forms are rarely seen at beginner level. Distinguish 質 (quality/nature of something) from 種 (type/kind, which is about classification).

examples.meaning_tr: pawn (game piece in Go or Shogi)

待.note_tr: Use the kunyomi ま.つ (matsu) for the standalone verb 'to wait' and everyday expressions. The ま.ち variant appears in compound words as a suffix (e.g., 待ち時間, waiting time). The onyomi た.い appears mainly in formal compounds like 期待 (expectation).

試.note_tr: The onyomi し appears in most compounds (試験 exam, 試合 game, 試作 prototype), while the kunyomi ためす appears in the verb 試す (to try/test), and こころみる in 試みる (to attempt). You'll encounter 試験 frequently in school settings and 試合 in sports or tournament scenes in anime and manga.

族.note_tr: 族 uses only the onyomi reading ぞく and appears primarily in compound words as a suffix meaning "group of" or "family of." It rarely stands alone. You'll encounter it frequently in history, anime, and cultural contexts (e.g., 皇族 in historical narratives, 一族 in manga/games).

銀.note_tr: The onyomi reading ぎん is used in nearly all modern compounds like 銀行 (bank) and 銀色 (silver color). The kunyomi しろがね is archaic and rarely appears in modern Japanese except in traditional names or poetry.

examples.meaning_tr: Ginza (famous shopping and entertainment district in Tokyo)

早.note_tr: Use the cunyomi reading (早い, 早起き) in everyday adjectives; use onyomi (そう) in formal compounds like 早朝 (early morning). Distinguish from 速い: while both mean 'fast', 早い emphasizes temporal earliness, while 速い emphasizes speed of action.

映.note_tr: 映 most commonly appears in 映画 (movie). Use うつす for the active action of projecting or reflecting; use うつる for something being reflected or appearing passively.

examples.meaning_tr: To project; to display on screen
To be reflected; to appear on screen
To look attractive; to stand out (in photos)

親.note_tr: Use the kun'yomi (おや) for basic words like '親' (parent), and the on'yomi (しん) for compounds such as '親友' (best friend) and '親切' (kindness). The classical readings した.しい and した.しむ rarely appear in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Oyakodon; rice bowl with chicken and egg (parent-child dish)

験.note_tr: The onyomi reading けん is predominant in common words; the kunyomi (ため.す, ためし) are rarely used in modern Japanese and typically written in hiragana. 試験 (exam) is by far the most frequently encountered compound with this kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: taking an exam, sitting for a test

英.note_tr: The on'yomi えい appears in nearly all modern words; the kun'yomi はなぶさ is archaic. 英雄 (hero) is frequent in anime, manga, and games.

医.note_tr: 医 uses the onyomi reading い in almost all modern compounds (e.g., 医者, 医学). Unlike 薬 (medicine/drug as a substance), 医 refers to medicine as a profession, field of study, or healthcare system.

仕.note_tr: The onyomi し is used in the most common compounds like 仕事 (work, job). The kunyomi つかえる means 'to serve' or 'to work for' and appears in verb forms. This kanji is essential for understanding occupation and service vocabulary in Japanese.

去.note_tr: The onyomi reading きょ appears mainly in time expressions like 去年 (last year); the kunyomi さ.る is the action verb meaning to leave or depart, often appearing in verb compounds like 立ち去る. Distinguish from 昨 (yesterday/last).

examples.meaning_tr: to leave; to depart; to go away
to depart; to leave (a place or person)

味.note_tr: The kunyomi あじ is used for the noun 'taste' or 'flavor,' while あじわう means 'to taste' or 'to savor.' The onyomi み appears in compounds like 趣味 (hobby) and 味噌 (miso).

写.note_tr: Onyomi しゃ (sha) dominates compound words; kunyomi うつす means 'to copy/photograph' (transitive) while うつる means 'to appear in photos' (intransitive). Essential for photography and art vocabulary.

examples.meaning_tr: appearance, how one looks in a photo

字.note_tr: The onyomi じ (ji) is most common in compounds like 漢字 (kanji) and 文字 (letter). The kunyomi あざ (aza) specifically refers to an administrative section or district of a town or village.

答.note_tr: Kun reading こたえ is used for everyday words: 答え (answer, noun) and 答える (to answer, verb). On reading とう appears in formal compounds: 回答 (response) and 答案 (answer sheet).

夜.note_tr: Use the kunyomi よる when 夜 stands alone or at the end of a compound. Use the onyomi や in compounds with other kanji, such as 昨夜 (last night) or 夜景 (night scenery). Don't confuse with 夕 (sunset/dusk).

音.note_tr: Use おと (kun'yomi) for the standalone word "sound." Use おん (on'yomi) in compound words like 音楽 (music) and 音量 (volume). The suffix -のん appears in specialized contexts like 促音便 (sound change in Japanese phonology).

注.note_tr: The onyomi 'chu' typically appears in compound words like 注意 (caution) and 注文 (order), where it conveys the sense of directing or focusing. The kunyomi 'sosogu' is used in the standalone verb 注ぐ, representing the kanji's most literal and physical meaning: to pour. The kanji's semantic core connects all meanings through the concept of channeling or directing a flow, whether of liquid, tears, or attention.

examples.meaning_tr: An order (especially for food or products)

帰.note_tr: The kunyomi かえる (to go home/return) is very common in daily speech and anime/manga. The onyomi き is used in formal compounds like 帰国 (returning to one's country) and 帰宅 (arriving home).

examples.meaning_tr: to come back, to return (to the speaker's location)
the way home, the return path

古.note_tr: The adjective 古い (ふるい) 'old' is most common in everyday speech. In compound words, 古 uses the onyomi reading こ (e.g., 古代 'ancient times', 古風 'old-fashioned').

歌.note_tr: Kunyomi うた is 'song' (noun), and うたう is 'to sing' (verb). Onyomi か appears in compounds like 歌手 (かしゅ, singer) and 歌詞 (かし, lyrics).

買.note_tr: The kunyomi 買う (かう) is used for the main verb 'to buy' and most common compounds. The onyomi ばい appears mainly in formal or business contexts like 買収 (acquisition). This kanji frequently appears in everyday situations related to shopping and commerce.

悪.note_tr: The kun'yomi わるい is the everyday adjective "bad"; the on'yomi あく appears in compound words and formal contexts like 悪魔 (demon) and 悪役 (villain role). For beginners, master わるい first, then gradually learn the on'yomi compounds.

図.note_tr: The on'yomi ず is most common in everyday words (図, 地図). The on'yomi と appears mainly in 図書 (books) and 図書館 (library). The kun'yomi readings (え, はかる) are rarely used in modern Japanese. Distinguish from 絵 (picture), which focuses on artwork.

週.note_tr: 週 always uses the onyomi reading しゅう in common words. It combines with prefixes (先 "last", 来 "next", 毎 "every", 今 "this") to specify which week. The word 週末 (weekend) is especially useful for daily conversation.

室.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 室 is almost always read as しつ (shitsu) when forming compound words for rooms and facilities. The kunyomi むろ (muro) is archaic and rarely used today.

歩.note_tr: The kunyomi reading あるく is the standard form for the verb "to walk" (歩く). The onyomi reading ほ is used in compounds like 散歩 (taking a walk) and 歩道 (sidewalk). The reading あゆむ means "to progress" or "to advance." This kanji also serves as a counter for paces or steps.

風.note_tr: The kunyomi reading かぜ (kaze) refers to physical wind or breeze; it also appears in 風邪 (かぜ) meaning 'cold' (illness). The onyomi reading ふう (fū) typically appears in compound words for style, manner, flavor, or customs, e.g., 和風 (Japanese style), 風味 (flavor).

紙.note_tr: The kunyomi reading (かみ) is used for the standalone word "paper" and most everyday compounds. The onyomi reading (し) appears primarily in formal or technical compounds like 新聞紙 (newspaper) and 色紙 (colored paper sheets). Do not confuse with 神 (kami = god) or 髪 (kami = hair), which are homophones with different kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: colored paper sheets (used in crafts and art)

黒.note_tr: The kunyomi くろ is the most common reading for standalone use and simple compounds. Use くろい for the i-adjective form meaning "is black." The onyomi こく appears in more formal or compound words like 黒板 (blackboard). Distinguish from 茶色 (brown) and 灰色 (gray).

meanings_tr: the finest or best part of something
花.note_tr: The kun'yomi はな is used in everyday speech for "flower" and most common noun forms. The on'yomi か appears frequently in compound words like 造花 (artificial flower) or words borrowed from Chinese. The on'yomi け is rare in modern Japanese. Related nature kanji: 草 (grass), 木 (tree), 葉 (leaf).

examples.meaning_tr: flower language; symbolic meaning of flowers

春.note_tr: The kun'yomi はる is used for the common word 'spring' and most everyday compounds. The on'yomi しゅん appears in literary or formal compounds like 青春 (youthfulness) and 早春 (early spring). Not to be confused with 秋 (autumn).

赤.note_tr: The kun-reading あか is most frequently used in everyday words; the い-adjective form 赤い (is red) is particularly common at beginner level. The on-readings せき and しゃく are rarely encountered in beginner materials.

meanings_tr: Green (especially fresh green, for plants and vegetables)
青.note_tr: Use kunyomi (あお-) for basic colors like 青い and 青空; use onyomi (せい) in youth-related compounds like 青春 and 青年, common in anime. Historically 青 meant both blue and green, but modern Japanese uses 緑 (midori) specifically for green.

館.note_tr: The onyomi 'kan' (かん) appears almost exclusively in compounds like 図書館 (library) and 映画館 (movie theater). The kunyomi 'yagata' (やかた) stands alone, meaning mansion or traditional residence. Best learned through common compounds.

屋.note_tr: The kunyomi や is highly productive and commonly combines with other words to form shop names (e.g., パン屋 = bakery, 花屋 = flower shop). The onyomi おく is less frequent but appears in compounds like 屋上 (rooftop). Distinguish from 家 (いえ), which also means house but emphasizes home and family rather than an establishment or business.

色.note_tr: The kunyomi reading いろ is most common in everyday Japanese and is the standard for this kanji at beginner level. The onyomi readings しょく and しき rarely appear in N4 contexts. The compound 色々 (いろいろ) meaning "various" or "all sorts of" is essential vocabulary and extremely common in daily conversation.

走.note_tr: The kunyomi 走る is extremely common in everyday Japanese and frequently appears in anime and manga (especially action scenes). The onyomi そう primarily appears in compound words like 走者 (runner) and 走行 (running; operation), which are more formal or technical. Beginners should prioritize learning 走る first.

秋.note_tr: The kunyomi reading あき is used for the standalone word and everyday contexts. The onyomi reading しゅう appears in compounds and formal/written Japanese (初秋, 秋分). Use あき when speaking casually about the season; use しゅう-compounds in more formal or poetic contexts.

夏.note_tr: The kunyomi なつ is used for standalone use and most common compounds, while the onyomi か appears in literary or formal compounds like 初夏 (early summer). No common kanji confusion.

習.note_tr: The kunyomi なら.う appears in everyday verbs like 習う (to learn from a teacher). The onyomi しゅう is common in formal compounds like 学習 (study), 習慣 (habit), and 練習 (practice). This kanji emphasizes repetition and becoming familiar with something through repeated action.

examples.meaning_tr: to learn, to be taught (by someone)
practice (especially for music, sports, or skills)
lessons, hobby class (such as piano, calligraphy, or martial arts)

駅.note_tr: 駅 always uses the onyomi reading えき with no kun'yomi alternative. This is one of the most essential kanji for transportation and frequently appears in location names, travel vocabulary, and navigation contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: In front of the station; the area before/near a station
Ekiben; station lunch box (traditional Japanese railway food)

洋.note_tr: 洋 (yō) primarily appears in compound words and contrasts with 和 (Japanese/domestic). It describes Western, foreign, or ocean-related things, making it essential for food (洋食), clothing (洋服), and geography (太平洋) vocabulary.

旅.note_tr: The onyomi 'りょ' commonly appears in compound words like 旅行 (ryokō = travel), while the kunyomi 'たび' is often used in more literary, poetic, or standalone contexts referring to a personal journey or adventure.

服.note_tr: 服 uses only onyomi (ふく) with no kunyomi. Though historically it can mean obey or admit, in modern Japanese it almost exclusively refers to clothing and garments in everyday speech.

examples.meaning_tr: To wear clothes, to get dressed

夕.note_tr: The kunyomi ゆう (yuu) is far more common than the onyomi せき (seki). The kanji 夕 rarely appears alone; it typically combines with other kanji to form words. Distinguish from 夜 (yoru), which refers to the darker, later nighttime.

examples.meaning_tr: sunset, glow of the setting sun

借.note_tr: Use kunyomi (かりる) for the main verb 'to borrow' or 'to rent.' Onyomi (しゃく) typically appears in nouns like 借金 (debt). The opposite action is expressed by 貸す (かす, 'to lend').

曜.note_tr: 曜 uses only the onyomi reading よう and almost always appears in the days-of-the-week compounds (月曜日, 火曜日, etc.). Essential for scheduling, timetables, and daily conversation. No common kun-reading exists.

飲.note_tr: Use the kunyomi のむ (nomu) for everyday actions like drinking beverages or taking medicine; use the onyomi いん/おん readings in formal compound words like 飲酒 (drinking alcohol) or 飲食 (eating and drinking). The 'smoke' meaning is primarily historical.

examples.meaning_tr: eating and drinking, food and beverage

肉.note_tr: The onyomi reading にく is used in nearly all modern common words. The kunyomi しし is archaic and rarely appears in contemporary Japanese.

貸.note_tr: The kunyomi か.す is the primary reading for the verb 'to lend' or 'to rent out' in everyday Japanese. Don't confuse 貸 (to lend) with 借 (to borrow); they express opposite actions. The onyomi たい is less common in beginner vocabulary.

examples.meaning_tr: to lend out; to check out (books, etc.)
rental book shop; manga/book lending library

堂.note_tr: This kanji is read as どう in virtually all compounds (no kunyomi). Be careful not to confuse it visually with 党 (とう, "party/faction"); they look similar but have different meanings and readings.

鳥.note_tr: The kunyomi (とり) is standard for everyday bird references and simple compounds; the onyomi (ちょう) appears primarily in formal or compound words, especially in nature-related contexts. Both readings are equally important at this level.

飯.note_tr: Use onyomi はん in formal contexts like 白飯 (white rice) and with the prefix ご in ご飯 (rice/meal); use kunyomi めし in casual meal references like 朝飯 (breakfast), 昼飯 (lunch), and 夜飯 (dinner). Most frequently encountered as ご飯.

勉.note_tr: The onyomi べん is the primary reading used in N4 vocabulary, especially in the very common word 勉強 (to study). The kunyomi つとめる is rarely encountered at beginner level.

冬.note_tr: The kunyomi ふゆ is used for the standalone word and most everyday compounds; the onyomi とう appears mainly in formal or specialized terms like 冬眠 (hibernation) and 冬至 (winter solstice).

昼.note_tr: The kunyomi ひる is used in everyday/casual compounds like 昼寝 (nap) and 昼間 (daytime), while onyomi ちゅう appears in formal or written contexts such as 昼食 (lunch) and 昼夜 (day and night). This kanji contrasts with 夜 (night).

茶.note_tr: The reading ちゃ (cha) is standard and common in modern Japanese; the reading さ (sa) is rarely used. This kanji refers to both the tea plant's leaves and the brewed drink, and forms the root of 茶色 (cha-iro), the standard Japanese word for brown.

弟.note_tr: The kun'yomi おとうと (younger brother) is the most common everyday usage. The onyomi readings てい, だい, and で appear in compound words like 兄弟 (siblings), 弟子 (disciple/apprentice), and 師弟 (master-student relationship), often expressing hierarchy or service relationships. Common in anime and manga featuring family or training arcs.

examples.meaning_tr: younger siblings; younger brother and sister

牛.note_tr: The onyomi reading ぎゅう is used in most compound words about cattle or beef products (牛乳 milk, 牛肉 beef), while the kunyomi うし is used when referring to a cow as an animal. The character's original pictographic form resembles a cow's head.

魚.note_tr: さかな is the most common everyday reading for fish. The onyomi ぎょ appears in compound words like 金魚 (goldfish), うお is a more formal reading, and -ざかな combines with descriptive prefixes such as 川 (river) or 小 (small).

兄.note_tr: The kunyomi あに is the most common reading in everyday speech and frequently appears in anime/manga. The onyomi けい and きょう are used in formal or compound words (like 兄弟 'siblings'). Easily confused with 弟 (おとうと - younger brother); 兄 always means the older sibling.

examples.meaning_tr: older brother (affectionate or polite form, common in anime)
big bro (casual, informal, common in manga)

犬.note_tr: Use いぬ (kun'yomi) when the word stands alone or combines with native Japanese words; use けん (on'yomi) in compounds with other Sino-Japanese terms. This is one of the most fundamental kanji and appears frequently in manga, anime, and everyday conversation about animals and pets.

妹.note_tr: Use the kunyomi いもうと for everyday speech about your younger sister; the onyomi まい appears mainly in compounds like 義妹 (stepsister). Do not confuse with 姉 (あね, older sister).

examples.meaning_tr: Younger sister (polite form, used when referring to others' sisters)
Younger sister character type (popular in anime and manga)

姉.note_tr: The kunyomi reading あね is used for "older sister" (especially as ねえさん in anime and casual speech). The onyomi し appears in compounds like 姉妹 (sisters). Distinguish from 妹 (younger sister).

examples.meaning_tr: older siblings; older brother and sister

漢.note_tr: Always read as かん (on'yomi). Commonly appears in words about Chinese language, culture, and medicine, with 漢字 being especially important for Japanese learners.

政.note_tr: The onyomi reading せい dominates in modern Japanese, appearing in virtually all common political and governmental vocabulary. The kunyomi readings (まつりごと, まん) are archaic and rarely encountered in contemporary usage. This kanji is a fundamental component of political/historical discourse.

議.note_tr: This kanji uses only the on'yomi reading ぎ and appears primarily in formal compounds. It is commonly found in political and governmental contexts, particularly in words related to parliaments, meetings, and formal discussions.

民.note_tr: The onyomi reading みん dominates in modern Japanese compounds; the kunyomi たみ is rarely used. Distinguish from 人 (person): 民 refers to people as a collective or nation, while 人 refers to individual persons.

連.note_tr: Use つれる as a verb meaning "to take someone along" or "to lead." Use れん in compound words for meanings like "connect" or "consecutive." In anime, 連れて行って (take me with you) is a common phrase.

examples.meaning_tr: a series of; a sequence of

対.note_tr: The on'yomi たい is the primary reading in modern Japanese, found in compounds like 対戦 (match), 対応 (response), and 対立 (conflict). The kunyomi are rarely used in contemporary contexts, so prioritize the on'yomi reading.

examples.meaning_tr: To respond; to correspond; to deal with

部.note_tr: The onyomi reading ぶ is the most common, especially in compound words like 全部 (all) and 部長 (department head). The kunyomi へ/べ appears mainly in 部屋 (room), one of the most frequent words with this kanji. Students often mix up へ and ベ readings, remember 部屋 uses へ (from the old word へや).

合.note_tr: Onyomi (ごう, がっ) is used in formal words like 合計 (total) and 合格 (pass); kunyomi (あ.う, あ.わせる) is used in everyday verbs like 合う (to fit). Note: 会 and 合 both can mean "to meet," but 会 refers to people gathering while 合 refers to things fitting or combining together.

examples.meaning_tr: To fit; to suit; to match
To combine; to match; to adjust
To get along with; to be compatible

市.note_tr: 市 primarily reads as し (shi) in compounds (都市 city, 市民 citizen), while the kunyomi いち (ichi) appears mainly in 市場 (ichiba - marketplace). The kanji often refers to an urban administrative area in modern Japanese.

内.note_tr: Use うち when referring to 'home' or 'inside' directly in spoken contexts; use ない in formal compound words like 内容 and 内部. Do not confuse with 中 (なか), which also means 'inside' but appears in different compound patterns and contexts.

相.note_tr: The kunyomi あい is most common in 相手 and other あい- compounds. The onyomi そう appears in formal words like 相談, while しょう is mainly used in words like 相性 and 首相.

定.note_tr: The onyomi てい dominates in compound words (定価, 定義, 限定). The kunyomi さだめる is transitive ("to set/decide"), while さだまる is intransitive ("to be settled"); the reading さだか is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese. For beginners: learn てい in nouns first, then kunyomi verbs.

examples.meaning_tr: To determine; to decide; to establish
To be determined; to be settled; to come to a decision

回.note_tr: かい is primarily used as a counter suffix (e.g., 3回 = 3 times), while the kunyomi まわ.る is the verb form meaning 'to turn/revolve.' In compound words like 回転 (kaiten), the onyomi かい appears in the beginning.

examples.meaning_tr: to turn; to revolve; to go around
to turn (something); to rotate; to pass around

選.note_tr: The kunyomi えら.ぶ is used in everyday speech for "to choose/select", while the onyomi せん appears in formal compounds like 選手 (athlete) and 選挙 (election). Commonly seen in anime and gaming contexts for character or option selection.

examples.meaning_tr: selection; chosen group (often used in sports or music)

米.note_tr: The kun'yomi reading こめ is used for the standalone word and simple compounds. The on'yomi reading まい appears in rice variety names (白米 white rice, 玄米 brown rice), while べい is used for America-related terms (米国 USA).

実.note_tr: The on'yomi じつ is most common in compounds like 実行 and 実験. The kunyomi み typically refers to fruit or ripening (as in みのる, to bear fruit). Do not confuse 実 (actual) with 質 (quality), which is a different kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: actually, in fact, the truth is
actual ability, true strength, real skill
to bear fruit, to ripen, to yield results

関.note_tr: Onyomi かん is most common in compound words (関係, 関心, 関連). Kunyomi かか.わる appears in the verb 関わる meaning 'to relate to or be involved with', while せき refers to gates or barriers in historical contexts (関所).

examples.meaning_tr: To be involved with, to relate to

決.note_tr: The kun'yomi 決める (kiru) means "to decide actively," while 決まる (kimaru) is its passive/intransitive counterpart meaning "to be decided or settled." The on'yomi けつ (ketsu) appears frequently in compound words like 決定 (decision) and 決勝 (final match).

examples.meaning_tr: to decide, to make a decision
to be decided, to be settled, to be determined
final match, finals (in sports or competition)

全.note_tr: The onyomi ぜん appears most frequently in modern compounds (全部, 全員, 全力). The kunyomi forms すべて and まったく occur in more formal or emphatic contexts respectively. Distinguish from 総 (sou), which also means 'total' but emphasizes aggregation or sums.

examples.meaning_tr: Full strength, all one's power, best effort

表.note_tr: Use おもて when referring to a physical surface or the front/outside of something. In compound nouns, the onyomi ひょう is typically used (例: 表紙 = book cover, 表情 = facial expression). The verb forms 表す (to express/show) and 表れる (to appear/be revealed) employ the arawasu/arawareru kunyomi readings.

戦.note_tr: The on-reading せん typically appears in formal compounds like 戦争 'war', 戦士 'warrior', and 戦場 'battlefield'. The kun-reading たたかう 'to fight' is used as a verb and is very common in anime, manga, and everyday speech; the less common kun-reading いくさ is archaic and rarely encountered in modern Japanese.

meanings_tr: experience; practical knowledge gained through doing something
management; administration; operation (of a business or organization)
longitude; distance measured along a line
経.note_tr: The on'yomi reading けい is overwhelmingly common in modern Japanese, appearing in almost all contemporary usage such as 経験 (experience), 経済 (economy), and 経営 (management). The reading きょう is reserved for classical and religious contexts, typically appearing in compounds like 経文 (Buddhist scripture). Note: Don't confuse this with 径 (径), which also means path or diameter but is a completely different kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: management; operation; running (a business, organization, or project)
passage of time; progress; lapse; the course of events
via; by way of; through (indicating a path or route)

最.note_tr: The onyomi さい is common in compounds (最高, 最新, 最近); the kunyomi もっとも is less common. This kanji forms essential superlatives and appears frequently in storytelling and casual speech.

現.note_tr: On-yomi げん appears in most compound words (現在, 現実, 現代), while kun-yomi forms like 現れる and 現す function as verbs. Use あらわれる when something appears naturally or comes into view; use あらわす when deliberately expressing, revealing, or indicating something."

examples.meaning_tr: Reality, the real world, actual fact
To appear, to show up, to come into view
Modern era, present-day period, contemporary times
To show, to express, to reveal, to indicate

調.note_tr: The kunyomi しら.べる means "to investigate or examine," while the onyomi ちょう appears in most compounds (especially in music, cooking, and formal nouns). The less common readings ととの.う and ととの.える mean "to be in harmony" or "to adjust."

examples.meaning_tr: to investigate, to examine, to check, to look up
condition, mood, tone, feeling; how someone is doing

化.note_tr: The native reading ば.ける emphasizes taking on a different form or transformation, especially common in anime/manga for magical or supernatural changes. The Sino-Japanese reading か is used in many compound words (化学, 進化, 文化).

examples.meaning_tr: to transform, to change shape, to assume a different form

当.note_tr: Onyomi (とう) appears in compounds like 本当 (truly) and 当番 (one's turn); kunyomi (あたる, あてる) express action meanings like 'to hit' or 'to guess.' The core meaning is hitting a target, extending to 'right' or 'true.'

examples.meaning_tr: To hit, to be correct, to win
To win, to be selected (in a lottery or election)

約.note_tr: The onyomi 'やく' is overwhelmingly common in everyday words like 約束 and 予約. The kunyomi forms (つづ.まる, つづ.める, つづま.やか) are rare in modern Japanese and appear mainly in formal or classical texts. No major lookalike kanji for beginners.

首.note_tr: The kunyomi reading くび is used for the physical neck body part and everyday compounds. The onyomi reading しゅ appears in formal and official terms, especially those meaning 'leader' or 'chief'. Distinguish 首 (neck) from 頭 (atama/head), where 首 refers specifically to the neck portion.

法.note_tr: The ほう reading dominates modern Japanese compounds. The kunyomi のり is archaic and appears mainly in classical or formal texts. Context matters: 魔法 (magic) is essential for anime/manga fans, while 法律 and related terms are critical for legal or formal discussions.

examples.meaning_tr: Legal; lawful; in accordance with law

性.note_tr: The reading 'sei' (せい) dominates modern Japanese and appears in nearly all common compounds. The 'shō' (しょう) and 'saga' (さが) readings are rare and literary. Note: 性 (sex/nature) should not be confused with 姓 (surname, family name), which also uses 'sei' but refers to family names.

examples.meaning_tr: Opposite sex; Person of opposite gender
Same sex; Person of same gender

要.note_tr: The onyomi よう dominates in modern Japanese; the kunyomi is rarely used. 要 most frequently appears in words expressing importance (重要) and necessity (必要). When you see this kanji in compounds, it typically signals something central, critical, or required.

制.note_tr: 制 appears primarily in compound words using the onyomi reading せい, and rarely stands alone. It frequently describes systems, laws, rules, or control mechanisms. Note that 規制 (regulation) and 制限 (restriction) share the general sense of "control" but distinguish by usage: 規制 emphasizes formal rules or restrictions, while 制限 emphasizes a quantitative limit or boundary.

examples.meaning_tr: uniform (especially school uniform; very common in anime)
production; creation; making (used for anime, music, art)

meanings_tr: To calm down, to settle, to be at peace
To govern, to rule, to reign
治.note_tr: Kun-readings なお.す/なお.る (to heal) are most common in everyday speech. The reading おさ.まる (to calm down, settle) appears frequently in narratives and dialogue. On-readings (じ/ち) are mainly used in compounds: じ in political/governance words like 政治 (politics), ち in medical terms like 治療 (treatment).

examples.meaning_tr: to calm down, to settle down

務.note_tr: The onyomi (む) primarily appears in compound nouns like 義務 (obligation) and 職務 (duties), while the kunyomi (つとめる) forms the verb meaning "to work at" or "to serve in a position." Both readings are essential for N3 mastery.

examples.meaning_tr: to work at, to serve in a position, to be employed
work, employment, to be on duty

成.note_tr: Onyomi readings (せい, じょう) typically appear in compounds like 成功 (success) and 成長 (growth). Kunyomi なる expresses 'to become' and is fundamental for describing transformation. Easily confused with 生 (life, to be born) which shares the reading せい but refers to birth and living things.

期.note_tr: 期 primarily uses the き reading in everyday words; ご is rare. Common in academic and work contexts for terms and deadlines: 学期 (school term), 期限 (deadline), 期末 (term end).

取.note_tr: The kun'yomi reading と.る is by far the most common in everyday speech and compounds. The on'yomi しゅ appears mainly in formal or technical terms (e.g., 取材 "gathering information"). Avoid confusion with 撮 (photograph) and 採 (select/pick), which use different readings despite surface similarity.

examples.meaning_tr: To tackle; to grapple with (common in sports and games)
The way or method of doing something
Gathering information or footage; interviewing; coverage
To take back; to recover; to reclaim

都.note_tr: The onyomi と is standard in modern Japanese and appears in common compounds like 都会 and 都市. The kunyomi みやこ is classical and rarely used in contemporary writing; the onyomi つ is also uncommon.

和.note_tr: Use onyomi わ in most common nouns and compounds like 和食 (Japanese food) and 平和 (peace); use kunyomi forms (やわらぐ, なごやか) for describing gentle qualities or the action of softening. The "Japanese" meaning comes from 和 historically meaning Japan.

機.note_tr: This kanji primarily uses the on'yomi reading き in modern Japanese compounds. The kun'yomi はた refers to the original meaning 'loom' but is rarely used today.

平.note_tr: On'yomi へい is standard in modern compounds like 平気, 平日, 平均. The kun'yomi forms (たいら, ひら) are archaic or literary. In conversation, 平気 (へいき) idiomatically means 'I'm fine / okay' regardless of the base meanings.

examples.meaning_tr: Heian period (historical era); peace and tranquility

加.note_tr: The onyomi か appears in most compounds (参加, 追加, 加工) and emphasizes the result or status of adding or joining. The kunyomi くわえる and くわわる appear as verbs and emphasize the action itself. Similar kanji to watch: 足 (foot; add to) and 増 (increase; grow).

examples.meaning_tr: to add; additional (very common in games, manga for bonus content)
to process; processing (food or tech contexts)
