受.note_tr: Use kunyomi う.ける for active verbs meaning "to receive" or "to undergo"; the onyomi じゅ appears in formal nouns and academic contexts like 受験 (exam). The same reading can convey receiving benefits or enduring hardship, context determines the interpretation.

examples.meaning_tr: To receive, to undergo, to take (a class), to suffer
Exam, entrance exam, taking an exam
To receive, to accept, to take receipt of

続.note_tr: The kunyomi 続く and 続ける are the most common in everyday speech meaning "to continue" or "to keep doing." The onyomi ぞく appears mainly in compound words like 続編 (sequel) and 連続 (series), with 続き especially popular in anime and manga communities for sequels or next installments.

進.note_tr: The kunyomi has two forms: すす.む (intransitive, something advances on its own) and すす.める (transitive, you advance or promote something). The onyomi しん appears in many academic compounds like 進化 (evolution) and 進路 (course/path), which are common in anime, games, and school contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: to advance, to progress, to move forward
to advance, to promote, to push forward
course, direction, path (of study or career)

数.note_tr: The onyomi すう (su) is used in most compounds like 数学 and 数字. The kunyomi かず (kazu) appears in simpler verbs like 数える (to count). Context determines which meaning applies, numerical contexts use "number," while classical or Buddhist texts may reference fate or destiny.

記.note_tr: 記 almost always appears in compounds using the onyomi reading き; the kunyomi しる.す is rare in modern Japanese. Key compounds like 記者 (journalist), 記録 (record), and 記事 (article) are very common in everyday text and media.

初.note_tr: The onyomi しょ is commonly used in formal compounds like 初心者 (beginner) and 最初 (first); the kunyomi はじめて is the most natural everyday phrase meaning 'for the first time'. Related to 始 (to begin) but with a focus on timing rather than action.

指.note_tr: Use ゆび when referring to fingers as body parts. Use the onyomi し in compounds like 指示 (instruction), and さす for the action of pointing or selecting something.

権.note_tr: The reading けん is by far the most common in modern Japanese, especially in compound words denoting types of rights or authority (権利, 人権). The ごん reading appears rarely, mainly in historical or religious contexts (権現). The kunyomi readings are almost never used in contemporary usage.

支.note_tr: The character 支 primarily uses onyomi し in compounds (支店 branch store, 支援 support), while the kunyomi ささえる appears in 支える (to hold up or support something physically). The concept extends to both concrete and abstract contexts.

産.note_tr: The on'yomi さん is used in compound words related to production, industry, and origins (産業 "industry", 生産 "production", 産地 "origin"). The kun'yomi う.む and う.まれる refer specifically to biological reproduction and childbirth contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Domestic product, made in one's own country

点.note_tr: The onyomi てん is the standard reading in modern Japanese and appears in nearly all compound words; the listed kunyomi are archaic or extremely rare in contemporary usage. Beginners should focus on compounds with てん, especially in contexts like scores in games/tests (点数), viewpoints in anime analysis (視点), and character weaknesses (弱点).

報.note_tr: The onyomi ほう dominates in common compounds like 報告 (report) and 情報 (information), while the kunyomi むく.いる appears in more formal or literary contexts meaning 'to reward' or 'to repay.' In anime and manga, watch for 報復 (retaliation) and 報道 (news reporting), which appear frequently in narratives.

meanings_tr: Finish, complete, come to an end
済.note_tr: The kunyomi す.む is the most common reading for learners, appearing prominently in 済みません (excuse me/sorry). Note that 済む describes when something is finished (intransitive), while 済ます means to finish something actively (transitive).

examples.meaning_tr: Excuse me, I'm sorry, pardon me
To finish, to be completed, to be over
To finish, to complete, to get through

meanings_tr: to utilize; to make use of
活.note_tr: The onyomi かつ primarily appears in Sino-Japanese compound words like 活動 (activity) and 活躍 (to flourish). The kunyomi い.きる means 'to live' and い.かす means 'to utilize' or 'to bring to life'; both essential for everyday Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to play an active role; to flourish; to be active
to utilize; to make use of; to put to good use
to live; to be alive; (of food) to be fresh

原.note_tr: The onyomi げん appears almost exclusively in compound words (原因, 原作, 原料) and is far more common in modern Japanese. The kunyomi はら is rare today but appears in place names and classical/poetic contexts. In anime/manga, 原作 (original work) is especially useful to know.

共.note_tr: The onyomi きょう is used in most compound words like 共通 (common) and 共和国 (republic). The kunyomi とも appears in the adverb 共に (together). The suffix -ども creates collective or plural forms (e.g., 私ども, we in humble speech).

得.note_tr: Use the onyomi とく in most compound words like 得意 (good at) and 得点 (score). The kunyomi える appears in the basic verb 得る (to obtain).

examples.meaning_tr: to obtain, to gain, to get
good at, one's specialty, strong point
not good at, weak point, poor at

解.note_tr: The on'yomi かい appears in compound words like 理解 (understanding) and 解説 (explanation). The kun'yomi verb form と.く means 'to solve' or 'to untie,' with と.ける as the intransitive form 'to be solved/to come untied.' Don't confuse 解く (to solve) with 開く (to open).

examples.meaning_tr: to come untied, to thaw, to melt
to undo one's hair, to let one's hair down

交.note_tr: The onyomi こう appears in most Sino-Japanese compounds like 交差点 (intersection) and 交通 (traffic). The kunyomi forms like 交わる emphasize the physical action of things mixing or crossing together.

examples.meaning_tr: To cross, to intersect, to mingle together
To mix in, to add by mixing, to blend

資.note_tr: 資 is read as し in all compounds and primarily appears in business, academic, and formal contexts. Distinguish it from 財 (wealth/money) and 材 (material/lumber).

予.note_tr: The onyomi よ appears in most everyday compounds carrying the sense of "in advance" or "pre-" (予定, 予約, 予報, 予算). The kunyomi あらかじめ is a standalone adverb meaning "beforehand," and in modern Japanese it's very commonly written in hiragana only rather than with the kanji. The onyomi しゃ is extremely rare and does not appear in any common everyday vocabulary, so no example is given for it.

examples.meaning_tr: Reservation, booking (e.g., booking a restaurant table or hotel room)
Forecast, as in 天気予報 (weather forecast)
Beforehand, in advance (often written in hiragana)

向.note_tr: This kanji expresses direction and orientation. In everyday speech, the kunyomi むかう (heading toward) and むこう (over there) dominate; the onyomi こう appears mainly in formal compounds like 向上 (improvement). The prefix 前向き (positive/forward-looking) is particularly common in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to head toward, to go in the direction of
over there, the other side, yonder
to turn toward, to direct, to point

際.note_tr: Use おんよみ さい in formal Sino-Japanese compound nouns like 国際 and 実際; use くんよみ きわ (often voiced ぎわ as a suffix) in native words about edges, sides, or timing, like 窓際 and 際立つ. Don't mix up 際 with the similar-looking 祭 (festival); 際 has the こざとへん (阝) radical on the left, while 祭 does not.

examples.meaning_tr: at this point, on this occasion

勝.note_tr: The verb 勝つ (to win) is very common in casual speech, anime, and games. In formal contexts or sports results, you'll see 勝利 (victory) or 優勝 (championship). The reading changes between verb forms (かつ) and compound forms (しょう).

面.note_tr: The on-reading めん dominates in compounds (画面, 仮面), while the kun-reading おも appears in the common adjective 面白い (interesting). All meanings, face, surface, mask, aspect, relate to the core idea of 'face' or 'appearance'.

告.note_tr: The kun'yomi form つ.げる (tsugeru) is used for direct communication like 'telling' someone something, while on'yomi こく (koku) primarily appears in compounds such as 告白 (confession) and 告知 (announcement). This kanji conveys a sense of making information known or revealing something.

反.note_tr: The on-yomi はん is most common in compound words. The kun-readings そ.る ("to bend/curve"), かえ.す, and かえ.る ("to return/change") appear in native Japanese words. The kanji fundamentally expresses opposition or reversal, useful in anime/manga for words like 反抗 (rebellion) and in technology/science contexts like 反射 (reflection/reflex).

判.note_tr: The on'yomi はん is used in most compounds related to judgement and decision-making (判断, 判定, 裁判). The kunyomi わか.る reflects the fundamental sense of 'to distinguish' or 'to understand', though it appears less frequently in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Stamp or seal (especially a personal seal used in Japan)

認.note_tr: The onyomi にん is standard in compounds like 認識 and 承認, while みとめる (kunyomi) forms the verb "to recognize" or "to acknowledge." The kanji conveys both understanding (recognition) and acceptance (approval).

examples.meaning_tr: To recognize; to acknowledge; to admit

meanings_tr: To go; to come (humble or casual)
参.note_tr: The onyomi さん (san) primarily appears in formal compound words like 参加 (participation) and 参考 (reference). The kunyomi まいる (mairu) expresses movement (to go/come) in humble or casual speech, and in modern usage often means 'to be exhausted' or 'to be overwhelmed.' Frequently appears in anime, manga, and casual conversation.

examples.meaning_tr: Participation; to join or take part
To go; to be beaten; to be exhausted
To worship (at a shrine or temple)
To enter a battle or competition; to join the fray

利.note_tr: The on'yomi り is used in most compounds (利用, 権利, 利益). The kun'yomi き.く appears in 利く, meaning 'to work well' or 'to be effective.' Distinguishable from 力 (strength/power) by its meaning of advantage or utility rather than raw power.

examples.meaning_tr: To work well, to be effective

meanings_tr: to assemble, to construct, to put together
組.note_tr: The kunyomi (くむ, くみ) forms express the verb "to assemble" or the noun "group/class," commonly seen in anime/manga school settings (e.g., 〇年〇組 = Grade 〇, Class 〇). The onyomi (そ) appears mainly in Sino-Japanese compounds like 組織 (organization). The verb 組む can also mean "to fold" (as in arms) or "to braid," depending on context.

examples.meaning_tr: to assemble, to put together, to fold (arms), to braid
to assemble, to construct, to build up
Group 1, Class 1 (common in schools and anime)

信.note_tr: The on'yomi しん (shin) dominates in everyday vocabulary. 信 conveys reliability and credibility in contexts ranging from personal trust to technical systems. Do not confuse with 伸 (shin: to extend/stretch), which sounds identical but has a different meaning.

在.note_tr: The onyomi ざい is used in most compounds (存在, 滞在, 在宅). The kunyomi あ.る is literary and rarely appears in modern usage; いる is used instead for living beings.

examples.meaning_tr: being enrolled in school; student status

件.note_tr: The onyomi けん dominates modern usage, appearing in compounds and as a counter for cases or items. The kunyomi くだん is archaic, appearing in literary contexts with the meaning 'the aforementioned.'

examples.meaning_tr: Number of cases, number of items

側.note_tr: Use がわ for directional sides (右側 - right side). Use そば for 'by/near' in phrases like 側に (by one's side). Onyomi そく appears in compound words like 側面 (aspect) and 両側 (both sides).

任.note_tr: The onyomi (にん) typically appears in duty/responsibility compounds like 任務 (mission) and 責任 (responsibility). The kunyomi (まかせる) is used as a verb meaning "to entrust" or "to leave to someone."

examples.meaning_tr: To entrust; to leave something to someone

引.note_tr: The kunyomi ひ.く is the primary everyday reading for basic "pulling" actions (引く, 引き込む, 引っ張る). In compound words, the noun form 引き (ひき) often appears, as in 引き分け (draw/tie in games). The onyomi いん is less common but surfaces in certain phrases. Distinguish from 抜く (ぬく - "pull out/extract") which refers to removing something completely.

examples.meaning_tr: a draw; a tie (in games, matches, or sports)
to pull in; to draw into; to involve
to draw a bow (archery; common in games and anime)
to turn back; to return; to retrace one's steps

求.note_tr: The kunyomi もとめる is used in everyday speech to mean seeking, requesting, or wanting something. The onyomi きゅう appears mainly in compound words like 要求 (demand) and 求人 (job opening).

examples.meaning_tr: to seek; to request; to want

所.note_tr: Use the kunyomi ところ when 所 stands alone meaning "place" (e.g. この所). The onyomi しょ appears in compound words borrowed with Chinese-style readings (e.g. 場所, 住所). The reading どころ/とこ shows up in casual speech or as a suffix attached to another word (e.g. 見どころ, ここんとこ). Don't confuse 所 with 場 (ば/じょう), which also means "place" but is used in different compounds like 会場, 市場.

次.note_tr: The kunyomi つぎ is the most common reading for "next" in everyday conversation (e.g., 次の日 "next day"). The onyomi じ is used in formal compounds like 次回 (じかい) "next time/episode," which is very common in anime and manga contexts. The kunyomi つぐ means "to succeed" or "to follow" in verb forms.

昨.note_tr: The kanji uses onyomi さく in time compounds (like 昨年 for last year and 昨晩 for last night), but the everyday word 昨日 (yesterday) uses the reading きのう.

論.note_tr: 論 is read exclusively as ろん (on'yomi) and appears primarily in formal, academic, and philosophical contexts. It does not have a standard kunyomi. The kanji rarely stands alone and is almost always used in compounds.

官.note_tr: This kanji uses only the onyomi reading かん and primarily appears in formal government and bureaucratic contexts. Look for it in compounds describing government positions, agencies, or officials.

増.note_tr: Intransitive 増える (ふえる) describes a natural increase; transitive 増やす (ふやす) means to actively increase something. Compound 増加 (ぞうか) appears frequently in formal contexts.

meanings_tr: Staff member, attendant, person in charge
To be involved, to concern oneself
係.note_tr: The kunyomi かかわる (to be involved) and かかる (to take/cost) appear in verbs; the onyomi けい appears mainly in compounds like 係員 (staff member) and 関係 (relationship). Focus on かかわる as a core verb for beginners.

examples.meaning_tr: Staff member, counter attendant, person in charge of a counter
To be involved (in), to be concerned (with), to relate to

感.note_tr: 感 uses only the on'yomi かん; there is no kun'yomi. It appears primarily in compound words and rarely stands alone. You'll encounter it frequently in anime, manga, and music contexts when expressing emotions or personal reactions.

examples.meaning_tr: To be moved, to be impressed

情.note_tr: The onyomi じょう dominates modern Japanese, appearing in frequent compounds like 感情 (emotion) and 情報 (information). The kunyomi なさ.け mainly appears in 情け (kindness/mercy). The onyomi せい is archaic in contemporary use. Note: 情 focuses specifically on emotion/feeling/sentiment, whereas 心 (heart/mind) covers broader mental states.

投.note_tr: The kunyomi なげる is used for the simple verb "to throw" in everyday contexts. The onyomi とう combines with other kanji in formal words like 投票 (voting) and 投資 (investment), commonly seen in sports, business, and modern Japanese.

示.note_tr: Kunyomi (しめす) forms the basic verb 示す (to show). Onyomi (じ/し) appear in compounds like 表示 (display) and 指示 (instruction). Avoid confusion with 指 (finger).

変.note_tr: The onyomi へん appears in compounds and adjectives like 変な (strange), while the kunyomi か.わる and か.える form verbs meaning to change. The word 変身 (transformation) is especially common in anime and manga.

打.note_tr: The reading う.つ (utsu) is used for the verb meaning 'to hit or strike,' while だ (da) appears in many compound words and nouns. This kanji differs from 撃 (shoot) or 討 (defeat) despite surface similarity in meaning.

examples.meaning_tr: to drive in, to hammer, to pour one's efforts into

直.note_tr: The on'yomi reading ちょく is most common in compound words and means 'straight/direct'. The kunyomi reading なお.す is used as a verb meaning 'to fix or correct'. The reading す.ぐ means 'immediately' or 'soon'. The じき reading emphasizes immediacy. Different readings carry distinct nuances, so context determines which applies.

examples.meaning_tr: Intuition, instinct (a frequent concept in anime and manga)
To fix, correct, repair (can be used for objects, mistakes, or behavior)
Immediately, right away, soon (very common in daily conversation)
Honest, frank, sincere (often used to describe character traits in anime)
Straight line (used in art, geometry, and technical contexts)

meanings_tr: Counter for vehicles or carriages (e.g., train cars)
両.note_tr: The onyomi りょう is used in nearly all common modern words; the kunyomi forms are rare in contemporary Japanese. This kanji typically appears in compound words expressing "both" of something, making it essential for everyday expressions.

式.note_tr: Reading しき appears almost exclusively in compounds. Meaning depends on context: 'ceremony' for rituals (儀式, 結婚式), 'style' for types (和式, 洋式), or 'formula' in mathematics (数式).

確.note_tr: The onyomi かく is used in formal compounds (確認 = confirmation). The kunyomi たしか is an everyday adverb meaning 'certain' or 'sure.' The こう reading is rare in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Certain, sure (adverb, used to express confidence)
To confirm, to verify, to check

果.note_tr: The on'yomi か appears in most compound words like 結果 (result) and 効果 (effect), common in everyday and academic contexts. The kun'yomi は.たす and は.てる are verb forms: は.たす means 'to carry out' or 'fulfill' (often in achievement contexts), while は.てる means 'to end' or 'be exhausted' (more literary).

examples.meaning_tr: to end, to come to an end

容.note_tr: The onyomi よう appears in almost all common compound words (内容, 容器, 美容). The kunyomi reading い.れる (容れる, "to accept/contain") is rare and mostly literary; in everyday writing, "to put in" is almost always written with 入れる instead, so don't mix the two up.

examples.meaning_tr: content, substance (e.g. the content of a story or anime episode)
container, vessel (e.g. a food storage container)
capacity, volume (e.g. phone storage or battery capacity)

必.note_tr: Onyomi (ひつ) appears in compound words like 必要 (necessity) and 必死 (desperate effort). Kunyomi (かなら.ず) stands alone as an adverb meaning 'definitely/certainly.' Use 必ずしも for 'not necessarily', a common negation pattern in everyday speech.

examples.meaning_tr: Desperate, all-out effort, with all one's might

演.note_tr: 演 uses only the onyomi reading えん. It appears frequently in entertainment contexts (anime, manga, theater) and in demonstration contexts. Not to be confused with 演る, which is a rare verb; use 演じる (to play a role) or 演ずる instead.

examples.meaning_tr: Acting, performance (especially in film or theater)
Musical performance, to play an instrument
Direction, production (of a film or play)

meanings_tr: Year (as a counter for age or years)
歳.note_tr: The reading さい is by far the most common in modern Japanese, especially for counting age (何歳 = "how old?"). Other readings (とし, よわい, せい) appear mainly in literary or archaic contexts; focus on mastering さい as a beginner.

examples.meaning_tr: Passage of time; years and months

争.note_tr: Use kunyomi 争う (あらそう) as a standalone verb meaning "to compete" or "to argue"; onyomi そう appears in compounds like 戦争 (war) and 競争 (competition). The nuance: 争う emphasizes conflict or serious rivalry, while 競う (from 競) emphasizes friendly racing or competition.

examples.meaning_tr: to compete, to argue, to dispute

談.note_tr: The kanji 談 uses the on'yomi reading だん and typically appears in compound words within formal or semi-formal contexts, anime, and news. For casual conversations, simpler words like 話す (hanasu) are more commonly used.

examples.meaning_tr: Consultation; to consult or ask for advice
Small talk; casual conversation or chat
Official meeting or conference between leaders

能.note_tr: 能 has two main readings: のう (on'yomi) appears in compound words like 能力 and 可能; よく (kun'yomi) means "well" or "skillfully" in formal/literary contexts. Don't confuse 能 (ability) with 脳 (brain); they sound similar but have different kanji and meanings.

位.note_tr: The onyomi い is used in compounds like 位置 (location) and 順位 (ranking). The kunyomi くらい/ぐらい means "about, approximately" and is mainly used as a suffix in phrases like 十人くらい (about 10 people).

置.note_tr: The kunyomi おく (oku) is used for the verb 置く 'to place' or 'to put down.' The onyomi ち (chi) typically appears in compound words such as 位置 (position), 配置 (arrangement), and 放置 (neglect).

examples.meaning_tr: To place, to put down, to leave
To leave as is, to neglect, to abandon

流.note_tr: Kunyomi (ながれ-, なが.す) appears in everyday words meaning 'flow' or 'current'; onyomi (りゅう) is used in formal compounds like 流行 (trend). Both derive from the core concept of something moving or spreading.

examples.meaning_tr: To drain; to flow away; to let go

格.note_tr: The reading かく is primary and appears in most common words (人格 personality, 資格 qualification, 格差 gap). The reading こう appears in 格好 (appearance/style), notably in the popular phrase 格好いい ('cool' or 'stylish'), which is very common in anime and casual speech.

疑.note_tr: Use onyomi ぎ in compounds like 疑問 (question) and 疑惑 (suspicion); use kunyomi うたが.う for the verb 'to doubt.' Don't confuse with 怪, which means strange or eerie rather than doubtful.

meanings_tr: To exceed; to surpass; to go beyond
過.note_tr: The reading すぎる (sugiru) is extremely common in anime and casual speech, meaning 'too much' or 'to go too far', often heard as a character reaction. Different readings create different meanings: 過去 (かこ) uses the onyomi for 'the past' (essential for history and storytelling), while 過ごす (sugosu) means 'to spend time.'

examples.meaning_tr: To exceed; to go too far; to be excessive
To spend (time); to pass (time); to live through

局.note_tr: The onyomi きょく is far more common in modern Japanese, used in compounds for offices and stations. The kunyomi つぼね is archaic, referring to palace apartments in classical texts and is rarely encountered in beginner materials.

放.note_tr: Most compounds use the onyomi ほう (放送, 放課後); verb forms use kunyomi (放す, 放つ). The core meaning centers on releasing, spreading, or transmitting, ranging from physical action to media transmission.

examples.meaning_tr: To shoot; to fire; to emit

常.note_tr: The on'yomi じょう appears in most modern compounds (日常, 常識, 非常). The kun'yomi つね is rarely used in everyday Japanese. Useful to pair with 異常 (abnormal) and 非常 (emergency) to understand opposite/related concepts.

examples.meaning_tr: Everyday life, daily routine; the mundane activities shown in slice-of-life anime
Always, constantly, all the time (basic adverb for describing ongoing actions)
Common sense, general knowledge (important social concept in Japanese culture)
Emergency, extraordinary, unusual (used in emergency announcements and opposite of 常)
Room temperature (commonly seen on food and beverage labels)
Abnormality, anomaly, abnormal (opposite concept; じょう reading shows up in antonyms)

状.note_tr: 状 is primarily used with the onyomi reading じょう and most commonly appears in compound words. It describes the external state or conditions of a situation, person, or thing.

球.note_tr: The onyomi きゅう is used in very common compounds like 野球 (baseball) and 地球 (Earth). The kunyomi たま is also used for the standalone word 球, though less frequently in beginner vocabulary.

職.note_tr: 職 (しょく) is typically used in compounds related to jobs and professions, most commonly in the on'yomi reading しょく. In anime and manga, you'll frequently encounter 職業 (occupation) when characters discuss their professions or work.

与.note_tr: The kunyomi 与える is by far the most common reading in everyday Japanese, meaning 'to give' or 'to grant.' The onyomi よ appears in formal compounds such as 与党 (ruling party) and 関与 (involvement). Other kunyomi readings are rare in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to give; to grant; to bestow

供.note_tr: The onyomi きょう is most common in formal compounds like 供給 (supply) and 供述 (testimony). The kunyomi そなえる means to offer or dedicate, and the suffix -ども marks plurality in pronouns and group nouns.

meanings_tr: Role, part (in drama, theater, or media)
役.note_tr: The reading やく (yaku) is standard in modern Japanese for 'role' and 'duty.' The reading えき (eki) is archaic and rarely used today. In anime and manga, 役 frequently appears in credits and character descriptions referring to roles and voice actor assignments.

examples.meaning_tr: To be useful, to serve a purpose

構.note_tr: The onyomi (こう) appears in compound words meaning 'structure' (e.g., 構造, 構成), while kunyomi forms action verbs: 構える means 'to take a stance or prepare', and 構わない is the everyday phrase 'doesn't matter' or 'I don't mind'. Do not confuse with 造 (to make/create), 構 emphasizes structure and arrangement.

examples.meaning_tr: to take a stance; to prepare; to set oneself
doesn't matter; I don't mind; never mind

割.note_tr: Primary readings fall in the waru/wari family (わ). The katsu reading (かつ) appears in specialized compounds. Use the wari reading to express proportions, rates, and percentages (割合, 二割).

examples.meaning_tr: To divide; to break; to cut
To break; to crack; to split
Disposable wooden chopsticks (commonly used in casual dining)

費.note_tr: Use ひ (on'yomi) in compound words for types of costs (e.g., 旅費 travel expenses). The kun'yomi 費やす means 'to spend time or money,' appearing frequently in anime and games when characters invest effort. Avoid confusing with 支出 (expenditure), which is more formal in accounting contexts.

付.note_tr: The kun'yomi つ.ける is most common, meaning to attach or turn on something. The on'yomi ふ appears in compounds like 付録 (appendix). When used with appliances or lights, つ.ける typically means 'to turn on' (e.g., ライトを付ける, to turn on the light).

examples.meaning_tr: to date; to spend time with
to notice; to become aware of

由.note_tr: 由 primarily uses on'yomi readings (ゆ/ゆう) in common words like 理由 (reason) and 自由 (freedom), while kunyomi readings (よし/よ.る) are rarely used in modern Japanese.

説.note_tr: The on'yomi せつ is used in most compounds like 説明 (explanation) and 小説 (novel); the kun'yomi と.く means "to explain" or "to teach" and is used as a standalone verb form.

examples.meaning_tr: To explain; to teach; to preach

難.note_tr: The kunyomi むずかしい is the most common reading for everyday 'difficult' (e.g., 難しい), while onyomi なん appears in compounds like 困難 (hardship) and 難易度 (difficulty level, common in games and anime). Distinguish 難 (difficult) from 易 (easy), which is its semantic opposite.

examples.meaning_tr: Difficulty level (used in games and anime)
Steep hurdle, difficult barrier (e.g., 難関大学 = competitive university)

優.note_tr: 優しい (yasashii) meaning 'kind and gentle' is the most commonly encountered form in manga and anime, making it essential for understanding character descriptions. In compound words, the onyomi ゆう- typically relates to superiority, priority, or excellence. Be careful not to confuse this with 憂 (yū), which sounds the same but means 'melancholy'.

夫.note_tr: The kunyomi おっと is the standard modern reading meaning 'husband.' The onyomi ふ and ふう appear mainly in compounds like 夫婦 (married couple). The archaic reading それ is rarely used in modern Japanese.

収.note_tr: The onyomi 'shuu' appears in abstract nouns like 収入 (income) and 収集 (collection). The kunyomi forms 'osame' and 'osamaru' describe physical actions: putting things away or fitting items into a space. Similar kanji 修 (repair/discipline) shares visual structure but means something entirely different.

examples.meaning_tr: To put away, to store, to settle
To fit, to be contained, to settle down
Recording, inclusion (used for music albums and anime releases)

断.note_tr: The reading ことわる is used for polite refusal in social situations; たつ emphasizes cutting or severing. The onyomi だん is common in formal and technical compounds like 中断 (interruption) or 断定 (assertion).

examples.meaning_tr: to refuse, to decline, to reject
to sever, to cut off, to break with
interruption, suspension, pause (in games, videos, etc.)

石.note_tr: The kun'yomi いし is used for standalone 'stone' and at the end of compounds, while the on'yomi せき is common in technical and compound words. Do not confuse 石 (stone/rock) with 岩 (いわ, boulder).

meanings_tr: to do incorrectly, to make a mistake
違.note_tr: The verb form ちがう (chigau) means 'to be different'; ちがい (chigai) is its noun form meaning 'difference'. The onyomi い appears mainly in formal words like 違法 (illegal).

examples.meaning_tr: to make a mistake, to do wrongly

消.note_tr: Use intransitive き.える ('to disappear') for 火が消える (the light goes out) and transitive け.す ('to extinguish') for 火を消す (turn off the light). Onyomi しょう appears in compounds like 消火 (firefighting) and 消費 (consumption).

examples.meaning_tr: To turn off, to extinguish, to erase
To disappear, to vanish, to go out (of lights/fire)

神.note_tr: Use かみ for 'god' or 'deity' in basic contexts. Use onyomi しん or じん in compounds, especially 神社 (shrine), 神話 (mythology), and 神経 (nerve). This kanji is very common in anime and manga, often representing gods or supernatural elements. Not to be confused with 霊 (spirit/ghost), which implies something more ghostly or departed.

examples.meaning_tr: Shinto shrine, shrine dedicated to kami

meanings_tr: Number in a series; turn, order
番.note_tr: 番 typically uses the onyomi reading ばん (ban) in compounds. When combined with numerals (一番, 二番), it expresses rank or position in a sequence. The kunyomi つがい is rarely used in modern Japanese; focus on ばん for everyday words.

規.note_tr: 規 is primarily read as き (ki) in formal and administrative contexts. Do not confuse it with similar-reading kanji such as 記 (ki - record) or 起 (ki - rise), which have entirely different meanings.

術.note_tr: The onyomi じゅつ dominates modern Japanese, appearing in nearly all common compounds. The kunyomi すべ is archaic and rarely used in contemporary texts.

meanings_tr: be furnished with, be endowed with
備.note_tr: The onyomi び is used mainly in compounds like 装備 (equipment) and 設備 (facilities), while the kunyomi そなえる means 'to prepare actively' and そなわる means 'to be equipped with' or 'to possess naturally.'

examples.meaning_tr: to prepare, to equip oneself with, to get ready
always kept on hand, standard stock
to be equipped with, to be endowed with naturally

宅.note_tr: The onyomi reading たく is standard for this kanji in compounds. Use 宅 in formal or commercial contexts (delivery services, real estate). Do not confuse with 家 (いえ), which is more colloquial, can refer to a household or family unit, and has multiple readings.

examples.meaning_tr: Home delivery, delivery to one's house
At home, remote work or studying from home

害.note_tr: The kanji 害 uses only the onyomi reading がい and typically appears in compound words rather than standalone. Do not confuse with 傷 (きず/しょう), which specifically refers to physical wounds or cuts; 害 is broader and encompasses any kind of harm, damage, or misfortune.

配.note_tr: Kunyomi 配る (kubaru) is the basic verb meaning 'to distribute' or 'hand out'; onyomi はい (hai) is used in compounds like 配送 (delivery) and 配置 (placement). Different compounds emphasize different aspects: 配信 highlights broadcast, 配慮 emphasizes consideration.

examples.meaning_tr: arrangement, placement, positioning (strategy, game boards, art)

警.note_tr: On'yomi けい dominates modern Japanese, especially in the common compound 警察 (police). Kun'yomi いまし.める appears in formal or classical contexts meaning 'to admonish' or 'to guard against'.

育.note_tr: Use transitive 育てる (sodateru, 'to raise') for active parenting and intransitive 育つ (sodatsu, 'to grow') for passive development. The on-reading いく commonly appears in compounds like 教育 (education) and 体育 (PE), while the kun-readings are used for standalone verbs or more poetic contexts with はぐくむ (hagukumu, 'to nurture').

examples.meaning_tr: to raise, to bring up, to grow (something)

席.note_tr: The on'yomi reading せき is used for "seat" in modern Japanese contexts (座席, 空席). The kun'yomi むしろ refers to a traditional woven mat and is rarely used in beginner materials or contemporary speech.

examples.meaning_tr: To stand up; to leave one's seat

訪.note_tr: The onyomi 訪(ほう) appears in formal or written contexts such as 訪問, while the kunyomi 訪(おとず)れる and 訪(たず)ねる are more common in conversation. Use 訪(おとず)れる for arrivals or visiting places; use 訪(たず)ねる for visiting a specific person.

examples.meaning_tr: to visit, to look for (a person)

乗.note_tr: The kunyomi 乗る (noru) is used in everyday speech for 'to ride or board.' The onyomi じょう appears in formal or compound words like 乗車 (boarding) and 乗客 (passenger).

examples.meaning_tr: To ride; to board (a train, bus, car, bike)
To give someone a ride; to load; to put on

残.note_tr: のこる (intransitive: something remains) vs のこす (transitive: you leave something behind). The onyomi ざん appears in formal/emotional words like 残念 (unfortunate), very common in daily speech.

想.note_tr: 想 almost always appears in compound words using the on'yomi そう; the kun'yomi おもう is rarely used to write this kanji alone in modern Japanese (思う is the standard way to write "to think"). Don't confuse 想 with the similar-looking 相 (also read そう), which means "mutual" or "phase"; a common mix-up for beginners.

examples.meaning_tr: impression, thoughts (e.g. about a movie or anime episode)
prediction, expectation (often used for game or sports results)

声.note_tr: Use こえ (kunyomi) for everyday speech about voice (e.g., 大声 'loud voice', 小声 'quiet voice'); use せい (onyomi) in compounds like 声優 (voice actor) and 音声 (audio). Note the distinction from 音, which also relates to sound but has different readings and usage patterns.

念.note_tr: 念 is almost always read as onyomi ねん and used in compounds, with meaning shifting by context: 念願 emphasizes wish or desire, 信念 emphasizes belief or conviction, and 念力 (common in anime) refers to psychic or mental power. Learn 念 words as complete phrases rather than trying to translate 念 alone in isolation.

examples.meaning_tr: just in case; as a precaution

助.note_tr: The kunyomi たすける and たすかる express the active verb "to help" and passive "to be saved/helped". The onyomi じょ primarily appears in compound words like 援助 (aid) and 助手 (assistant).

examples.meaning_tr: to be saved; to be helped

meanings_tr: To appreciate or thank for hard work
労.note_tr: The onyomi ろう dominates in modern Japanese, appearing in most work-related compounds. The phrase ご苦労さま is a key polite expression meaning "thank you for your hard work"; this usage derives from appreciating or rewarding someone's labor.

examples.meaning_tr: thank you for your hard work (polite expression commonly heard in anime)

例.note_tr: The onyomi れい is used for nouns and compounds like 例外 (exception) and 先例 (precedent). The kunyomi たとえる appears in the verb meaning 'to compare' or 'to exemplify,' and in the common phrase たとえば 'for example.'

examples.meaning_tr: to compare, to give as an example

meanings_tr: like that; in that manner; so
然.note_tr: This kanji appears mainly in compounds with the on'yomi ぜん/ねん, but also as the very common kunyomi しかし meaning 'but.' The fundamental meaning 'like that' or 'in that manner' gives rise to the senses of 'naturally' and 'completely.'

meanings_tr: To the best of one's ability
限.note_tr: The onyomi げん typically appears in formal compound words (限定, 期限, 限界), while the kunyomi かぎる/かぎり is used in simpler phrases like できる限り. The suffix -かぎり carries the meaning 'to the extent that' or 'as far as'.

examples.meaning_tr: To the best of one's ability, as much as possible

追.note_tr: The kunyomi 追う means 'to chase' or 'to follow' in standalone verbs. The onyomi つい- is used mainly in compounds like 追加 (addition) and 追放 (exile). In anime and action games, 追う and 追跡 appear frequently.

商.note_tr: The onyomi しょう dominates in modern Japanese compounds (商品, 商売, etc.). The kunyomi あきな.う is archaic/literary but appears in the classical word 商い (dealings, commerce). Both readings refer to commercial activity, so context determines which is used rather than meaning differences.

葉.note_tr: The kunyomi reading は is used for the standalone word 'leaf' and in most native compounds. The onyomi reading よう appears in Sino-Japanese compounds like 紅葉 (autumn leaves). Do not confuse with 片 (kata, meaning 'one side').

伝.note_tr: The onyomi でん appears in compound words (伝説, 伝統, 伝言). The kunyomi 伝える (tsutaeru) means "to actively tell/convey," while 伝わる (tsutawaru) means "to be passively transmitted or spread to someone." Both are common in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Legend; Myth (very common in anime and manga)
To tell; To convey; To communicate
To be transmitted; To spread; To be conveyed

働.note_tr: The kunyomi reading (はたら.く) is used almost exclusively in modern Japanese for everyday 'work' and is common in anime and manga. The onyomi (どう) rarely appears in standard vocabulary. Note: This is a kokuji (Japanese-created kanji), not borrowed from Chinese.

examples.meaning_tr: prime working years; in one's prime

形.note_tr: The kunyomi reading かたち is the most common, used for the standalone word 'shape' in everyday speech. The onyomi reading けい appears in compounds and formal contexts (形式 'format/style', 三角形 'triangle', 図形 'figure'), while ぎょう is mainly found in 人形 'doll/puppet'.

examples.meaning_tr: Doll; puppet; figure (very common in anime, games, and traditional arts)
Form; format; style; manner (used in technology, writing, and formal contexts)
Triangle (geometric shape commonly studied in art and mathematics)
Figure; geometric shape; diagram (essential term for art and design)

景.note_tr: The onyomi reading けい appears in most common compounds about scenery. You will frequently encounter 景色 (scenery/landscape), which is an essential everyday word.

落.note_tr: Kun'yomi お.ちる (to fall) is the most common reading in everyday use; on'yomi らく appears mainly in formal compounds like 落第 (to fail an exam). The phrase 落ち着く (to calm down) is especially frequent in daily conversation.

examples.meaning_tr: to drop; to cause to fall
to calm down; to settle; to become composed
to feel down; to become depressed

好.note_tr: The reading す.く (好き) is by far the most common in everyday speech for expressing preference or liking something; この.む (好む) is more formal and literary. The onyomi こう appears mainly in compound words. Similar kanji: 良 (good/fine) emphasizes objective quality, while 好 stresses personal preference or taste.

examples.meaning_tr: to really like, to love very much

退.note_tr: The on-reading たい is used in formal compounds like 退職 (retirement) and 退院 (hospital discharge). The kun-reading しりぞく means to physically withdraw or retreat; しりぞける is the transitive form meaning to push back or refuse.

examples.meaning_tr: To retire from work; to resign from a position
To withdraw, to retreat, to back down
To be discharged from a hospital
Exit, being sent off the field or stage (sports, theater, anime)
To push back, to refuse, to reject

頭.note_tr: あたま is used for the body part "head" in daily speech. とう and ず primarily appear in compound words, while かしら (less common) means "leader."

負.note_tr: The kunyomi reading 負ける (makeru, 'to lose') is most common in everyday contexts, especially sports and games. The onyomi form appears in formal words like 負担 (futan, 'burden') and 負債 (fusai, 'debt').

渡.note_tr: わたる (to cross) and わたす (to hand over) are the most common everyday uses. The onyomi と appears mainly in compounds like 渡航 (voyage); distinguish from 度 (degree), which sounds similar but means frequency or degree.

失.note_tr: The kunyomi (うしなう) is primarily used in the verb 失う (to lose). The onyomi (しつ) dominates in compounds like 失敗 and 失礼, commonly appearing in written and formal Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: To lose; to be deprived of

差.note_tr: 差 primarily conveys 'difference' or 'discrepancy.' Use the onyomi さ in noun compounds like 時差 (time difference). The kunyomi readings さ.す and さ.し appear in verbs: 差す (to point/shine), and compound forms like 差し出す (hold out).

examples.meaning_tr: to point; to hold (umbrella); to shine
a treat or snack brought for someone

末.note_tr: The onyomi reading まつ is standard in compounds denoting the end of time periods (週末 'weekend', 月末 'month-end'). The kunyomi すえ is used for the standalone word meaning 'end' or 'tip'. The ばつ reading is rare and appears in specialized terms. Not easily confused with similar-looking kanji when context is clear.

meanings_tr: Keep (as in a promise or secret)
守.note_tr: The kunyomi まもる is the most common reading; onyomi しゅ appears in compounds like 守備 (defense). Means both 'to protect' and 'to obey', frequently used with rules, promises, and laws. Often appears in manga/anime when characters vow to protect someone.

meanings_tr: Or (formal, as in 若しくは)
若.note_tr: The everyday kun-yomi わかい means "young" (as in the adjective 若い), while わか- shows up as a prefix in compounds like 若者. The on-yomi じゃく appears in more formal/written words such as 若干, and にゃく mainly survives in the set phrase 老若男女. The rare reading にゃ is essentially unique to 般若 (Hannya), the famous demon-woman Noh mask often referenced in anime and manga. もし/もしくは ("if"/"or") exist as readings of 若 but are almost always written in plain kana in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Hannya (demon-woman mask/wisdom in Buddhism, iconic in Japanese art and anime)
people of all ages and genders

種.note_tr: The kunyomi reading たね refers to a literal seed. The onyomi reading しゅ appears in compound words like 種類 (type) and 種族 (race), conveying more abstract meanings.

美.note_tr: The kunyomi うつくしい functions as an adjective meaning 'beautiful.' The onyomi び is primarily used in compound words like 美女 (beautiful woman) and 美術 (fine arts), where it often refers to aesthetics or excellence. Beginners should master the standalone adjective form first.

命.note_tr: The kunyomi いのち (life) is used standalone or in simple phrases; the onyomi めい appears in compounds and can mean either "command" (命令) or "fate/destiny" (運命) depending on the context.

examples.meaning_tr: At the risk of one's life; risking one's life

福.note_tr: 福 uses only the onyomi reading ふく and frequently appears in compounds expressing wishes for good luck or well-being, especially in Japanese celebrations and New Year traditions. It has no kunyomi reading in standard usage.

examples.meaning_tr: lucky bag; mystery bag (popular Japanese shopping tradition)
gastronomic pleasure; the joy of eating good food

望.note_tr: The kunyomi のぞ.む (to hope, to wish) is the primary reading in basic verbs. The onyomi ぼう appears frequently in compounds like 希望 (hope) and 望遠鏡 (telescope). The reading もち is mainly used in 望月 (full moon). Be careful not to confuse 望 (hope) with similar-looking 忘 (forget).

examples.meaning_tr: to hope for, to desire, to wish

非.note_tr: 非 functions primarily as a prefix meaning 'not' or 'non-' in compounds. The onyomi ひ is standard; the kunyomi あら.ず is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese. Most compounds use the onyomi reading.

観.note_tr: The on'yomi かん appears in most compounds (観光, 観客, 観察). The verb 観る ('to watch') uses the kun'yomi and means active observation or viewing of an event, unlike basic 見る ('to see').

察.note_tr: This kanji appears mainly in onyomi compounds with さつ. It emphasizes understanding through careful observation or reasoning, distinct from more general thinking verbs like 想 and 考.

examples.meaning_tr: To sense; to guess or perceive someone's feelings
To perceive; to sense or detect something

段.note_tr: The onyomi だん is used in almost all common words with this kanji; the reading たん is extremely rare. 段 represents both physical steps (stairs) and metaphorical progression (levels, stages).

横.note_tr: Kunyomi よこ is commonly used in everyday compounds and nouns. Onyomi おう appears in more formal or technical terms like 横断 (crossing). The opposite of 横 is 縦 (vertical/lengthwise).

examples.meaning_tr: Profile; side view of someone's face

深.note_tr: The kunyomi ふかい is the standard adjective form for "deep." The onyomi しん appears mainly in compounds like 深夜 (late night) and 深海 (deep sea). The verbs 深める (transitive) and 深まる (intransitive) convey both literal deepening and figurative intensification.

meanings_tr: to say, to mention, to state (humble form)
to apply for, to propose, to offer
monkey; the ninth sign of the Chinese zodiac
申.note_tr: 申す (もうす) and its derivative 申し込む are the most common in everyday speech; use the onyomi しん mainly in formal Sino-Japanese compounds like 申請. The standalone meaning 'monkey' is rarely used, see 申年 (さるどし) for the zodiac sign. Easily confused with 猿 (さる, 'monkey').

examples.meaning_tr: to apply for, to sign up, to register
I'm sorry, excuse me, pardon me
to say, to tell (polite humble form)

様.note_tr: The よう reading (on'yomi) expresses manner and style in words like 様式 and the common grammar pattern ～ように (in the manner of), while the さま reading (kun'yomi) appears in respectful or playful contexts like 王様 (king). Avoid confusing with 状 (state/condition).

examples.meaning_tr: appearance, situation, manner, how things seem
king (often used in fairy tales, games, and anime)
everyone, ladies and gentlemen (polite/honorific, common in formal speech and anime)
form, style, format, type of arrangement

財.note_tr: Onyomi ざい (zai) is most common in compounds like 財布 (wallet) and 財宝 (treasure); さい is used in formal words like 財産 (wealth) and 財政 (finance). Don't confuse 財 (wealth/property) with 材 (material/lumber), they sound similar but differ in meaning.

港.note_tr: The reading みなと is used for the standalone word and compounds like 港町 (port town). The reading こう appears in compound words like 空港 (airport) and maritime terms like 入港 (entering port).

識.note_tr: The onyomi (しき) is commonly used in compounds like 常識 (common sense) and 認識 (recognition), while kunyomi readings are less frequent in modern Japanese. Similar kanji 知 (know) also means 'to know,' but 識 emphasizes recognition, discrimination, and awareness.

呼.note_tr: The kunyomi よ.ぶ (yobu) is the primary reading used in the verb "to call" and is very common in everyday conversation. The onyomi こ appears mainly in compound words like 呼吸 (breathing). Both readings are practical for beginners; watch for this kanji in anime dialogue when characters call each other.

examples.meaning_tr: to call someone by their name
to call out loudly; to shout
to call out; to summon; to page

達.note_tr: The suffix form -たち is used to pluralize nouns (friend → friends = 友達). The on'yomi たつ appears mainly in formal or compound words like 達成 (achievement) and 達人 (master/expert). 友達 is one of the most essential N3 vocabulary words.

examples.meaning_tr: To reach; to arrive at; to attain

良.note_tr: Use the kunyomi reading (よい) for standalone adjectives like 良い (good); use the onyomi (りょう) for compound words like 良心 (conscience) and 良質 (quality). Unlike 善, which emphasizes moral virtue, 良 describes general quality or condition.

候.note_tr: The on'yomi こう dominates modern compounds relating to weather, climate, and seasons. The kun'yomi そうろう is archaic and rarely appears in contemporary Japanese. In compounds like 候補 (candidate), 候's meaning integrates with other characters to create derived meanings.

meanings_tr: Degree, extent, the amount or level to which something is true
Law, regulation, formal or legal sense (rare)
程.note_tr: Two main readings: onyomi tei (てい) appears in compounds like 程度 'degree/level' and 工程 'production process,' while kunyomi hodo (ほど) is used in extent and degree expressions (程々 'moderately', 程よい 'moderate'). The compound 程度 is by far the most frequently encountered.

満.note_tr: In compounds, use onyomi (まん); for verbs, use kunyomi (みちる/みたす). The kanji expresses reaching a state of fullness, whether of time (full moon), quantity (packed train), or emotion (satisfied).

敗.note_tr: On'yomi (はい) is used in most compound words. Kun'yomi (やぶれる) forms the verb 敗れる, meaning to be defeated or ruined. Unlike 負ける (makeru, to lose at a game), 敗 emphasizes comprehensive defeat or collapse.

examples.meaning_tr: To be defeated, to be ruined
To be eliminated, to retreat in defeat

値.note_tr: 値 uses the reading ね in everyday commercial contexts about prices and shopping (値段, 値札, 値引き). The ち reading appears in formal or technical terms like 価値 (value) and 数値 (numerical value).

突.note_tr: The kunyomi つ.く is the basic verb form. The onyomi とつ appears in compounds, especially 突然 (suddenly), which is very common in modern Japanese and manga. This kanji describes both action (piercing, thrusting) and state (protruding).

examples.meaning_tr: to poke; to pierce; to stab
to stick out; to protrude; to jut out
to charge; to rush forward; to dash ahead

光.note_tr: Use ひかり (kunyomi) for the standalone noun 'light'; use こう (onyomi) in compound words like 光速 (speed of light) and 日光 (sunlight). The verb 光る means 'to shine' or 'to glitter', common in describing sparkles or stars in anime and manga.

路.note_tr: The onyomi ろ is used in most compounds (道路, 路線, 進路). The suffix -じ appears in 路地 (alley). The kanji 道 is often preferred for the reading みち in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: On the street; on the road

科.note_tr: This kanji primarily uses the onyomi reading か and appears commonly in two main contexts: educational subjects and courses (教科, 科目) and medical specialties (歯科 dentistry, 内科 internal medicine). No kunyomi is provided.

meanings_tr: To stack, pile up, or load (something)
積.note_tr: Use つむ to actively stack or load, and つもる for passive accumulation (like snow piling up). The onyomi せき is used in technical terms like 面積 (area) and 体積 (volume). Be careful not to confuse 積 with 績 (achievement), which shares the onyomi pronunciation but has a different meaning.

examples.meaning_tr: To accumulate, pile up (snow, dust, feelings)
Area, acreage (of land, floor, or shape)
Volume (of a container, object, or liquid)

他.note_tr: 他 has two readings: ほか (kunyomi) for simple uses like 他の (other) and 他に (besides), and た (onyomi) for compounds like 他人 (another person). The kunyomi is more common in everyday conversation.

処.note_tr: The onyomi しょ is most common in formal and technical compounds: 処理 (processing), 処分 (disposal), 処方 (prescription). The kunyomi ところ means "place" or "situation," but is usually written in hiragana in modern Japanese.

太.note_tr: When used as kunyomi (ふとい/ふとる), 太 describes physical thickness or gaining weight. As onyomi (たい), it appears mainly in compound words and proper names. Distinguish from 大 (large/big in general), 太 specifically means thick or fat.

examples.meaning_tr: To gain weight; to become fat

客.note_tr: The onyomi きゃく (kyaku) is the standard reading used in almost all common compounds and is the only reading a beginner needs to learn. The kanji appears frequently in travel and hospitality contexts (guest room, passenger) as well as in business/technology vocabulary (customer, client). No kunyomi exists.

否.note_tr: Onyomi ひ is used in formal compounds like 否定 (negation) and 否認 (denial). Kunyomi いや appears in the phrase 否応なく, meaning 'perforce' or 'whether willing or not.' Don't confuse 否 with 不 (general negation) or 非 (injustice); 否 specifically means 'to deny' or 'refuse.'

examples.meaning_tr: Perforce, willy-nilly; whether willing or not
Yes or no; approval or rejection

師.note_tr: The onyomi し is far more common in modern Japanese than the kunyomi いくさ. This kanji appears frequently in anime, manga, and martial arts contexts, especially in 師匠 (master/mentor). Practical everyday words include 医師 (doctor) and 教師 (teacher).

examples.meaning_tr: instructor, master trainer (especially in martial arts)

登.note_tr: Kunyomi のぼ.る (to climb) is used for physical climbing action; onyomi とう appears mainly in compounds like 登場 (appearance, very common in anime/games) and 登録 (registration). Distinct from 上 (up/above), which describes location rather than the action of ascending.

meanings_tr: Ready to; prone to; inclined to
易.note_tr: Kunyomi やさしい (easy/simple/kind) is the most common reading in everyday speech. Kunyomi やすい means "easy to" or "prone to" and typically appears as a suffix (e.g., 壊れやすい = easy to break). Onyomi えき appears in formal and specialized terms like 易経 (I Ching) and 易者 (fortune-teller).

examples.meaning_tr: I Ching, Book of Changes (classical divination text)

速.note_tr: Use kunyomi 速い (はやい) for the everyday adjective "fast," but note this is written with a different kanji than 早い (はやい, "early"); they sound the same but mean different things. The onyomi そく appears in compound words like 速度 (speed) and 高速 (high speed, often seen on highway signs in Japan).

存.note_tr: The onyomi そん dominates in modern Japanese compounds like 存在 (existence). Kunyomi forms are archaic and rarely appear in contemporary texts.

飛.note_tr: The kunyomi と.ぶ (tobu) and its causative form と.ばす (tobasu) are common in everyday verbs. The onyomi ひ (hi) appears in formal compounds like 飛行機 (airplane) and 飛行 (flight). The causative reading と.ばす also means "to skip" when referring to pages or sections.

examples.meaning_tr: to jump out; to rush out

殺.note_tr: The kunyomi ころす is the everyday form 'to kill.' The on'yomi さつ appears in common compounds like さつじん (murder) and さっき (killing intent, very common in anime/manga), while さっきん denotes sterilization in food and technology contexts.

号.note_tr: The reading ごう (onyomi) dominates modern Japanese and appears in nearly all common compounds. The kunyomi readings さけぶ and よびな are rarely used in contemporary contexts.

単.note_tr: The kanji 単 almost always uses the onyomi reading たん in modern Japanese, appearing in common compounds like 単語 (word) and 単純 (simple). The kunyomi ひとえ is archaic and rarely encountered. When you see 単 in compounds, expect the たん reading.

examples.meaning_tr: Manga volume, standalone book (perfect for anime & manga fans!)

座.note_tr: The kunyomi すわ.る is the verb meaning "to sit." The onyomi ざ appears in nouns related to sitting, such as 座席 (seat) and 座布団 (cushion).

examples.meaning_tr: seat (on a train, plane, or in a theater)
floor cushion (used in traditional Japanese rooms)
tatami room, sitting room (traditional Japanese-style room)
seiza, formal sitting position with knees on the floor

破.note_tr: Kunyomi (やぶ.る/やぶ.れる) is used for verbs; onyomi (は) appears in compounds like 破壊 (destruction) and 破裂 (explosion).

examples.meaning_tr: to break; to tear; to rip
to be broken; to be torn

除.note_tr: The onyomi じょ appears in compounds like 除外 (exception) and 駆除 (elimination). The kunyomi 除く (nozoku) means 'to remove or set aside' in everyday speech, while the mathematical 'division' sense is archaic.

examples.meaning_tr: to remove; to exclude; to set aside

完.note_tr: The kanji 完 uses only the onyomi reading かん and appears almost exclusively in compounds. It emphasizes not just finishing or ending something, but completing it fully and perfectly. Distinguish from 終 (おわる/しゅう – to end) which simply means 'end' without the connotation of perfection or wholeness.

examples.meaning_tr: Completion; finished product (especially art, games, buildings)
Completion; finished (common in tech and gaming contexts)
Conclusion; end (often used when manga or anime series concludes)

降.note_tr: The kunyomi おりる and ふる are everyday conversational words: おりる appears when getting off trains or vehicles, and ふる describes rain or snow falling. The onyomi こう tends to appear in formal or technical compounds like 降参 (surrender). Distinguish from the similar kanji 下 (below/under), which is purely about position.

examples.meaning_tr: To descend, to get off (a train, bus, car)
To lower, to bring down, to take down
Surrender, capitulation; to give up (used in martial arts, games, history contexts)

責.note_tr: The onyomi せき typically appears in compounds referring to responsibility or duty (e.g., 責任). The kunyomi せめる functions as a verb meaning to blame, censure, or condemn. Both readings center on the concept of accountability or fault.

examples.meaning_tr: To blame; to censure; to condemn

捕.note_tr: The kunyomi forms (つかまる, つかまえる) are common everyday words frequently used in anime and conversation. The onyomi ほ appears mainly in formal compounds like 捕虜 (prisoner of war) and 捕獲 (capture).

危.note_tr: The kun'yomi あぶない is most common in everyday speech and anime/games. The on'yomi き is used in formal compounds like 危険 (danger) and 危機 (crisis). The reading あやうい expresses precariousness or uncertainty, while あやぶむ means to fear or suspect.

給.note_tr: Onyomi きゅう is standard in modern Japanese, used in compounds like 給料 (salary) and 給食 (school lunch). Kunyomi forms (たまう, たもう) are archaic and rarely appear in contemporary texts.

苦.note_tr: This kanji has two main reading patterns: the onyomi 苦 (く) used in most compound words (苦労, 苦手), and the kunyomi forms expressing suffering (くる.しい) or bitterness (にが.い). In anime, you'll frequently encounter 苦しい when characters express emotional pain or struggle.

examples.meaning_tr: weak point, something one is poor at

迎.note_tr: The kunyomi むか.える is used in most everyday expressions for "to meet" or "to welcome." The onyomi げい appears in formal compounds like 歓迎 (welcome) and 迎撃 (intercept). Context determines which reading applies.

examples.meaning_tr: To meet, to welcome, to greet
Going to meet someone, greeting on arrival
Pickup (polite way to say picking someone up)
Interception, to intercept (used in gaming and military contexts)
To welcome the new year (common cultural reference)

園.note_tr: The on'yomi えん is used in almost all modern compound words (公園, 動物園, etc.); the kun'yomi その is rarely seen in contemporary usage and appears only in classical or poetic contexts. When you see 園 in a word, expect えん pronunciation.

具.note_tr: In almost all everyday words, 具 is read with its onyomi ぐ (as in 道具, 家具, 具合). The kunyomi そなえる is rare in modern Japanese; the meaning "to possess/equip" is usually written with 備える instead. The other kunyomi つぶさに (meaning "in detail, fully") only appears in formal/literary writing as 具に, so don't worry about it for daily conversation.

examples.meaning_tr: tool, implement (e.g. art supplies, sports gear, cooking tools)
condition, state (often used for health, e.g. 具合が悪い = feeling unwell)

meanings_tr: To quit; to stop; to cease
To resign from a position or office
To refuse; to decline; to reject
辞.note_tr: The onyomi じ is used in most compound words such as 辞書 (dictionary) and 辞職 (resignation). The most common kunyomi, や.める, appears in 辞める (to quit or stop), which is very frequently used in everyday Japanese. The other kunyomi いなむ is archaic and rarely appears in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: To quit; to stop; to resign from
Resignation from a position of office
To decline; to refuse an invitation or offer

因.note_tr: On'yomi いん appears most frequently in everyday compounds like 原因 (cause) and 因縁 (karma/fate). Kun'yomi 因む (ちなむ, to be related to) appears in more formal contexts. Focus on the on'yomi reading for early learning.

馬.note_tr: The reading うま is used for the standalone noun 'horse', while ば is the onyomi used in Sino-Japanese compounds like 競馬 (horse racing) and 馬力 (horsepower). Note that 馬鹿 (fool) comes from an old idiom rather than the literal kanji meaning.

examples.meaning_tr: Fool; idiot (common in anime and manga)

愛.note_tr: The on'yomi あい dominates modern usage (愛する to love, 愛情 affection). The kun'yomi いとしい appears in 愛しい (beloved, darling), common in anime; a deeper emotional connection than 好 (like/prefer).

examples.meaning_tr: to appreciate; to admire (beauty or art)

富.note_tr: The onyomi ふ appears mainly in fixed phrases like 富士山 (Mount Fuji). The kunyomi readings とむ and とみ are more commonly used for everyday words about wealth and abundance.

examples.meaning_tr: to be rich in, to abound with

彼.note_tr: The kunyomi かれ is the most common reading for the pronoun meaning "he," and appears frequently in anime and manga. The form かの is more formal or archaic. The kanji is often found in compounds like 彼氏 (boyfriend) and 彼女 (girlfriend).

未.note_tr: The onyomi 未 (み) is typically used in compounds to mean "not yet" or as a negative prefix (e.g., 未来, future). The kunyomi ま.だ/いま.だ emphasizes "still not" and is often written in hiragana alone (まだ). The reading ひつじ (sheep) appears mainly in zodiac contexts like 未年 (year of the sheep).

examples.meaning_tr: minor; person who is not yet an adult
undecided; not yet determined or fixed
year of the sheep; eighth year in the zodiac cycle
person from the future; time traveler

舞.note_tr: The onyomi ぶ appears primarily in compound words (舞台 'stage', 舞踊 'dance'); the kunyomi ま.う is the standalone verb 'to dance'. 舞台 is one of the most frequently encountered words with this kanji in entertainment, theater, and media contexts.

亡.note_tr: The kunyomi なくなる is the standard, polite way to express that someone has died. The onyomi ぼう appears in formal, literary compounds like 亡命 (exile) and 亡国 (collapse). Compared to 死 (to die), the kanji 亡 with なくなる sounds more respectful and is the preferred term when referring to someone's passing.

examples.meaning_tr: to pass away; to die (polite and respectful)
the late; deceased (formal; e.g., 亡き父 = my late father)
ruin of a nation; collapse of a country

冷.note_tr: The kunyomi つめたい describes physical coldness (cold to touch), while the onyomi れい appears in compounds like 冷蔵庫 (refrigerator) and 冷房 (air conditioning). Related action verbs are ひえる (to become cold) and さめる (to cool off or lose enthusiasm).

examples.meaning_tr: to cool down, to cool off

適.note_tr: On'yomi てき is used in compounds expressing suitability, qualification, or application (e.g., 適切, 適応, 適用). Kun'yomi かなう appears mainly in the pattern ...に適う, meaning 'suited to' or 'fitting for.' Do not confuse 適 with 敵 (enemy, also てき).

examples.meaning_tr: Suited to the times, timely, appropriate for the era
Suitable person, right person for the job, qualified person

婦.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 婦 is almost always read with its on'yomi ふ inside compound words; the kun'yomi よめ is rare and mostly limited to classical or formal contexts. For everyday "bride / daughter-in-law", the separate kanji 嫁 (also read よめ) is the one actually used; don't confuse the two.

寄.note_tr: In everyday contexts (especially anime/manga), you'll mostly encounter the kunyomi よる (approach) and よせる (bring near). The onyomi き appears in more formal compounds like 寄付 (donation). Note: 寄る is intransitive (characters approach), while 寄せる is transitive (bring objects near).

examples.meaning_tr: to approach, to come near; to stop by
to bring near, to move closer; to gather
detour, stopping by somewhere (on the way)
to snuggle close to, to be near someone (romantic/supportive)

meanings_tr: to cram, to stuff, to pack in
to involve, to roll up, to wrap up in
to surge, to well up (of emotions)
込.note_tr: こ.む is primarily intransitive or used with を (to stuff into something). こ.める is transitive (to pack something in, to include). The suffix -こ.み means 'including' or 'including the fact that.' Commonly appears in expressions of overwhelming emotions and situations, especially in manga and anime.

examples.meaning_tr: to apply for, to sign up, to submit an application
to stuff in, to cram, to pack tightly
to involve, to roll up in, to get caught up in
to surge up, to well up, to rise (of emotions or tears)
to send in, to dispatch into
to be crowded, to be packed with people

顔.note_tr: The kun-reading かお is used in most everyday words about faces (such as 笑顔 "smiling face" and 真顔 "serious face"). The on-reading がん appears mainly in formal or technical terms (such as 顔面 "facial surface"). Not easily confused with other kanji.

類.note_tr: The onyomi るい predominates in modern compounds, while the kunyomi たぐい appears mainly in formal contexts. Distinguish from 種 (しゅ/たね), which emphasizes individual varieties or botanical 'seeds' rather than classification.

examples.meaning_tr: the same kind, same type, alike

余.note_tr: The kunyomi reading あま appears in everyday expressions like 余る (to be left over) and 余り (remainder; also means 'not much' with negatives). The onyomi reading よ appears in formal compounds like 余計 (unnecessary) and 余震 (aftershock).

examples.meaning_tr: to be left over, to remain
remainder; not much, not very (with negatives)

王.note_tr: 王 uses the onyomi reading おう and appears frequently in anime and manga (especially 王様, meaning king). Don't confuse it with 皇 (emperor, こう), which refers to the supreme imperial ruler.

examples.meaning_tr: King (used in fairy tales and anime)

返.note_tr: Kunyomi かえす and かえる are used for concrete actions like returning or reversing. The onyomi へん appears in formal vocabulary, such as 返事 (reply) and 返金 (refund). Do not confuse this with 帰 (to return home), which shares the reading かえる but has a different focus.

妻.note_tr: The kunyomi つま is used for everyday reference to 'wife,' while the onyomi さい primarily appears in formal compounds like 妻帯者 (married person). This kanji carries a respectful, formal nuance compared to casual alternatives.

背.note_tr: Use the せ or せい reading for physical meanings like "back" and "height" (especially in せが高い 'is tall'). The はい reading appears in abstract or technical compounds like 背景 (haikei, 'background'), very common in anime and art contexts. The そむ reading means 'to go against' or 'betray' and is more literary.

熱.note_tr: Use ねつ for 'fever' or 'heat' (nouns); use あつい for 'hot' (adjective). The compound 熱心 (ねっしん, 'enthusiastic/passionate') is extremely common in anime and everyday conversation. Note: don't confuse with 温 (warm), which is milder.

宿.note_tr: Use しゅく in compounds like 宿泊 (lodging) and 宿題 (homework). The kunyomi やど means 'inn' or 'lodge' and is used for the standalone word. Similar to 家 but implies commercial or temporary lodging rather than a permanent home.

薬.note_tr: The kunyomi reading (くすり) is used for the standalone word and many common compounds like 目薬 (eye drops) and 風邪薬 (cold medicine). The onyomi reading (やく) appears in more formal compounds like 薬局 (pharmacy). No common kanji confusion.

険.note_tr: The onyomi けん is primarily used in compound words, while the kunyomi けわしい appears as an i-adjective meaning 'steep' or 'precipitous'. In compounds like 危険, 冒険, and 保険, the けん reading is standard.

頼.note_tr: The kun-reading 頼む (to ask/request) is very common in everyday speech and anime, often meaning "please." Use 頼る for "to rely/depend on." The on-reading らい appears mainly in formal compounds like 信頼 (trust).

examples.meaning_tr: to request, to ask, to count on someone
to rely on, to depend on

覚.note_tr: 覚える means to learn or memorize; さめる and さます relate to waking up (さめる is intransitive, さます is transitive). The onyomi かく appears in compounds like 覚悟 (determination).

examples.meaning_tr: to learn; to memorize; to remember
to learn a song; to memorize music

船.note_tr: The kunyomi ふね (fune) is the everyday reading for boats and ships in conversation. The onyomi せん (sen) appears in compounds and formal contexts, and is commonly seen in anime and manga titles (e.g., 海賊船 – pirate ship).

途.note_tr: The onyomi reading と dominates modern Japanese in compounds like 途中 (on the way); the kunyomi みち is rarely used. Distinguish 途 from similar kanji 道 (dō/michi, 'way') and 路 (ro, 'path'), which are more commonly used.

examples.meaning_tr: On the way, in the middle of, during

許.note_tr: The kunyomi ゆる.す (yurusu) is used in everyday speech meaning 'to allow' or 'to forgive.' The onyomi きょ (kyo) appears in formal compound words like 許可 (kyoka, permission). The reading もと (moto) is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to permit, to allow, to forgive
won't forgive, won't allow, won't permit

抜.note_tr: The reading ぬく means 'to pull out,' while ぬける means 'to slip out' or 'to be omitted.' The reading ばつ appears mainly in fixed words like 抜群 (outstanding). Particle phrases like 気が抜ける shift the meaning to 'lose' or 'escape.'

examples.meaning_tr: to slip out, to escape, to come out
to lose one's concentration, to go limp
to pull out hair, to pluck hair
a name is omitted, to forget a name

便.note_tr: The onyomi べん is most common in the everyday word 便利 (convenient). The びん reading appears in service compounds like 宅配便 (parcel delivery), which is relevant to modern life and technology. Though the kanji originally referred to bodily waste, modern Japanese primarily uses it to mean convenience or services.

examples.meaning_tr: convenience; the quality of being convenient

留.note_tr: 留 has paired transitive/intransitive verbs: 留める (to stop or detain something) versus 留まる (to stay or remain, intransitive). The on'yomi りゅう is common in compounds like 留学 (study abroad) and 留年 (repeating a school year, frequently seen in anime/manga). The reading る appears in 留守 (being away).

examples.meaning_tr: To stop, to fasten, to hold back
Grade retention, repeating a school year

罪.note_tr: Kunyomi つみ is used for the standalone word; onyomi ざい is used in compounds (犯罪, 有罪). This kanji is common in crime stories, legal contexts, and moral dilemmas in anime and manga.

努.note_tr: The onyomi ど is used in the frequently seen noun compound 努力 (どりょく, 'effort' or 'hard work'). The kunyomi つとめる is a verb meaning 'to endeavor' or 'to try one's best.' When expressing effort as a noun or general concept, use 努力; when describing the action of striving, use つとめる.

examples.meaning_tr: To endeavor, to strive, to try one's best
To make an effort, to work hard

精.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 精 is primarily used with onyomi readings せい and しょう in compound words. The meaning varies by context: せい appears in words related to spirit or essence (精神), vigor or energy (精力), and refined precision (精密). The kunyomi readings (しらげる and くわしい) are rarely found in contemporary Japanese text.

examples.meaning_tr: Spirit, mind, willpower, common in anime and manga for describing character determination
Vigor, energy, vitality, describes physical or mental stamina
Precision, accuracy, detailed, used in technology and engineering contexts
Rice milling, rice polishing, important in Japanese cuisine and sake brewing
Fairy, spirit being, a supernatural creature common in fantasy stories and anime

散.note_tr: The reading ち.る emphasizes graceful or natural scattering, especially in anime/manga contexts like cherry blossoms falling in spring. The onyomi さん appears in many everyday compound words like 散歩 (stroll) and 散乱 (disorder).

examples.meaning_tr: To scatter; to fall (of petals or leaves)

静.note_tr: Kunyomi (しず-) forms are used in everyday contexts to express "quiet" and "calm." Onyomi せい appears mainly in formal compounds like 冷静 (calm/cool-headed). The reading じょう is less common in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: To calm down, to quiet, to silence
To become quiet, to calm down (intransitive)
Calm, composure, cool-headedness (useful in anime/character contexts)

婚.note_tr: This kanji is almost always used in compounds with the onyomi こん. It rarely appears alone. You'll encounter it frequently in anime, manga, and drama depicting relationships and romantic storylines.

examples.meaning_tr: marriage hunting; searching for a spouse

喜.note_tr: The kunyomi reading (よろこぶ) is used in everyday verbs and expressions like 喜ぶ (to be glad). The onyomi reading (き) appears in compound words such as 喜劇 (comedy). Both express the sense of being happy or pleased.

examples.meaning_tr: to be glad; to rejoice; to be pleased
great joy; being very happy; jubilation

浮.note_tr: Master 浮く (to float) as the core meaning. 浮かぶ adds 'comes to mind,' while 浮かべる means 'to put on' (e.g., 笑顔を浮かべる, 'to smile'). These forms are very common in anime and manga dialogue.

examples.meaning_tr: to float; to rise; to emerge
to float; to come to mind; to occur to
to float; to put on (an expression)
to be in high spirits; to be in a festive mood

絶.note_tr: The onyomi ぜつ forms compounds meaning 'absolute' or 'extreme' (絶対, 絶景), while the kunyomi たえる is a verb meaning 'to cease' (絶える). Unlike 切 (cut), 絶 emphasizes complete severance or an absolute state rather than just physical cutting.

examples.meaning_tr: To cease; to end; to stop existing

幸.note_tr: Kunyomi さいわい (fortunately) is formal, while しあわせ (happiness) is everyday speech. Onyomi こう appears mainly in compounds like 幸運 (good luck) and 幸福 (happiness).

押.note_tr: 押 primarily uses the kun'yomi reading お.す (to push/press) in everyday contexts. The reading お.さえる means to hold down or suppress, often with a more figurative sense of restraint. Don't confuse 押 with 推 (to recommend/push forward) or 圧 (pressure).

examples.meaning_tr: To hold down; to suppress; to restrain
Closet; built-in storage space (traditional Japanese-style closet)

倒.note_tr: The kunyomi たおれる (fall) and たおす (knock down) are common in action contexts like anime and games. The onyomi とう typically appears in formal compounds such as 倒産 (bankruptcy) and 倒立 (handstand).

等.note_tr: The kunyomi ひとしい appears as the verb/adjective 等しい meaning "equal," while など and -ら are common suffixes attached to nouns (など for listing items "etc.", -ら for pluralizing people like 彼ら "they"). The onyomi とう shows up in compound words like 平等 (equality) and 等級 (grade/class), where it conveys the idea of rank or category rather than simple equality.

examples.meaning_tr: etc.; and so on (used after a list of items)
they; them (plural suffix -ら on 彼)

老.note_tr: On-reading ろう (rō) is most common in compounds like 老人 (old person) and 老化 (aging). Kun-reading お.いる forms the verb 老いる (to grow old), used when describing someone aging over time.

曲.note_tr: The onyomi きょく is used for music-related meanings such as songs, melodies, and compositions. The kunyomi ま.がる (intransitive) and ま.げる (transitive) mean to bend, curve, or turn, used for physical actions or directions. These meanings align clearly with their respective readings.

examples.meaning_tr: To bend; to curve; to turn (as in turning at an intersection)
To bend; to fold; to twist

払.note_tr: The kunyomi はらう is most common for 'to pay' or 'to brush/sweep away.' The onyomi ふつ appears in more formal or literary terms like 払拭 (to dispel). In formal contexts, 支払う is the standard way to express payment.

examples.meaning_tr: To pay; to brush away; to clear off
To refund; to pay back; to return (money)
To dispel; to wipe away (doubts, fears, concerns)

庭.note_tr: The kunyomi reading (にわ) is used for everyday 'garden' or 'yard', while the onyomi reading (てい) appears in formal compound words like 庭園 (garden park).

徒.note_tr: The on'yomi 「と」 dominates in modern compounds like 徒歩 (on foot) and 徒労 (futile effort). The kun'yomi 「いたずら」 means mischief or prank, common in manga and anime when characters play tricks, though this reading appears less frequently in modern Japanese than in classical texts. The kun'yomi 「あだ」 relates to vanity or impermanence and is rarely used today. Beginners should focus on the on'yomi compounds first.

examples.meaning_tr: futile effort; vain labor; wasted work
gang; clique; group of followers or associates

meanings_tr: To work; to serve; to be employed
勤.note_tr: The onyomi きん is common in compound words related to work and employment (勤務, 出勤, 皆勤), while the kunyomi つと.める/つと.まる function as standalone verbs. The onyomi ごん is rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to work for; to serve; to be employed
to be suited for; to manage; to be capable of
to come to work; to go to work; attendance

遅.note_tr: The on-reading ち is common in formal contexts like 遅刻 (being late for school). The kun-reading おそい describes slowness as an adjective. The kun-reading おくれる means to fall behind or be delayed as a verb. Avoid confusion with 後 (ato/behind), which refers to sequence or position rather than slowness or lateness.

examples.meaning_tr: to be late; to fall behind; to be delayed
being late (especially for school or work); tardiness
delay (technical or formal term used for flights, trains, etc.)
slow to reply; takes a long time to respond
slow movement; sluggish action (common in anime and gaming)

meanings_tr: to be; to exist; to stay
to reside; to live; to dwell
to sit; to remain in place
居.note_tr: い.る (to be/exist) is the most common everyday reading, appearing constantly in conversation and anime. Other readings appear mainly in formal or compound words. Often confused with 有る (ある); use 居る for living beings in a location, and 有る for objects or possessions.

examples.meaning_tr: to be; to exist; to stay (for living things)
dozing off while sitting; nodding off
comfort; sense of a place's atmosphere
to sit stubbornly; to stay put; to occupy

雑.note_tr: The onyomi ざつ is used in most common words like magazines and conversations. The alternative readings are less frequently seen in modern Japanese.

招.note_tr: The kunyomi form 招く (to invite/beckon) is the base verb, commonly used in everyday situations. The onyomi しょう appears in formal compounds like 招待 (invitation), used for official invitations and formal contexts. Both readings share the core sense of drawing someone toward you.

examples.meaning_tr: Lucky cat; beckoning cat (iconic Japanese figurine)

困.note_tr: The kunyomi こまる forms the basic verb 困る and its conjugations, commonly used in everyday situations and anime dialogue. The onyomi こん appears in compound words like 困難 (difficulty) and 困惑 (perplexity), essential for reading comprehension at the N3 level.

examples.meaning_tr: to be in trouble; to be troubled
I'm in trouble; how troublesome (very common phrase in anime and manga)
to trouble; to bother; to cause trouble for someone

欠.note_tr: The onyomi けつ is used in formal nouns (欠点, 欠席), while the kunyomi か- forms appear in verbs (欠ける, 欠かす). Both readings are equally important for this level.

examples.meaning_tr: To lack, to be missing, to chip (of a cup or dish)
Absence, being absent from school or work
To miss, to skip, to fail to do (often: ～ことを欠かさない = never fail to ~)
Defect, flaw, or fault in something

meanings_tr: To update, to renew, to refresh
To grow late (of the night), the passage of night
更.note_tr: The kunyomi さらに (sara ni) works as an adverb meaning 'furthermore,' common in formal and narrative writing. The onyomi こう appears primarily in compounds like 更新 (update). The kunyomi ふける conveys 'to grow late' and appears frequently in anime/manga descriptions of nighttime. Do not confuse 更 with 再 (sai, 'again') or 又 (mata, 'also'), each has a distinct nuance and usage pattern.

examples.meaning_tr: Update, renewal, refresh (commonly used in technology and gaming contexts)
Furthermore, moreover, even more; in addition
Late night, the dead of night
Changing room, locker room, dressing room
To grow late (of the night), to pass (of time)

刻.note_tr: The kunyomi きざ.む is used for physical actions like chopping (food) or engraving, while the onyomi こく appears mainly in compounds related to time (時刻 "time of day") or formal/artistic contexts (彫刻 "sculpture"). これが helpful for distinguishing usage contexts in anime, cooking, and art.

examples.meaning_tr: to chop, to carve, to engrave

賛.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 賛 appears mainly in compounds with the reading さん, with meanings that vary by context: 賛成 (approval), 称賛 (praise), 協賛 (sponsorship).
