憲.note_tr: This kanji primarily appears in formal compound words related to laws and constitutions. It uses only the onyomi reading けん and is rarely used standalone. The most common compound is 憲法 (Constitution), widely used in legal, political, and educational contexts.

離.note_tr: Use kunyomi (はな-) for verb forms like 離れる and 離す; use onyomi (り) for compounds like 離婚 and 離島. The kanji expresses distance or disconnection between things.

examples.meaning_tr: To separate; to move away; to leave
To release; to separate; to distance

激.note_tr: The kunyomi reading はげ.しい appears in the common adjective 激しい (intense/fierce), while onyomi げき is used mainly in compound words like 激怒 (rage) and 激励 (encouragement). This kanji emphasizes strong, vigorous action or feeling and appears frequently in anime and action scenes.

摘.note_tr: The kunyomi つむ (tsu-mu) means "to pick or pluck" and is common in action contexts like picking flowers or leaves. The onyomi てき appears mainly in formal compounds such as 摘発 (exposure) and 摘出 (extraction), which are more literary or technical.

examples.meaning_tr: Exposure, revelation, to expose (a crime or deception)
To pick, pluck, harvest (more emphatic form)

系.note_tr: This kanji uses only the onyomi reading けい and appears most often in compound words. Commonly used as a suffix meaning "related to," "genre," or "type" (e.g., アニメ系 = anime-related, 音楽系 = music-related). Not to be confused with 径 (diameter) or 茎 (stem), which share similar pronunciations.

批.note_tr: This kanji uses only on'yomi (ひ) in modern Japanese and appears mainly in formal, Sino-Japanese compounds. 批判 emphasizes direct criticism or disapproval, whereas 批評 suggests professional analysis or critique.

郎.note_tr: 郎 appears primarily in male given names, with onyomi ろう being the standard reading. While historically used to count sons (first son, second son), this usage is archaic and now typically uses 男 instead; the kunyomi おとこ is also rare in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Tarō (an extremely popular male given name, very common in anime and manga)
Jirō (the second son; traditionally used to indicate a second male child)
Ichirō (the first son; a common male given name)
Shirō (the fourth son; used as a male given name)

健.note_tr: The onyomi けん dominates in common words like 健康. The kunyomi すこやか is less frequent, appearing mainly in poetry and literary texts. Not to be confused with 賢 (wise, clever), which sounds similar but has a different meaning.

盟.note_tr: 盟 uses only the on'yomi reading めい, no kun'yomi. It typically appears in compound words related to alliances, agreements, or sworn pacts. Frequently encountered in historical contexts, games, and anime/manga when discussing formal unions or blood oaths.

従.note_tr: The kun'yomi したがう means to follow or obey in everyday speech, while the on'yomi じゅう appears in formal compounds like 従来 (traditionally) and 従事 (to engage in). The kanji emphasizes willing submission and compliance rather than just being physically present.

examples.meaning_tr: to follow, to obey, to comply with
to engage in, to work in, to be employed in

修.note_tr: Uses onyomi しゅ/しゅう in most compounds (修行 training, 修理 repair, 修正 correction) and kunyomi 修める (おさめる, to master). Often confused with 習 (to learn by repetition); 修 emphasizes active self-discipline and skill mastery through training.

examples.meaning_tr: Training, practice; ascetic discipline and training, very common in anime about martial arts or magic
Repair, maintenance; to repair or fix something
Correction, revision; to correct or amend an error or draft
To master, to perfect; to acquire skill or knowledge through dedication

隊.note_tr: 隊 reads as たい (onyomi only; no common kunyomi). It indicates organized groups, units, or teams, and appears frequently in anime/manga for military squads and expeditions. Often combined with words like 長 (leader) or 消防 (firefighting).

織.note_tr: The kunyomi お.る and its variants (お.り) are used in the basic verb "to weave"; the onyomi しょく appears in technical terms like 織機 (loom), while しき appears in abstract compounds like 組織 (organization).

拡.note_tr: The on'yomi かく is the primary reading in modern compounds like 拡大 (expansion) and 拡張 (extension); こう is rare. Kun'yomi forms are less frequent in contemporary written Japanese than their 広 kanji alternatives.

故.note_tr: 故 primarily uses the onyomi こ in compound words describing reasons, intentional actions, and conditions. The phrase 故に (ゆえに, 'therefore') is essential and uses the kunyomi ゆえ. When modifying nouns, 故 often means 'deceased' or 'late'. The kunyomi ふる.い (old) is less common in modern Japanese than similar kanji like 古.

examples.meaning_tr: deceased person, the late (used respectfully when referring to someone who has passed away)

振.note_tr: The kunyomi ふ.る is most common for the physical action of shaking or waving. The onyomi しん appears in formal or technical compounds like 振動 (vibration). The -ぶり suffix reading describes manner or style, as in 手振り (gesture).

examples.meaning_tr: To shake; to wave; to swing
To turn back; to look back; to glance back

meanings_tr: to distinguish, to separate, to divide
弁.note_tr: べん is the most common reading in everyday words like 弁当 (bento) and 弁護士 (lawyer). The kanji originally means to distinguish or divide. わ.ける and わきま.える are less frequent in modern usage. Do not confuse 弁 (petal/valve) with 弁 (speech) when learning compound words, context matters. See also 弁 in medical terms (弁膜).

examples.meaning_tr: valve (medical/anatomical term, as in heart valve)
to know one's place, to understand and accept a situation

meanings_tr: To take a position or job; to assume office
To depart; to set out on
就.note_tr: Modern usage strongly favors the on'yomi しゅう, especially in formal compound words about employment and positions. The kun'yomi and alternate reading じゅ are rare. Not to be confused with 付く (つく, 'to attach'), which is far more common in everyday speech.

異.note_tr: The onyomi い appears in most formal compounds (異常, 異国). The kunyomi ことなる is used in the verb 異なる (to differ). This kanji is especially popular in anime and manga, particularly in fantasy contexts for 異世界 (another world / isekai).

examples.meaning_tr: Another world; isekai (different world common in fantasy and anime)
To differ; to be different from

献.note_tr: The onyomi けん is used in most compounds (献血, 献上, 献金), while こん appears in the common word 献立 (menu). The kunyomi たてまつる is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese.

厳.note_tr: The kunyomi reading きびしい (harsh, strict) is most common for beginners in the adjective 厳しい. The onyomi reading げん appears in formal compound words like 厳選 (carefully selected) and 厳禁 (strictly forbidden). The reading いつくし appears primarily in the place name 厳島 (Itsukushima).

examples.meaning_tr: Strict, harsh, severe, describes rules, conditions, or a person's demeanor
Carefully selected, hand-picked, often seen in food and product descriptions
Strictly forbidden, used on warning signs and rules
Solemn, grave, serious, describes formal or serious atmospheres
Itsukushima (famous shrine island in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan)

維.note_tr: 維 is an advanced character that appears almost exclusively in compounds like 維持 (maintenance) and 維新 (restoration/reform). Although the character originally referred to rope or fiber, modern Japanese uses it primarily through these fixed expressions with the on'yomi reading い.

examples.meaning_tr: Maintenance, preservation; to maintain, keep, sustain
Restoration, reform, modernization (e.g., Meiji Restoration in Japanese history)
Life support, life preservation (often seen in medical or sci-fi contexts)

浜.note_tr: The kunyomi はま (hama) is the standard reading used in most common words. The onyomi ひん (hin) is rarely encountered in modern Japanese. This kanji frequently appears in place names and words related to coastal areas.

遺.note_tr: The onyomi い is the predominant reading in modern Japanese, appearing in common words like 遺言 (will) and 遺産 (inheritance). The reading ゆい is rarely used in contemporary vocabulary, while the kunyomi のこす is less common in everyday usage.

塁.note_tr: The onyomi るい dominates in modern Japanese, especially in baseball where it names the four bases. The kunyomi とりで (fort or fortified position) is more literary or historical and less frequently used. Similar kanji: 砦 (とりで, fort, usually appears in compounds) and 塞 (barrier/fortress).

邦.note_tr: The onyomi ほう is productive in modern Japanese, primarily appearing in compounds related to Japanese culture and things (邦画 = Japanese film, 邦楽 = Japanese music). The kunyomi くに exists etymologically but is rarely used in contemporary Japanese; 国 is the standard character for the general meaning "country." Use the ほう reading in modern compounds.

examples.meaning_tr: Japanese title (given to a foreign work)

素.note_tr: Both onyomi (so and su) are common in compounds, with the specific reading determined by the word itself rather than a fixed pattern. The kunyomi (moto) is rarely used in modern Japanese.

遣.note_tr: The onyomi けん is most common in 派遣 (dispatch/temporary employment). The kunyomi forms frequently appear in emotional or relational compounds: 気遣い and 心遣い both express care or thoughtfulness. The や reading appears in 遣る (colloquial: "to do/give") and 遣り取り ("exchange").

抗.note_tr: The kunyomi あらがう is used for the verb "to resist" or "to oppose." The onyomi こう appears in compounds like 抗議 (protest) and 抗菌 (antibacterial).

examples.meaning_tr: to resist; to oppose; to defy

模.note_tr: 模 primarily uses the も reading in common compounds and rarely uses ぼ in modern usage. It often expresses intentional imitation or creating a model based on something. Similar kanji 似 (に, "resemble") describes accidental or natural resemblance, while 模 emphasizes deliberate copying or modeling.

examples.meaning_tr: model, mockup, scale model (common in anime figures, architecture, games)
pattern, design, figure (used in art, nature descriptions, textiles)
copying, imitation (especially in art and drawing)
mock exam, practice test, trial examination

雄.note_tr: The おす/お- readings refer to male animals or gender (e.g., 雄 = male animal). The ゆう reading appears in formal/literary compounds expressing heroism or magnificence (英雄 hero, 雄大 grand) and is more common in written Japanese and anime/manga contexts.

益.note_tr: The onyomi えき (eki) is most common in compound words like 利益 (profit) and 有益 (beneficial). The kunyomi ます (masu) appears in the adverb 益々 (ますます, increasingly).

緊.note_tr: In almost all modern words this kanji is read with the onyomi きん (as in 緊張 or 緊急); the kunyomi し.める／し.まる are essentially never used with this kanji on its own in practice, so focus on learning it through compound words. Don't confuse 緊 with the more common 締 (also read しめる, meaning "to tie/fasten"); they look similar but are different kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: tension, nervousness (e.g. before a performance or game)
emergency, urgent (e.g. emergency alert while traveling)
tense, strained (a tense situation, e.g. in a story or historical event)
close, tight-knit (a close relationship or connection)

標.note_tr: The onyomi reading 'hyō' (ひょう) is most common in compound words and is the default for this kanji. The kunyomi readings 'shirube' (しるべ) and 'shirushi' (しるし) are less frequent but appear in traditional or poetic contexts such as 道標 (wayside signpost).

宣.note_tr: The on-reading せん appears in nearly all modern words with 宣; the kun-reading のたま.う is classical and rarely used in contemporary Japanese. Do not confuse with 言 (to say, general speech) or 述 (to state, narrate), 宣 specifically means formal proclamation or public announcement.

examples.meaning_tr: Declaration, proclamation, statement (e.g., 'I declare war' or 'a musical artist's debut announcement')
Advertising, publicity, promotion (e.g., a movie ad, tech product marketing)
Announcement, verdict, sentence (e.g., court ruling or sports official's call)
Declaration of war (formal diplomatic or historical context)
Proclamation, promulgation (official governmental or legal announcement)

昭.note_tr: This kanji is most famous in the era name 昭和 (Showa). Always use the onyomi reading しょう. Do not confuse with the similar kanji 照, which emphasizes the action of shining rather than the quality of brightness.

examples.meaning_tr: Showa era (1926-1989), a major period in Japanese history
it is obvious; it is manifest

廃.note_tr: The on'yomi はい is used in formal compound words (廃止, 廃棄) commonly seen in technology, history, and business contexts. The kun'yomi すたれる means 'to become obsolete' or 'to fall into disuse' and appears in literary or narrative descriptions of decline.

examples.meaning_tr: To become obsolete, To fall into disuse, To decay

伊.note_tr: This kanji is primarily used in its onyomi reading (い) meaning "Italy", appearing in place names and words related to Italian culture. The kunyomi reading (かれ) is archaic and rarely seen in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Izu (scenic region in Japan, famous for hot springs and travel)

江.note_tr: 江 predominantly uses the kunyomi え in common words and place names, especially in 江戸 (Edo). The onyomi こう appears mainly in more formal or literary compounds and is relatively uncommon in everyday speech.

examples.meaning_tr: Edo (former name of Tokyo; also refers to the Edo period, 1603–1868)
Edo period (a major historical era frequently featured in anime and manga)
Enoshima (a scenic island and popular travel destination near Tokyo)

僚.note_tr: This kanji is read exclusively as りょう and appears almost entirely in compound words. The most common modern usage is 同僚 (colleague/coworker). The character conveys a sense of working alongside or standing with someone.

吉.note_tr: The onyomi (きち・きつ) appears primarily in compounds indicating good fortune and luck, such as 大吉 (great luck, common in fortune-telling omens shown in anime/manga). The kunyomi (よし) is used in names and means "good" or "favorable." Both readings carry auspicious and positive connotations.

examples.meaning_tr: Great luck, supreme luck (the highest rating on fortune-telling slips, often seen in anime shrine scenes)
Good omen, good sign, harbinger of good fortune
Yoshino (famous mountain region in Japan known for cherry blossoms, cultural heritage)

meanings_tr: Peak, height, at the height of
盛.note_tr: The kunyomi さか.ん is most commonly seen in the adjective さかん (thriving, active); も.る is used for serving/heaping food and in the common phrase 盛り上がる (to get excited); onyomi せい appears in formal compounds like 繁盛 (prosperity) and 盛夏 (midsummer).

examples.meaning_tr: to get excited, to heat up (mood/energy); to become lively
vigorous, active, thriving; in full swing
great success; packed or crowded event
midsummer, height of summer; the dead of summer

皇.note_tr: The こう reading is standard and appears in most modern compound words (皇帝, 皇族, 皇太子, 皇后). The おう reading is rare in contemporary Japanese. When you encounter 皇 in anime, manga, or historical texts, it almost always uses the こう pronunciation.

臨.note_tr: On'yomi (りん) dominates in compounds (臨時 "temporary," 臨床 "clinical"), while kun'yomi (のぞむ) functions as a standalone verb meaning "to face" or "to approach directly." Useful in formal written contexts, news, and classical literature.

examples.meaning_tr: To face, to confront, to approach
On a war footing, war readiness

meanings_tr: Carry through, persist, hold one's ground
Base on, take into account, consider
踏.note_tr: 踏む (kunyomi) is used for everyday stepping and treading. 踏ん張る means to hold one's ground or persist. 踏まえる means to use as a base or to take into account. The onyomi 踏 (tō) appears in formal compounds like 踏襲 (tōshū, follow/adopt) and 踏査 (tōsa, survey).

examples.meaning_tr: to take a step forward, to make a move
to hold one's ground, to persist
to base on, to take into account
to follow, to adopt, to continue a tradition

壊.note_tr: Kunyomi こわ.す (transitive: to break) and こわ.れる (intransitive: to be broken) are far more common in daily Japanese than the onyomi かい, which appears mainly in formal compounds like 破壊 (destruction). Distinguish from 割る (to split/break brittle things) and 折る (to bend/break).

examples.meaning_tr: Broken (past participle, used as an adjective)

債.note_tr: This kanji is primarily used in formal and financial contexts, employing only the on'yomi reading さい. It frequently appears in compound words related to financial instruments and debt obligations.

興.note_tr: きょう dominates modern interest/entertainment words; こう appears in formal contexts. おこ.す 'to start/arouse' (transitive) vs おこ.る 'to flourish/arise' (intransitive).

examples.meaning_tr: to start, to begin, to bring about
to flourish, to prosper, to arise

源.note_tr: The onyomi げん dominates in compound words (源泉, 源流, 水源); the kunyomi みなもと appears in proper names like 源氏 (Genji) and classical literature. As a standalone noun, 源 means "source" and is common in nature and technology contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: water source; origin of a river
Genji (famous clan from The Tale of Genji; popular in anime & manga)

儀.note_tr: 儀 uses only the onyomi reading ぎ (gi) and appears almost exclusively in formal and ceremonial contexts. It is most commonly encountered in compound words like 儀式 (ceremony) and 儀礼 (etiquette).

創.note_tr: The onyomi そう is the most common reading in compound words like 創造 (creation) and 創作 (creative work). This kanji typically conveys bringing something new into existence or establishing an institution. The reading しょう appears in 創傷 (wound), and the kunyomi つく.る shows up in literary or poetic writing, though less frequently in modern usage.

examples.meaning_tr: First publication, launch of a magazine or newspaper

障.note_tr: The onyomi しょう appears in most compound words (障害, 障子), while the kunyomi さわる is primarily used in phrases describing sensory disturbance (目障り 'eyesore', 耳障り 'grating sound'). Both readings convey the sense of interference or unpleasantness.

examples.meaning_tr: shoji (traditional Japanese sliding screen or door)
eyesore, something unpleasant to look at
grating, harsh or unpleasant to the ear

継.note_tr: Use kunyomi つ.ぐ for verbs meaning 'to inherit/continue.' Onyomi けい forms compounds like 継続 (continuation) and 継承 (succession). The prefix ままー means 'step-/foster-' in family relations (継母 'stepmother').

examples.meaning_tr: to inherit; to succeed; to continue
to refill; to replenish; to add more to

筋.note_tr: The on'yomi きん is used in modern vocabulary related to muscles and anatomy (筋肉, 筋トレ). The kun'yomi すじ is used for abstract or idiomatic meanings, such as the plot of a story or the phrase 筋が通る (makes sense).

闘.note_tr: The onyomi (とう) typically appears in compounds like 戦闘 (combat) and 格闘 (grappling). The kunyomi (たたかう) forms the standalone verb 闘う (to fight). The second kunyomi reading あらそ.う emphasizes competing or quarreling rather than fighting.

examples.meaning_tr: to fight; to battle; to combat
to struggle hard; to fight valiantly; to strive

葬.note_tr: This kanji primarily appears in the onyomi (そう) reading in formal compounds related to funeral ceremonies and burial practices. The kunyomi (ほうむる) is less common in everyday contexts but appears in literary or formal expressions meaning 'to bury.'

避.note_tr: The kunyomi さ.ける is used for everyday verbs like 避ける (to avoid). The onyomi ひ appears primarily in compound words such as 避難 (evacuation) and 回避 (evasion). The reading よ.ける is an alternate kunyomi, less common in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to avoid looking at, to avert one's eyes

meanings_tr: To preside over, to govern, to manage
司.note_tr: The onyomi し is used in most modern compounds (司会, 司法, 司書). The kunyomi つかさどる (to preside over) is rare in contemporary usage. Distinguish from 裁 (judge/referee), which focuses on judgment rather than direction.

康.note_tr: 康 appears primarily in formal and medical compounds using its onyomi こう. The most common everyday word containing this kanji is 健康 (health), which pairs this kanji's sense of wellness with 健 (robust) to mean "good health."

善.note_tr: The kanji 善 typically appears in formal or ethical contexts, primarily using the on-reading ぜん in compounds. The kun-reading よい/いい is rarely used in modern Japanese; for everyday "good," use the simple adjective いい instead.

examples.meaning_tr: Good and evil (common in anime and manga)

逮.note_tr: This kanji appears almost exclusively in formal and legal contexts, with the compound 逮捕 (arrest) being by far the most common usage. Although marked JLPT N1, you'll encounter it frequently in crime-related anime, manga, news reports, and historical texts.

迫.note_tr: The kun-yomi せまる is used for the standalone verb 迫る (to draw near, to press someone, to be imminent), while the on-yomi はく appears mainly inside two-kanji compound words like 迫力 or 脅迫. Note the similar-looking kanji 追 (おう, "to chase"); both share the 辶 radical but have different right-hand parts, so don't mix them up.

examples.meaning_tr: to draw near; to press (someone) urgently; to be imminent
power, force, impact (e.g. of a scene or performance)
imminence, urgency, being pressed for time

惑.note_tr: The on'yomi わく appears primarily in compound words (迷惑 'nuisance', 惑星 'planet'), while the kun'yomi まど.う is used for the verb meaning 'to be perplexed or bewildered.' Both readings are stable and unlikely to be confused with other kanji.

meanings_tr: Die (of emperors; archaic usage in 崩御)
崩.note_tr: The on'yomi ほう appears in formal compounds like 崩壊 (collapse), while the kun'yomi くずれる/くずす describes gradual crumbling or breakdown of structures, systems, or health. Distinguish from 壊 (to break/destroy), which implies more sudden or general damage rather than structural/systemic collapse.

examples.meaning_tr: Collapse; disintegration of a system, society, or structure
To crumble; to fall apart; to break down
Shape becomes distorted; form falls apart
Physical health deteriorates; body breaks down

examples.reading: せかいかんがほうかいする
examples.meaning_tr: Worldview collapses; perspective shatters (frequent in anime and manga)

紀.note_tr: 紀 (き) primarily appears in Sino-Japanese compounds related to history and time periods. Most commonly encountered in 世紀 (century), which occurs frequently in everyday contexts including history, anime, and media. Historical dating terms like 紀元前 (BC) and 紀元後 (AD) are standard usage.

examples.meaning_tr: era; epoch; the beginning of an era

聴.note_tr: The kunyomi 聴く (to listen/hear) is the everyday form. The onyomi ちょう appears in formal compounds like 聴衆 (audience) and 聴診 (medical examination). This kanji should not be confused with the far more common 聞く (to listen/ask), which uses different kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: auscultation; medical examination by listening with a stethoscope
observing a trial or class as a visitor; auditing

脱.note_tr: ぬぐ and ぬげる (kunyomi) refer to physically removing items, especially clothing. だつ (onyomi) appears in compounds with abstract meanings like 'escape' or 'get free from.' Note the difference: 脱ぐ is specific action (taking off), while 脱出 emphasizes the concept of breaking free.

examples.meaning_tr: to remove, to take off (clothes, shoes)
to come off, to be removed
prison break, jailbreak (common in anime and games)

級.note_tr: The kanji 級 is always read as きゅう (on'yomi) and appears in compound words to indicate proficiency levels, grades, or classifications. Commonly found in language learning contexts (初級 beginner, 中級 intermediate, 上級 advanced), school systems, and product descriptions (高級 luxury).

博.note_tr: The はく reading is standard in most words (博士, 博物館). The ばく reading appears in specialized, less common contexts such as 博打 (gambling). The core meaning, "broad" or "extensive", underlies all uses, including 博学 (broad knowledge) and terms for institutions that encompass wide collections.

締.note_tr: Transitive 締める (to tighten/close/fasten) differs from intransitive 締まる (to become tight/close). Common usage includes the everyday compound 締切 (deadline) and formal onyomi words like 締結 (to conclude an agreement).

examples.meaning_tr: To close, to shut; to become tight (intransitive verb)
To close, to fasten, to tighten (transitive verb)
To keep one's mouth shut; to remain silent

救.note_tr: The kunyomi すくう is used for the direct verb meaning 'to save' or 'to rescue.' The onyomi きゅう appears in compounds related to emergency and rescue services, such as 救急車 (ambulance) and 救助 (rescue operation).

meanings_tr: To grasp, grip, or hold firmly
To persist stubbornly; to be tenacious or obstinate
To administer or execute (an action or policy)
To hold onto or cling to
執.note_tr: The on'yomi しゅう (shū) typically appears in abstract nouns related to persistence or attachment (執着, 執念), while しつ (shitsu) is commonly used in compound verbs and concrete actions (執筆, 執行). The kun'yomi と.る is rare in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Writing; authorship; the act of writing (a book, article, etc.)
Attachment; obsession; clinging (to something emotionally or mentally)
Execution; enforcement; implementation (of a law, policy, or plan)
Persistent desire; obsession; strong determination to achieve something
Butler; steward; a male servant who manages a household

房.note_tr: The kanji 房 has two readings: ぼう (mainly in compounds like 茶房 'café') and ふさ (for tassels, bunches, or locks of hair). The ふさ reading is more common in contemporary Japanese.

撤.note_tr: This kanji typically appears in formal contexts, politics, military, business, and law. In compounds, the on'yomi often becomes てっ (with consonant assimilation), as in 撤退 and 撤回. Commonly seen in anime/games with military or political scenarios.

examples.meaning_tr: Removal (of an obstacle, structure, or roadblock)
Withdrawal (of a statement, claim, or proposal)
Withdrawal, breaking camp (military or event context)
Abolition, repeal (of a law, rule, or system)

削.note_tr: On'yomi (さく) appears in formal/modern compounds like 削減 (reduction) and 削除 (deletion). Kun'yomi kezuru is most common in daily use, seen in 削る (to whittle/shave) and 鉛筆削り (pencil sharpener). Other kun'yomi readings are less frequently encountered in everyday contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: to whittle, to shave, to carve
shaved dried bonito (common ingredient in Japanese cooking)

密.note_tr: On'yomi (みつ) is commonly used in compounds like 密度 (density) and 親密 (intimate); kun'yomi (ひそか) appears in 密かに (secretly) and is very frequent in anime. Note that the compound 秘密 (secret) is one of the most common kanji words for beginners.

examples.meaning_tr: Secret; extremely common in anime and manga
Secretly, on the sly, in secret

措.note_tr: On'yomi そ dominates in modern Japanese, appearing primarily in 措置 (measures/action taken). Kun'yomi お.く is archaic; the modern equivalent おく is written with 置 instead. The character 措 appears mainly in formal and official contexts.

志.note_tr: The onyomi し appears in compounds like 志望 (aspiration) and 意志 (will), while kunyomi こころざす/こころざし serve as the verb and noun forms respectively. Though similar to 思 (think) and 願 (wish) in meaning, 志 specifically emphasizes intention and aspiration rather than mere thinking or wishing.

載.note_tr: ON-yomi (さい) appears mainly in compounds like 掲載 'publish' and 搭載 'equip'; KUN-yomi (の.る/の.せる) appears in patterns like '新聞に載る' (appear in newspaper) and '情報を載せる' (post information). Often confused with 乗 (ride), which emphasizes personal transportation, while 載 emphasizes placement and installation.

examples.meaning_tr: To appear in a newspaper, to be in the news
To appear in a magazine, to be published in a magazine
To post/place information, to upload, to list
Serialization, serial publication (of a manga/story), (to) serialize

陣.note_tr: 陣 is read only as じん (jin, on'yomi) and appears almost exclusively in compounds. It is frequently found in historical contexts, military narratives, and anime/manga depicting battles or conflicts.

我.note_tr: The on'yomi が is most common in modern compounds like 我慢 (patience); the kun'yomi われ (ware) appears in formal/archaic 我々 (we). The prefix わが- (waga-) marks possession (my, our). Distinguish from 自 (self) and 私 (I), which carry different connotations, 我 emphasizes strong personal identity or ego.

為.note_tr: 為 most commonly means 'for' (reading: ため) and appears in everyday phrases like そのため (therefore). When used in compounds, it often uses the onyomi い, as in 行為 (act/conduct).

examples.meaning_tr: to make, to do, to accomplish
for the sake of, in order to

抑.note_tr: The kunyomi おさえる (osae-ru) is used in everyday contexts meaning 'to hold down,' while the onyomi よく appears mainly in compounds like 抑制 (suppression). This is an N1 kanji, so beginners typically encounter it through common phrases rather than standalone characters.

examples.meaning_tr: To hold down; to suppress; to restrain

examples.reading: おんりょうをおさえる

examples.meaning_tr: To keep prices down; to hold down costs

幕.note_tr: The onyomi ま-く is used when 幕 stands alone or in phrases like 幕が上がる (curtain rises). The onyomi ば-く is used in many compounds such as 幕府 (shogunate) and 開幕 (opening). The kunyomi と-ばり is an archaic, poetic reading rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: the curtain rises; a show or performance starts
the curtain falls; a show or performance ends
shogunate; the feudal military government that ruled Japan historically
opening; the beginning of a performance, match, or tournament
first act; the opening scene of a play or dramatic performance

染.note_tr: The kunyomi そ.める (active) and そ.まる (passive) express dyeing or staining directly. The reading し.み refers to physical stains or marks. The onyomi せん appears in compound words with extended meanings such as 感染 (infection) and 汚染 (pollution).

奈.note_tr: This kanji appears almost exclusively in the proper noun 'Nara' (奈良), where it contributes the on'yomi reading な. The classical kun'yomi いかん ('what') is archaic and rarely seen in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Nara (prefecture in central Japan, famous for temples and deer)
Nara Park (popular tourist destination with sacred deer and temples)
Nara Period (8th-century era of Japanese history, 710–794)

傷.note_tr: The kunyomi きず is used for physical wounds and scars. The kunyomi いためる/いたむ describes damage or deterioration, especially of food. The onyomi しょう appears in formal or legal compounds such as 傷害 (bodily injury).

examples.meaning_tr: to be hurt; to get wounded

択.note_tr: The onyomi たく appears in compound words like 選択 (selection) and 採択 (adoption). The kunyomi えらぶ is rarely written with this kanji alone (択ぶ) in modern Japanese; the everyday verb "to choose" is almost always written as 選ぶ instead, so you'll mainly encounter 択 in two-kanji compounds.

examples.meaning_tr: adoption (of a proposal, plan, or textbook)

秀.note_tr: The onyomi しゅう dominates compound words (秀才 'prodigy', 秀逸 'excellence'), while the kunyomi ひいでる forms the verb 秀でる ('to excel'). You'll encounter this kanji often in manga and anime when describing talented characters or exceptional works.

examples.meaning_tr: To excel, to stand out, to surpass

徴.note_tr: The reading ちょう is used in almost all common compounds (特徴, 象徴, 徴収, 徴兵); the reading ち is rare and mostly appears in older/formal vocabulary. The kunyomi しるし (meaning "sign/mark") is literary and rarely used alone in modern Japanese. Be careful not to confuse 徴 with the visually similar kanji 微 (meaning "slight, minute"); they look alike but have completely different meanings and readings.

examples.meaning_tr: sign, symptom (e.g. of an illness or change)

meanings_tr: To play an instrument, to pluck
弾.note_tr: The onyomi だん appears most often in compounds like 弾丸 (bullet) and 弾力 (elasticity), while the kunyomi ひ.く means 'to play' for stringed instruments. Other kunyomi relate to elastic or bouncy motions (はず.む) or sharp snapping actions (はじ.く, はじ.ける).

examples.meaning_tr: To play an instrument; to pluck strings

償.note_tr: The onyomi しょう is used in most compound words (代償, 補償, 報償, 弁償). The kunyomi つぐなう functions as a standalone verb meaning to make amends or compensate for something.

examples.meaning_tr: to make amends; to atone; to compensate

功.note_tr: The reading こう is by far the most common in modern Japanese; the alternative readings く and いさお are quite rare and unnecessary for beginners. This kanji frequently appears in words describing success, achievements, and military or heroic feats, contexts common in anime, history, and sports narratives.

拠.note_tr: The onyomi きょ typically appears in compounds meaning 'base' or 'stronghold' (like 拠点), while こ is used in 'grounds' or 'evidence' contexts (like 根拠, 証拠). The kunyomi よ.る means 'to rely on' or 'to lean on,' appearing in words like 拠り所.

examples.meaning_tr: Foothold, support, something to rely on

秘.note_tr: The onyomi ひ is used in compound words like 秘密 (secret). The kunyomi forms ひ.める (to hide/conceal in verbs) and ひそ.か (secretly in adverbial phrases) are commonly seen. Do not confuse this kanji with 隠す (to hide), which uses the different kanji 隠.

examples.meaning_tr: to hide, to conceal (in one's heart)
secret technique, hidden skill, special move

拒.note_tr: The onyomi reading (きょ) is primarily used in compound words like 拒否 (refusal) and 拒絶 (rejection). The kunyomi reading (こば.む) is used in the verb form 拒む (to refuse).

examples.meaning_tr: To refuse, to reject, to turn down

刑.note_tr: Formal legal kanji used primarily in official contexts. Only the onyomi けい is used; no kunyomi. Frequently appears in crime dramas and legal discussions, making it useful for anime, manga, and crime genre content.

塚.note_tr: The kunyomi つか is the primary reading in modern Japanese; the -づか suffix form is very common in place names and surnames. The onyomi ちょう is rarely used in contemporary texts. This kanji typically appears in historical and archaeological contexts, especially when referring to ancient burial sites or earthen mounds.

致.note_tr: The onyomi reading (ち) is predominant in modern Japanese, appearing mainly in compound words. The kunyomi reading (いた.す) is used primarily in formal or polite speech, especially in the phrase いたします (I will do/shall do).

examples.meaning_tr: to do; to cause (formal or humble form)

繰.note_tr: The kunyomi く.る is used in most common compounds, especially 繰返す (to repeat) and 繰越 (carryover). This kanji almost always appears as part of compound words rather than standing alone.

尾.note_tr: Use kunyomi (お) when referring to a tail as a noun or by itself; use onyomi (び) in compound words like 尾行 (tailing) and formal/scientific terms. This kanji is frequently seen in anime with animal characters and in cooking when describing whole fish presentations.

examples.meaning_tr: Served whole with head and tail (used in food/cooking contexts)

描.note_tr: The kunyomi えが.く is used for everyday drawing and sketching activities, especially popular in manga and anime contexts. The onyomi びょう appears in formal compounds like 描写 (depiction) and 描画 (graphics). Both readings convey the core sense of visually representing or capturing something through drawing or written depiction.

鈴.note_tr: The kunyomi すず is standard for the standalone noun and common compounds, including the widespread surname Suzuki (鈴木). The onyomi り appears mainly in compounds like wind chime (風鈴). Distinguished from 鐘 (かね/しょう), which refers to larger bells or gongs.

examples.meaning_tr: bell cricket (an insect known for its chirping)

盤.note_tr: 盤 uses only onyomi reading (ばん) and typically appears in compounds related to games (碁盤, 将棋盤) or records (音盤). No kunyomi reading exists.

項.note_tr: The onyomi こう appears in formal/written compounds meaning "item," "clause," or "term" (common in legal, academic, and math contexts, e.g. documents or contracts). The kunyomi うなじ is a standalone reading meaning "nape of the neck," though this word is more often written in kana alone in everyday text.

examples.meaning_tr: item, entry (e.g. on a list or form)
essential points, outline (e.g. of an exam or event)
clause, article (in a law or contract)

喪.note_tr: The kunyomi も is used in compounds related to mourning rituals and attire (喪中 mourning period, 喪服 mourning clothes). The onyomi そう appears in more formal, literary contexts such as 喪失 (loss). This kanji is formal and deals exclusively with serious contexts involving death and bereavement.

examples.meaning_tr: To mourn, to observe a period of mourning
Chief mourner, head of the bereaved family at a funeral

伴.note_tr: 伴う (ともなう) is the most frequently used form in everyday Japanese, meaning "to accompany" or "to occur together with." The onyomi readings はん and ばん appear primarily in formal compounds like 伴侶 (spouse/partner) and 伴奏 (musical accompaniment), making them useful for anime, manga, and music contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: To accompany; to occur together with; to be accompanied by
Musical accompaniment; backing music or instrumental support
Spouse; life partner; companion (often appears in anime and literature)
Going together; being accompanied by; traveling with someone
Running alongside; pacing; supporting from the side

養.note_tr: The kunyomi 養う emphasizes deliberate nurturing or raising (a child, animal). The onyomi よう and りょう appear mainly in compounds. Distinguish 養 from 育つ (grow naturally), 養 is about actively supporting development.

examples.meaning_tr: to raise, to foster, to support (a person or animal)
training, development, fostering (of skills or people)

meanings_tr: To be suspended, to depend on
懸.note_tr: The kunyomi かける (transitive) and かかる (intransitive) express everyday actions, to hang something or to be hanging. The onyomi けん appears in formal compounds like 懸念 (concern) and 懸命 (earnest effort). This kanji pairs naturally with action verbs and abstract nouns in both written and spoken contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: To hang, to suspend (transitive); to risk or stake
To hang, to be suspended; to depend on, to rely on

街.note_tr: Kunyomi 'machi' is the most common reading for standalone use, giving the basic meaning of 'town' or 'city.' Onyomi 'gai' typically appears in compound words like 街道 (highway) and 商店街 (shopping street). The context usually makes the reading choice clear.

examples.meaning_tr: Town; a place with buildings and streets
Shopping street; a street lined with shops and restaurants
Street corner; where two streets meet
Street lamp; a light mounted on streets
Highway; a major road or street
Bustling district; a lively area full of shops and entertainment

契.note_tr: The onyomi けい dominates modern usage, especially in business and legal contexts. The kunyomi ちぎ.る (to break/tear an agreement) is archaic and rarely encountered in contemporary Japanese.

掲.note_tr: As a kunyomi verb (掲げる), it means to raise or hold up something visibly, such as a flag or sign. With onyomi readings in compounds (掲示, 掲載), it means to display or publish information, commonly seen in notices and announcements.

examples.meaning_tr: publication; to be published; to be featured (in a magazine or newspaper)
to raise; to hold up; to display; to hoist
a notice; a bulletin; an announcement

躍.note_tr: The kunyomi おど.る is used for the standalone verb "to dance/leap"; the onyomi やく appears in formal compounds like 躍進 (rapid progress) and 躍動 (dynamism). The radical 足 (foot) helps with recall.

examples.meaning_tr: to spring out, to surge forth

棄.note_tr: The on-reading き appears primarily in compound words (放棄, 廃棄, 棄権). The kun-reading す.てる is less common than the similar kanji 捨 (す.てる); 棄 implies more formal or deliberate abandonment, while 捨 is used for casual discarding or everyday disposal.

examples.meaning_tr: Abandonment, desertion (of a person or duty)
Dumping, throwing away (often in illegal disposal context)
To throw away, to discard (kun-reading form, less common than 捨てる)

邸.note_tr: The onyomi reading てい dominates in modern Japanese compounds like 邸宅 (mansion) and 官邸 (official residence). The kunyomi やしき is rarely seen today; use 屋敷 instead for everyday reference to a house or property.

examples.meaning_tr: Within the residence, on the estate grounds

縮.note_tr: The on-reading しゅく (shuku) appears in compound words like 縮小 (shrinkage) and 圧縮 (compression). The kun-readings using ちぢ are more common in verbs, 縮む (to shrink) and 縮める (to make smaller) describe the action directly. This kanji frequently describes fabric wrinkles, size reduction, or data compression.

examples.meaning_tr: To shrink, to contract, to become smaller
To shorten, to reduce, to make smaller

還.note_tr: The kunyomi かえる expresses the action of returning or coming back (e.g., 還る 'to return'). The onyomi かん appears in compounds where the meaning emphasizes cyclical return or restoration (e.g., 還元 'reduction,' 還暦 '60th birthday').

examples.meaning_tr: Traffic; passage; going back and forth

属.note_tr: Primary reading is ぞく (to belong, be affiliated). The on'yomi しょく appears in formal compounds like 所属. This kanji is frequently used in gaming and anime contexts to describe character attributes or element types.

examples.meaning_tr: attribute, trait, property (especially character elements in games and anime, fire attribute, water attribute, etc.)
to belong to, to be affiliated with

慮.note_tr: Appears almost exclusively in onyomi compounds (りょ) meaning 'consideration' or 'reflection.' The kunyomi forms (おもんぱく.る, おもんぱか.る) are archaic literary expressions, rarely seen in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: unexpected, unforeseen (as in 不慮の事故 'unexpected accident')

枠.note_tr: 枠 has only the kunyomi reading わく. It is used for both literal frames (picture frames, window frames) and figurative frameworks (time slots, system structures).

恵.note_tr: The kunyomi readings (めぐみ/めぐむ) are most common in everyday speech and typically describe blessings or bounty from nature, while the onyomi reading けい appears in formal compounds like 恩恵 (benefit). This kanji often expresses grace from either divine or natural sources.

examples.meaning_tr: Bounty of nature, gifts of nature

露.note_tr: The kunyomi つゆ (tsuyu) primarily refers to dew and appears in nature-related compounds. The onyomi ろ is used in more formal compounds like 露出 (exposure) or 露骨 (frank). Russia is now typically written in katakana as ロシア.

沖.note_tr: The kunyomi おき is the most frequently used reading in everyday contexts, particularly in maritime vocabulary. This kanji is useful for students interested in travel, nature, and food, appearing commonly in Japanese geography (Okinawa), fishing terminology, and food preparation methods.

examples.meaning_tr: Salt-dried fish preparation; a traditional Japanese preservation method

緩.note_tr: Kunyomi readings (ゆる-) dominate everyday speech; かん appears mainly in formal compounds. The transitive pair ゆる.める (to loosen) and intransitive ゆる.む (to become loose) are both common in conversation and media.

examples.meaning_tr: To loosen, to ease, to relax (transitive)
To loosen, to become loose, to ease (intransitive)

節.note_tr: Onyomi せつ appears in formal compounds: 季節 (season), 節度 (restraint/moderation), 節約 (economizing). Kunyomi ふし or ふしぶし refers to physical joints, knots (in bamboo/wood), or turning points in time.

examples.meaning_tr: Joints, knots; multiple points or sections

需.note_tr: This kanji uses only the on'yomi reading (じゅ) and appears primarily in formal or business contexts. The most common word is 需要 (じゅよう, demand/need), frequently seen in economic discussions.

examples.reading: きょうきゅうとじゅよう

射.note_tr: The onyomi しゃ dominates modern compounds like 射撃 (shooting) and 射手 (archer). The kunyomi さ.す appears mainly in poetic or literary contexts meaning 'to shine', common in anime and manga descriptions of light scenes. This kanji is frequent in action anime and game terminology.

examples.meaning_tr: Archer; marksman; also Sagittarius zodiac sign
Light shines through; sunlight streams in
Sunlight pours in; daylight breaks through
Shooting range; effective range of a weapon

購.note_tr: The kanji 購 (こう) is used mainly in formal or written contexts and almost always appears in compound words with other kanji. There is no kunyomi reading for this kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: subscription (to a magazine, newspaper, or online service)

揮.note_tr: The kunyomi ふるう is used for direct waving or brandishing actions; the onyomi き appears in formal compounds like 指揮 (conducting) and 揮発 (evaporation). Distinguish from the more common 振 (ふる), which is more casual; 揮 suggests a more deliberate or flourishing motion.

examples.meaning_tr: to wave; to brandish; to swing

充.note_tr: The on'yomi じゅう dominates in modern compounds such as 充電 (charging) and 充実 (fulfilling). The kun'yomi あてる appears in formal or less frequent expressions like 充てる (to allocate). Note the distinction: 充 emphasizes active filling or supply, while 満 emphasizes being completely full or satisfied.

examples.meaning_tr: fulfilling, enriching, substantial; full and meaningful
to allocate, to assign, to devote to a purpose
fulfillment, satisfaction, meeting of needs or desires
bloodshot eyes, congestion (medical term, common in manga)

貢.note_tr: The こう reading is standard in modern Japanese compounds like 貢献 (contribution). The みつぐ kun'yomi is used for the classical sense of 'to offer tribute' and commonly appears in historical, fantasy, and period anime. The く reading is archaic and rarely seen in contemporary Japanese.

鹿.note_tr: The kunyomi reading しか (shika) is the standard, everyday word for 'deer' and is most commonly used. The onyomi reading ろく (roku) is less frequent and appears mainly in compound words or medicinal/traditional contexts. This kanji also frequently appears in Japanese place names like 鹿児島 (Kagoshima), where it uses the か reading.

examples.meaning_tr: Nara deer (the famous semi-wild deer in Nara, Japan)

meanings_tr: to reject, to refuse, to dismiss
却.note_tr: The onyomi reading きゃく commonly appears in formal compound words like 却下 (rejection) and 退却 (retreat). The kunyomi readings (しりぞく, しりぞける) are less frequent in modern Japanese but still used to mean "to withdraw" or "to refuse." The kanji emphasizes deliberate withdrawal or formal rejection.

examples.meaning_tr: retreat, withdrawal; to withdraw (often used in military/game contexts)
to reject, to refuse, to push away

端.note_tr: The reading はし is most common in everyday contexts, meaning 'edge' or 'tip'. The onyomi たん appears in technical compounds like 端末 (terminal). Similar kanji 橋 (はし, bridge) has the same pronunciation but different meaning and different stroke patterns.

賃.note_tr: Onyomi reading チン (ちん) only; no kunyomi. Almost always appears in compounds. The meaning shifts based on context: 家賃 refers to house rent, 賃金 to wages/salary, and 賃貸 to rental arrangements. Note: 賃 is rarely used as a standalone character in modern Japanese.

獲.note_tr: The onyomi かく is mainly used in formal compounds like 獲得 (to acquire). The kunyomi える appears in simpler verb forms like 獲る (to catch). Note: 奪 (take by force) has overlapping meaning but implies forceful taking.

examples.meaning_tr: To acquire, to obtain, to gain

examples.reading: しょうをかくとくする
examples.meaning_tr: To win a prize, to obtain an award

郡.note_tr: The on'yomi ぐん is used in all modern Japanese compounds and place names. The kun'yomi こおり is archaic and rarely appears in contemporary texts. The kanji often identifies rural administrative districts in Japanese geography and historical contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: North County (common in Japanese place names)

併.note_tr: The kunyomi あわ.せる (as in 併せて) appears more frequently in everyday conversation than the onyomi へい- compounds. Onyomi forms typically appear in formal or technical contexts, such as 併用 (concurrent use) in technology or medicine, and 併設 (having both facilities together).

examples.meaning_tr: together with; in addition to; at the same time
concurrent use; using two things together
having two facilities together; established concurrently

徹.note_tr: 徹 uses only the on'yomi てつ and rarely appears as a standalone character. It most commonly appears in compounds like 徹夜 (all-nighter, common in gaming and study contexts) and 徹底 (thorough/complete, frequently used in formal writing and instructions). The kanji conveys the sense of going all the way through something to completion.

examples.meaning_tr: To carry out completely, to accomplish fully

貴.note_tr: Onyomi (き) appears in formal compounds: 貴重 (precious), 貴族 (nobility). Kunyomi (たっとい, とうとい) forms the adjective 貴い (precious, noble). Note: 貴方 (あなた) is the polite pronoun for "you," while 貴様 (きさま) is a rude form popular in anime.

衝.note_tr: The onyomi reading しょう dominates in compound words describing collisions, conflicts, and impulses. The kunyomi reading つ.く is rare, appearing in specialized terms like 衝立 (folding screen).

焦.note_tr: The on'yomi (しょう) is used mainly in compound words like 焦点 (focus). The most common reading is あせ.る (to hurry/be impatient), while こ.げる refers to charring or burning in food contexts.

奪.note_tr: The kunyomi うば.う (ubaう) is used in everyday language and often describes forcibly taking something from someone. The onyomi だつ appears mainly in formal compound words (奪還, 奪取). This kanji emphasizes forceful or violent taking, not gentle transfer.

examples.meaning_tr: To rob; to seize; to take by force
To take someone's life; to cost a life
To snatch away; to wrest from someone
To be robbed; to be taken away from (passive)

災.note_tr: The on'yomi さい is predominant in modern Japanese compounds and appears in most everyday contexts. The kun'yomi わざわい (woe, misfortune) is found mainly in literary or classical texts and is rarely used in contemporary Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: To be affected by disaster; to suffer disaster damage

浦.note_tr: The kunyomi うら is far more common in modern Japanese than the onyomi ほ. This kanji primarily appears in geographical terms, place names, and in the famous fairy tale 浦島太郎 (Urashima Tarō), where it represents sheltered bays and inlets.

examples.meaning_tr: Urashima Tarō; protagonist of a famous Japanese fairy tale
Urayasu; a city in Chiba Prefecture, home to Tokyo Disney Resort

析.note_tr: 析 is almost always read せき and rarely appears as a standalone character; it dominates in compound words expressing analysis or division. Most common pairing is 分析 (analysis). Focus on the on-reading せき in compounds.

譲.note_tr: Kunyomi 譲る (yuzu-ru) is used for everyday actions of yielding or giving way; onyomi じょう appears in formal terms like 譲渡 (transfer) and 譲歩 (concession). Both readings express the core idea of passing something to another party.

examples.meaning_tr: to give up one's seat (common on trains/buses)
to yield the way, to step aside
to make concessions to each other, to compromise

称.note_tr: The onyomi しょう is used in most compounds, especially for names and formal titles (名称, 称号). The kunyomi たたえる emphasizes praising or celebrating achievements. Distinguish from 名 (name): 名 is simpler and more basic, while 称 emphasizes titles, roles, or earned reputations.

examples.meaning_tr: To call oneself, to be known as

納.note_tr: The onyomi readings のう and なっ appear mainly in compound words (like 納期, 納豆, 納得), while the kunyomi おさめる/おさまる are used in verb forms. 納豆 (natto) is a well-known food term where the なっ reading appears.

樹.note_tr: The onyomi reading じゅ is used in most compound words (樹木, 樹海, 樹立), while the kunyomi reading き appears when standing alone. This kanji refers both to the physical tree and the abstract concept of establishing in formal contexts.

挑.note_tr: The onyomi ちょう dominates modern usage in compounds like 挑戦 (challenge) and 挑発 (provocation). The kunyomi いど.む appears mainly in formal or literary contexts. For beginners, mastering 挑戦 is most valuable, as it appears frequently in sports, games, and motivational content popular in anime and manga.

examples.reading: あたらしいちょうせん

誘.note_tr: Kunyomi さそう is used for the standalone verb 誘う 'to invite or tempt'. Onyomi ゆう appears primarily in compounds like 誘導 and 誘惑. The meaning can range from friendly invitation to seductive temptation depending on context.

examples.meaning_tr: to invite; to tempt; to lure
to trigger; to provoke; to cause

meanings_tr: be mistaken for, look like, resemble
紛.note_tr: Use onyomi ふん in compounds like 紛争 (conflict) and 紛失 (loss). Use kunyomi ま- forms for verbs and adjectives: 紛らわしい (confusing), 紛れ込む (slip in), 紛れる (be mistaken for). Be careful not to confuse with 粉 (powder), which also reads ふん but means flour or powder.

examples.meaning_tr: to slip in, to sneak in, to infiltrate, to blend in
to be mistaken for, to look like, to escape notice

至.note_tr: This kanji primarily appears in compounds using the on'yomi し (shi), especially in formal or technical contexts like 至急 (urgent). The kun'yomi いた.る (itaru) is used when the character stands as a verb meaning "to reach" or "to arrive at." Frequently appears in written Japanese and formal announcements.

examples.meaning_tr: everywhere, here and there, all over

宗.note_tr: The on'yomi しゅう is most common, appearing frequently in 宗教 (religion). The on'yomi そう is used in contexts like 本宗 (main sect) and 宗家 (head of a school). The kun'yomi むね is rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Founder/Head/Master of a school or lineage (especially in traditional arts like tea ceremony or martial arts)

促.note_tr: The onyomi そく (soku) appears in formal compound words such as 促進 (promotion) and 催促 (urging). The kunyomi うなが.す (unaga.su) is the basic verb 'to urge or encourage.' Both readings are frequently used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: To urge, to encourage, to press
Small tsu (doubled consonant sound in Japanese); geminate

慎.note_tr: Use onyomi しん for compounds like 慎重 (careful), and kunyomi つつしむ/つつましい for standalone words; つつしむ means 'to be careful or refrain,' while つつましい means 'humble or modest.'

examples.meaning_tr: To be careful; to refrain from; to avoid
To be careful with one's words; to speak prudently

控.note_tr: The kunyomi ひかえる means 'to hold back or refrain' in verb form; ひかえ is the noun meaning 'spare or backup.' The onyomi こう is used in formal compounds like 控室 (waiting room).

examples.meaning_tr: To hold back, refrain from, abstain

智.note_tr: Always read as ち (onyomi only, no kunyomi). 智 overlaps in meaning with the more everyday kanji 知 (also read ち, as in 知る 'to know' or 知識 'knowledge'), but 智 tends to appear in more formal or literary compounds emphasizing deep wisdom rather than simple knowledge; you'll often spot it in fantasy game/anime lore (e.g. 叡智, 智将) and in given names.

examples.meaning_tr: profound wisdom, sagacity (often used in fantasy/RPG settings)
a brilliant tactician/general known for wisdom

握.note_tr: The kunyomi にぎる is the everyday verb form meaning "to hold firmly" or "grip." The onyomi あく mainly appears in compounds like 握手 (handshake) and 握力 (grip strength). In food contexts, 握り refers to nigiri sushi because the rice is hand-molded into shape, perfect for your food interests!

宙.note_tr: 宙 is mainly used in compound words and phrases rather than as a standalone noun. The reading ちゅう remains consistent across all common words. This kanji appears frequently in anime and manga, especially in the essential word 宇宙 (universe/cosmos).

examples.meaning_tr: Somersault; a mid-air flip or tumble
To float in mid-air; to hover
Suspended in mid-air; undecided or left hanging

俊.note_tr: This kanji is used almost exclusively with the onyomi reading しゅん. It frequently appears in names (e.g., 俊介 Shunsuke) and formal compounds denoting exceptional talent or ability. The character emphasizes superiority and brilliance.

examples.meaning_tr: Talented person; a capable or able person
Great man; superior person; outstanding figure
Shunsuke (common given name meaning excellent and helpful)

銭.note_tr: The on'yomi せん is most common in modern Japanese, especially in the term 銭湯. The kunyomi ぜに appears less frequently but shows up in compounds like 小銭 (small coins).

渋.note_tr: Kunyomi forms (shibu-i, shibu-ru) express astringent or reluctant meanings; onyomi じゅう appears in 渋滞. Note that 渋い can describe taste, attitude, or aesthetic style depending on context.

銃.note_tr: 銃 is read as じゅう (onyomi) in virtually all modern compounds; the kunyomi つつ is archaic and rarely used. Common in action anime, manga, video games, and historical contexts.

操.note_tr: The onyomi そう is typically used in formal and technical compounds (e.g., 操作 'operation'). The kunyomi あやつる emphasizes control through manipulation, as seen in 操り人形 'puppet.' Especially useful in technology, gaming, and anime contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Operation; control; manipulation (of machines, systems, devices)
Steering; piloting; maneuvering (of aircraft, ships, vehicles)
Puppet; marionette; a person being controlled by someone else

meanings_tr: To bring along, To have with you
To be involved in, To engage in
携.note_tr: The onyomi 携帯 (けいたい) is overwhelmingly common in modern Japanese, especially in technology contexts. The kunyomi readings 携える and 携わる are more literary or formal; use 携える when "carrying/bringing along" and 携わる when "being involved in." Easily confused with 持つ (carry/hold, physical possession) versus 携わる (participate/be involved, more abstract).

examples.meaning_tr: Mobile phone, Cell phone, Portable device
To be involved in, To take part in, To work with
To carry, To bring along, To hold
For portable use, For mobile use

診.note_tr: The onyomi しん dominates in compound words (診断, 診察) which are most common in everyday use. The kunyomi み.る appears in verbs like 診る (to examine), but is less frequently used. This kanji is essential medical terminology.

examples.meaning_tr: to be examined by a doctor; to see a doctor

託.note_tr: The onyomi たく appears in formal compounds like 委託 (commission). The kunyomi 託す is common in narratives and speech for genuine entrustment, while かこつ/かこつける means to use as an excuse or pretend.

examples.meaning_tr: to entrust, to place in someone's care

撮.note_tr: The kunyomi と.る is standard for the everyday verb 撮る (to take photos/shoot video). The onyomi さつ appears in formal compounds like 撮影 (photography, cinematography), common in anime/manga and technology contexts. The third kunyomi つま.む (to pinch) is archaic and rarely seen in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to take a photo, to shoot (video)

誕.note_tr: This kanji uses only the onyomi reading たん with no kunyomi. It is most commonly encountered in compound words, especially 誕生日 (birthday), which appears very frequently in anime and manga.

侵.note_tr: The onyomi しん appears primarily in compound words like 侵入 (invasion) and 侵略 (conquest), while the kunyomi おかす is the base verb form. Both convey unauthorized entry or violation.

括.note_tr: The kunyomi くくる describes the physical action of tying or binding objects together. The onyomi かつ appears primarily in compounds and formal contexts with meanings related to gathering, collecting, or arresting.

謝.note_tr: The kunyomi あやまる is used when 謝 acts as a standalone verb ('to apologize'). The onyomi しゃ appears mainly in compound words, particularly those expressing gratitude (感謝) or formal apology (謝罪). Both 'apologize' and 'thank' relate to acknowledging another's action or one's own responsibility.

examples.meaning_tr: thank-you gift, honorarium, token of appreciation

駆.note_tr: The kunyomi かける is most common in verbs and compounds (駆ける 'to run'), while the onyomi く appears mainly in Sino-Japanese noun compounds like 駆動 (operation) and 駆除 (elimination). The reading かる is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to run; to gallop; to dash
running; quick pace; at a gallop
to rush in; to dash into

透.note_tr: Onyomi 透(とう) typically appears in formal, technical, or compound terms (透明, 透視); kunyomi 透(す)く and 透(す)かす suit everyday, descriptive contexts. 透き通る describes crystalline clarity, often seen in anime scenes with water or glass. Not easily confused with other kanji, but 薄 (うすい, thin) differs, it implies thinness rather than transparency.

examples.meaning_tr: Transparent; clear (commonly used for glass, water, or air)
To show through; to be see-through (describes clothing or thin materials)
The water is crystal clear (describes pristine, perfectly clear water, common in travel and nature contexts)
Translucency; light transmission (used in art, photography, and materials science)

津.note_tr: The kunyomi reading つ is far more common in modern Japanese than the onyomi しん. This kanji is most frequently encountered in the compound 津波 (tsunami), which appears regularly in anime, manga, and nature-related content. It also appears in many Japanese place names and classical literature.

examples.meaning_tr: Tsunami; a large ocean wave caused by earthquakes or underwater eruptions
Port; harbor; a place where ships dock and cargo is loaded or unloaded
Every port and inlet; every corner of the land (classical/literary expression)

壁.note_tr: The kunyomi かべ is used for everyday 'wall'; the onyomi へき appears in specialized compounds like 壁画 (mural).

examples.meaning_tr: Walls have ears (idiom; secrets are easily overheard)
Hitting a ball against a wall (sports practice method)

稲.note_tr: The kunyomi いね and いな- are used in everyday compounds, while onyomi とう appears in formal terms like 稲作 (rice cultivation). The word 稲妻 (lightning) is etymologically interesting: 妻 originally meant 'brightness', not 'wife'.

仮.note_tr: Most words use the on'yomi か (as in 仮想, 仮説). The kun'yomi かり is less common and appears in phrases like 仮住まい. The core concept is something "not real" or "not permanent."

裂.note_tr: Use the transitive reading さ.く (saku) to actively tear or rip something; use the intransitive さ.ける (sakeru) when describing something that splits or tears on its own. The character also appears frequently in compound words with the onyomi reading れつ (retsu).

敏.note_tr: The onyomi びん is standard in modern compounds (敏感, 敏速, 敏腕). The kunyomi さとい, meaning 'clever' or 'wise,' is rarely used in contemporary Japanese and appears mainly in classical or historical texts.

是.note_tr: This is a formal, classical kanji rarely used in modern Japanese. The kunyomi readings (these, this, here) are typically written in hiragana instead. In modern usage, 是 primarily appears in compounds like 是非 (ぜひ, meaning "by all means" or "right and wrong"), which is common in manga dialogue and formal writing.

排.note_tr: 排 uses only the onyomi はい and appears mainly in compounds about removal, exclusion, and emission. Related kanji 除 (remove) and 棄 (discard) share some meanings but are used in different contexts.

裕.note_tr: This kanji uses only the onyomi reading ゆう, most commonly appearing in compounds like 裕福. No kunyomi reading is standard; this kanji typically appears in formal or literary contexts and in personal names.

examples.meaning_tr: Affluence, wealth; being wealthy or well-off
Abundant, ample, plentiful, having room to spare

堅.note_tr: The kunyomi かた.い is the most common in everyday speech and adjective forms, expressing physical hardness or figurative firmness. The onyomi けん appears in formal compounds (like 堅実, 堅持) used in written contexts and abstract meaning.

examples.meaning_tr: To harden; to strengthen; to make firm
Sound; reliable; solid (of plans, decisions, character)
Firm conviction; unwavering adherence to a belief or principle

訳.note_tr: Use やく in compound words related to translating or interpreting (like 翻訳 or 通訳), and use わけ as a standalone word meaning "reason" or "circumstance" (like in 訳 or 言い訳). Don't confuse 訳 with 約 (やく, meaning "approximately" or "promise"); they look similar but have different meanings.

examples.meaning_tr: translation (e.g. of a book, anime subtitles, or game text)
to translate (a sentence, word, or text)
interpretation / interpreter (spoken language, e.g. at a concert or sports event)
translator (person who translates, e.g. manga or novels)

芝.note_tr: Refers to grass or lawns in nature contexts. The kunyomi (しば) appears in 芝生 (lawn), while the onyomi (し) appears in 人工芝 (artificial turf).

綱.note_tr: The kunyomi つな refers to literal rope or cord; the onyomi こう appears in compounds like 綱領 (principles). The word 綱引き (tug of war) appears frequently in anime and manga school scenes.

典.note_tr: This kanji primarily uses the てん (ten) reading and is typically found in formal or academic compound words like 典型 (typical case) and 古典 (classics). The でん reading is rare in modern usage.

賀.note_tr: This kanji is mainly used in formal congratulatory contexts, particularly for New Year greetings (like 賀状). It's read as が and rarely appears in casual, everyday conversation.

扱.note_tr: The kunyomi 扱う (あつかう) and its noun form 扱い (あつかい) are by far the most common in modern Japanese, used to mean 'handle/deal with' in various contexts, handling objects, discussing topics, or treating people. The onyomi readings (そう, きゅう) and less common kunyomi (こ.く) are rare in everyday speech and not recommended for beginners.

examples.meaning_tr: to handle; to deal with; to treat
handling; treatment; the way something is dealt with
to handle/treat carefully; to take care of

顧.note_tr: The kunyomi かえりみる is used for the verb 顧みる (to review or look back). The onyomi こ appears in business and formal compounds like 顧客 (customer) and 顧問 (advisor).

examples.meaning_tr: to look back on, to review, to reconsider
to examine oneself, to look back on oneself
to look back on the past, to reflect on the past

弘.note_tr: The onyomi こう is primarily used in Buddhist or formal contexts (e.g., 弘法, 弘大); the kunyomi ひろ appears mainly in proper nouns like place names and given names. Avoid confusing this kanji with 広 (also meaning 'wide'), which is much more commonly used in everyday language.

examples.meaning_tr: Kobo Daishi; the founder of Shingon Buddhism and a revered historical figure in Japan
Hirosaki; a city in Aomori Prefecture famous for its cherry blossoms and castle
a common male given name (frequently seen in Japanese media like anime and manga)

看.note_tr: 看 (かん) is primarily used in onyomi compounds, especially in medical and care-related contexts. The kunyomi み.る is rare; the standard kanji for "to see" is 見 instead. 看 emphasizes deliberate watching or caring for someone's welfare.

examples.meaning_tr: nursing the sick, attending to an ill person
to watch over until the end, to see someone through

訟.note_tr: 訟 is used in formal legal contexts with only the onyomi しょう. It typically appears in compounds like 訴訟 (lawsuit) and related legal terminology. You'll encounter this kanji in news articles about court cases and in anime/manga featuring legal disputes or trial scenes.

戒.note_tr: The onyomi かい appears primarily in compound words expressing rules and discipline (戒律, 戒厳), while the kunyomi いまし.める forms the verb meaning 'to warn' or 'to admonish.' Both readings emphasize guidance or restraint of behavior.

examples.meaning_tr: rules and regulations; code of conduct

祉.note_tr: Read only as し (shi); this kanji appears almost exclusively in compound words, most commonly in 福祉 (welfare). It does not have a kunyomi reading.

誉.note_tr: The kunyomi reading ほめる serves as the active verb 'to praise'; ほまれ is the noun 'honor/reputation.' The onyomi よ appears in formal compounds like 名誉 (meiyō) and 栄誉 (eiyo). Watch out: 栄 (sakae, splendor) and 誉 (honor) often appear together in 栄誉 but have different kanji.

歓.note_tr: The kunyomi よろこ.ぶ (rejoice) appears in the standalone verb 歓ぶ, while the onyomi かん is used in compounds like 歓迎 (welcome) and 歓喜 (joy). This kanji always expresses positive emotions and is common in anime, games, and celebratory contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Cheer; shout of joy (often heard at sports events or concerts)

奏.note_tr: The on'yomi そう (sou) appears primarily in compound words like 演奏 (musical performance) and formal contexts. The kun'yomi かなでる has a more poetic or literary quality, meaning 'to play an instrument' or 'to produce sound.' This kanji is most commonly encountered in music-related contexts, making it especially relevant for anime and manga featuring musicians, orchestras, or performances.

examples.meaning_tr: To play (an instrument), to produce sound
To be effective, to have the desired effect

勧.note_tr: Use the kun'yomi 勧める (すすめる) as a verb meaning 'to recommend' or 'to encourage.' The on'yomi かん appears in formal compound words like 勧告 (advice/counsel) and 勧誘 (solicitation/invitation). This kanji expresses positive persuasion across contexts from personal recommendations to formal notices.

examples.reading: ともだちにえいがをすすめる
examples.meaning_tr: to recommend a movie to a friend

examples.word: 新しいゲームをお勧めします
examples.reading: あたらしいゲームをおすすめします
examples.meaning_tr: I recommend a new game (polite form)

examples.reading: せんせいがべんきょうをすすめた

騒.note_tr: Onyomi そう appears mainly in compounds like 騒音 (noise); kunyomi さわぐ/さわぎ are used in verbs and descriptive forms. Watch for the adjective reading さわがしい (noisy/boisterous) in dialogue and scene descriptions.

examples.meaning_tr: to make noise, to cause a commotion

閥.note_tr: Used primarily in compounds with the onyomi ばつ. Commonly appears in historical and political contexts (e.g., 財閥 zaibatsu during the Meiji era, 派閥 factions within political parties, 軍閥 military cliques). No independent kunyomi reading.

examples.meaning_tr: Faction, clique (within an organization or political party)
Zaibatsu; large financial and industrial conglomerate (historically important in Japan)
Military clique or faction (important in early 20th-century Japanese history)
Academic faction; preference or favoritism based on alma mater
Clan; family lineage or family faction

甲.note_tr: こう is the standard onyomi in most compounds like 甲虫 (beetle) and 甲板 (deck). かん appears specifically in 甲高い (high-pitched or shrill voice). The kunyomi きのえ refers to the first heavenly stem in traditional East Asian calendars and appears in dated contexts like 甲子 (first of the 60-year cycle).

examples.meaning_tr: A and B; Option A versus Option B
Koshien Stadium (famous baseball stadium in Japan)
Armor; Suit of armor; Protective metal gear

縄.note_tr: The native reading なわ is standard for referring to a rope or cord. The on'yomi じょう appears in compounds like 縄文時代 (Jomon period).

郷.note_tr: The onyomi reading きょう dominates in modern compounds (e.g., 故郷 'hometown', 郷土 'home region'); the ごう reading is rare, and the kunyomi さと is archaic.

揺.note_tr: The kunyomi ゆれる is the most common form in everyday Japanese, especially when describing earthquakes or physical motion. ゆらぐ can mean both literal swaying and figurative wavering (as in 心が揺らぐ meaning "one's heart wavers"). The onyomi よう appears mainly in formal compounds and is less frequently used in casual speech.

examples.meaning_tr: to shake, to sway, to rock
to sway, to waver, to fluctuate

免.note_tr: The onyomi めん is commonly used in compound nouns like 免許 (license) and 免除 (exemption), while the kunyomi まぬか/まぬが appears mainly in the verb 免れる (to escape or avoid). Most uses relate to being freed from or exempted from something.

examples.meaning_tr: License; permit (driver's license, fishing license, etc.)
To escape; to evade; to avoid

既.note_tr: The kanji 既 most commonly appears with on'yomi き in formal compounds (既成, 既出, 既婚, 既知) meaning 'already' or 'previously.' The kun'yomi すで.に stands alone as an adverb and is more conversational, frequently appearing in everyday speech and writing.

examples.meaning_tr: Already mentioned, previously stated or appeared

薦.note_tr: Kunyomi すす.める is used in 薦める (to recommend); onyomi せん appears in 推薦 (recommendation), especially in educational settings. Note: 勧める (same meaning and pronunciation) uses different kanji.

隣.note_tr: Use the kunyomi となり in casual speech to describe position or someone as a neighbor; the onyomi りん appears in formal compounds like 隣人 and 隣室. Straightforward kanji, rarely confused with others.

examples.meaning_tr: next to each other; sitting side by side
adjacent room; the room next door

華.note_tr: The onyomi reading か is most common in compounds and literary contexts (華麗, 華道, 中華). The kunyomi はな appears mainly in 華やか, meaning 'showy, gorgeous, or magnificent'. Distinguish from the similar kanji 花: while 花 refers to a literal botanical flower, 華 emphasizes splendor and elegance.

examples.meaning_tr: ikebana, the art of flower arrangement

範.note_tr: 範 only has the on'yomi はん and primarily appears in compounds. The most useful compound to learn first is 範囲 (はんい, range/scope), it's essential and very common in everyday usage.

隠.note_tr: Use かくす for actively hiding something and かくれる for hiding oneself or being hidden. Distinguished from 秘 (secret) in that 隠 emphasizes physical concealment rather than confidentiality.

徳.note_tr: 徳 is primarily read as とく (onyomi) and appears mostly in compounds related to morality, virtue, and governance. Similar kanji 得 (oku/toku, "to gain/obtain") has a different character and meaning; do not confuse them.

examples.meaning_tr: Virtue, admirable quality or character trait
Tokugawa (famous samurai clan and shogunate; important dynasty in Japanese history)
Benevolent decree (historical term for debt forgiveness edicts issued in medieval Japan)

哲.note_tr: The onyomi reading (てつ) dominates modern Japanese, especially in the compound 哲学 (philosophy). The kunyomi readings (さとい, あきらか) are rarely encountered in everyday usage, making the onyomi essential to master first.

杉.note_tr: This kanji predominantly uses the kunyomi reading すぎ for the cedar tree in everyday Japanese. The onyomi reading さん is rarely used in modern vocabulary. Cedar pollen (杉花粉) is a significant cultural reference in Japan due to widespread seasonal allergies.

釈.note_tr: The on'yomi しゃく (shaku) is commonly used in formal, academic, and Buddhist contexts, especially in compound words. The kunyomi forms (とく, す.てる, ゆる.す) are less frequent in modern Japanese but appear in classical or literary texts.

examples.meaning_tr: annotation; commentary; explanatory note (useful for manga and anime with footnotes)

己.note_tr: The onyomi こ is most common in modern compounds like 自己 (self) and 利己 (egoism). The kunyomi おのれ is used in formal or archaic contexts, often for dramatic effect in anime and literature.

妥.note_tr: The onyomi だ appears in all common compounds. This kanji frequently appears in anime and manga dealing with negotiations, conflict resolution, and agreement, characters reaching peaceful settlements use these words constantly.

examples.meaning_tr: Conclusion or settlement of an agreement

威.note_tr: The onyomi い is the primary and most productive reading, used in nearly all modern compounds. The kunyomi readings (おど.す, おど.し, おど.かす = to intimidate/threaten) are traditional but rarely appear in contemporary written Japanese.

豪.note_tr: Onyomi ごう is far more common in modern Japanese; kunyomi えら.い is archaic and rarely encountered. Compounds with 豪 frequently describe something magnificent, expensive, or severe (as in 豪雨, torrential rain).

熊.note_tr: The kunyomi くま is the standard reading for 'bear' as an animal. The onyomi ゆう appears mainly in specialized or classical compounds and is less commonly encountered at beginner levels. This kanji is especially recognizable in Japanese place names like Kumamoto (熊本) and Kumano (熊野).

滞.note_tr: The onyomi たい is used in most compounds (渋滞 traffic jam, 滞在 stay). The kunyomi とどこおる is the verb form meaning "to be delayed" or "to stagnate."

微.note_tr: Onyomi び is used in compounds like 微妙 and 微風; kunyomi かすか typically appears in い-adjectives like 微かな. This formal kanji appears frequently in literature and technical writing.

隆.note_tr: The kanji 隆 is primarily used in compound words with its onyomi reading りゅう. It commonly appears in historical and literary texts. While it originally represented a physical raised area, in modern Japanese it is mainly used abstractly to denote prosperity and greatness.

症.note_tr: 症 (しょう) primarily appears in compound medical terms describing specific conditions and symptoms. Common pattern: [type/adjective] + 症 = [type of] condition (e.g., 花粉症 pollen allergy, 自閉症 autism).

暫.note_tr: The kun'yomi しばらく is most common in everyday speech and manga dialogue. The on'yomi ざん typically appears in formal compounds like 暫定 (temporary, provisional). The kanji denotes a brief or temporary period, not an extended duration.

examples.meaning_tr: it's been a while (since we last met)

忠.note_tr: 忠 uses almost exclusively the onyomi reading ちゅう and appears in formal, literary, and historical contexts. It is common in anime and manga when describing character loyalty or samurai honor.

倉.note_tr: The kunyomi reading くら is used as a standalone noun, while the onyomi そう appears in compounds like 倉庫 (warehouse). Do not confuse with 蔵 (くら), a different kanji also read as 'storehouse' but used for sake breweries and treasure houses.

彦.note_tr: This archaic kanji appears mainly in names and classical literature. The kunyomi reading ひこ is more common in modern Japanese, especially in 彦星 (Altair, the Weaver Boy from the Tanabata legend, a fixture in anime). The onyomi げん is rare in contemporary usage.

examples.meaning_tr: Altair; the Weaver Boy in the Tanabata legend, frequently referenced in anime and manga
Hikone; a city in Shiga Prefecture known for its historical castle
Hikone Castle; a famous feudal castle and UNESCO World Heritage site in Japan
The Weaver Princess and the Weaver Boy; the central myth of Tanabata

肝.note_tr: The onyomi かん appears mainly in compounds like 肝心 (essential, vital) and 肝臓 (liver organ). The kunyomi きも is used for the literal liver and in courage-related expressions, such as 肝試し (test of courage).

examples.meaning_tr: Test of courage (often a dare or challenge game)
To be startled; to lose one's nerve

喚.note_tr: The onyomi かん is used in compounds like 喚起 (to evoke), commonly appearing in formal or written contexts. The kunyomi わめく stands alone as a verb meaning to yell or cry out loudly.

examples.meaning_tr: To yell; to scream; to cry out
Evocation; arousal; the act of evoking

examples.reading: かんどうをかんきする

meanings_tr: Follow along; run alongside; go along with
Lie along; extend along; be positioned along
沿.note_tr: Onyomi えん is used in compound words (沿線, 沿岸). Kunyomi そう forms the verb 'to follow along'; the suffix form -ぞい creates location expressions such as 川沿い (along the river).

examples.meaning_tr: railway line; areas along a railway
to follow along; to go with

妙.note_tr: みょう is the dominant reading in modern Japanese and appears in most compounds. びょう and kunyomi たえ are rare and archaic. In compounds, 妙 expresses both the sense of something peculiar or strange (奇妙) and something wonderfully skillful or excellent (妙技).

唱.note_tr: Onyomi (しょう) appears primarily in formal compound words (e.g., 合唱 'chorus', 提唱 'to advocate'). Kunyomi (となえる) is the main verb form meaning 'to chant' or 'to sing aloud'. Both readings relate to vocal expression and are frequently seen in music, anime, and school contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: To sing loudly; to shout in song

阿.note_tr: The onyomi reading あ dominates modern usage; kunyomi forms are archaic. 阿修羅 (Asura), a popular term in anime and manga, is by far the most common compound.

examples.meaning_tr: Asura; a deity or demon in Buddhist and Hindu mythology
A-un; the first and last sounds; the beginning and end
Amitabha Buddha; one of the principal deities in Buddhism
