脈.note_tr: The onyomi みゃく is predominant in modern usage and appears in medical and technical compound words. The kunyomi すじ represents the basic concept of a line or vein and is rarely used in contemporary Japanese.

滝.note_tr: The kunyomi たき is the standard, everyday reading and appears in words like 滝行 (waterfall meditation practice). The onyomi readings ろう and そう are less common and typically found in specialized or literary contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Waterfall meditation; an ascetic training practice performed under a waterfall
Waterfall basin; the pool of water at the base of a waterfall

軌.note_tr: This kanji uses only the on'yomi reading き and has no kunyomi. It appears most often in scientific and technical contexts, especially when describing orbits, trajectories, or "being on track." The phrase 軌道に乗る (to get on track) is a common idiom meaning to be progressing well or following the right path.

examples.meaning_tr: to get on track; to be progressing well; to be proceeding as planned

俵.note_tr: The kunyomi たわら refers to a bale or sack as an object. The onyomi ひょう appears in compound words like 米俵 (rice bale) and when counting bags or bales. This kanji is commonly found in historical and agricultural contexts in manga and anime.

examples.meaning_tr: Rice bale; a sack of rice

妨.note_tr: The onyomi ぼう typically appears in compound nouns like 妨害 (obstruction, interference), while the kunyomi さまたげる forms the main verb 妨げる meaning to prevent or hinder. In everyday conversation, 妨げる is more frequently used than 妨害する.

examples.meaning_tr: to prevent; to hinder; to obstruct

examples.reading: すいみんをさまたげる

examples.meaning_tr: obstructive conduct; obstruction (especially in sports or official contexts)

擦.note_tr: The kunyomi す.る is used in basic verbs like 擦る (to rub), while the onyomi さつ appears in compounds like 摩擦 (friction). The form 擦れ違う (to pass by/miss each other) is very common in anime and everyday conversation.

examples.meaning_tr: to pass by, to miss each other

鯨.note_tr: The kun'yomi (くじら) is the standard everyday reading for the animal. The on'yomi (げい) appears mainly in the literary compound 鯨飲 (excessive drinking), where it has figurative meaning unrelated to actual whales.

荘.note_tr: The onyomi そう is most commonly used in modern contexts (e.g., 別荘), while しょう appears mainly in historical and classical texts (e.g., 荘園). The kunyomi readings and ちゃん are rare in contemporary Japanese. This kanji frequently appears in architecture, travel, and history contexts, relevant to your interest in both anime/manga and Japanese history.

諾.note_tr: This N1 kanji appears primarily in formal, written Japanese, especially in business and legal documents. It rarely stands alone and is typically found in compounds carrying the だく reading. Unlike 同意 (mutual agreement/understanding) and 了承 (passive acknowledgment), 諾 emphasizes active, deliberate consent.

examples.meaning_tr: Cheerful consent; willing agreement or acceptance
Silent assent; tacit agreement without explicit words
Refusal; rejection of a request or proposal
Yes or no; answer indicating consent or refusal

雷.note_tr: The kunyomi かみなり is the everyday, natural reading used in speech and very common in anime and manga contexts. The onyomi らい is more formal and technical, appearing in compound words like 雷雨 (thunderstorm) and 雷神 (thunder god). The variant readings いかずち and いかづち are archaic or poetic forms rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Thunder god (common in anime, manga, and mythology)
Lightning strike; thunderbolt (used in gaming and military contexts)

漂.note_tr: The onyomi ひょう appears in compound words (e.g., 漂流 'adrift'); the kunyomi ただよう is the standalone verb meaning 'to drift' or 'to float.' This water-related kanji is common in adventure and fantasy stories, making it especially relevant to anime and manga contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: adrift; being stranded at sea; castaway
to drift; to float; to wander
to wash ashore; to be cast ashore

meanings_tr: To become attached to, to grow fond of
懐.note_tr: The on'yomi reading かい is used in compound words and formal terms. The kun'yomi reading なつ- relates to nostalgic feelings and attachment, with なつかしい being especially common in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: To become attached to, to grow fond of, to tame

meanings_tr: To check; to calculate; to examine
To guess; to infer; to surmise
勘.note_tr: The kanji 勘 is read only with the onyomi かん (no kunyomi). It appears frequently in everyday Japanese, especially in expressions related to intuition, miscalculation, and casual speech, very common in anime and manga for expressing character traits or misunderstandings.

examples.meaning_tr: Bill; account; calculation; check (at a restaurant)
To have sharp intuition; to be perceptive; to be quick to sense things
To suspect; to guess; to surmise; to have misgivings about

栽.note_tr: The onyomi さい is rarely used standalone; it appears mainly in compounds like 栽培. Don't confuse it with 植 (plant) or 育 (nurture), 栽 specifically refers to agricultural planting and growing crops.

拐.note_tr: Reads only as かい (on'yomi). In modern Japanese, primarily means 'kidnap/abduct,' especially in legal and news vocabulary; 'falsify' and 'bend' are archaic or specialized.

駄.note_tr: The reading だ dominates modern usage; た is rarely seen. 駄目 (だめ), meaning 'useless' or 'no good,' is the most common word with this kanji and appears in everyday conversation.

添.note_tr: The onyomi てん is used mainly in compound words (添付 means 'attachment'; 添加 means 'additive'). The kunyomi そ.える is the primary verb form meaning 'to add' or 'to serve with,' especially in food contexts. The reading そ.う appears in combined verbs like 付き添う (to accompany).

examples.meaning_tr: To add; to serve with (often with food/condiments)
To accompany; to attend to someone
Addition; additive (as in 食品添加物: food additive)

冠.note_tr: The kunyomi かんむり (kanmuri) refers to a crown or coronet shape and is also the name of the radical that appears at the top of many kanji. The onyomi かん is typically used in compound words. In sports contexts, 冠 often indicates a championship or title.

examples.meaning_tr: To lead, to be at the head of, to champion
To win a championship or title

斜.note_tr: The kunyomi ななめ is used in everyday expressions and standalone words (e.g., 斜めがけ bag, 斜め読み skimming); the onyomi しゃ appears in formal compounds (斜線 line, 斜面 slope). Both readings are equally common depending on context.

examples.meaning_tr: diagonal line, slant line (used in art, geometry, manga)
slope, incline, inclined plane (mountain slope, ski slope)
wearing diagonally across the body (e.g., a shoulder bag or messenger bag)
skimming, glancing through (reading quickly without detail)

鏡.note_tr: The kanji 鏡 primarily uses kunyomi かがみ (kagami) for everyday reference to mirrors. The onyomi きょう (kyō) and けい (kei) appear mainly in formal or compound words. A notable cultural reference is 鏡餅 (kagami mochi), a round rice-cake decoration traditionally displayed during New Year celebrations.

examples.meaning_tr: kagami mochi, a round rice-cake offering displayed for New Year
ceremony of breaking and sharing kagami mochi on New Year

聡.note_tr: The onyomi そう is used in formal compounds like 聡明 (wise and intelligent). The kunyomi さとい is the standalone adjective form. The specialized kunyomi みみざとい (keen-eared) emphasizes being perceptive to sounds and subtleties, as seen in 耳聡い.

examples.meaning_tr: Wise, intelligent, clever; quick to understand things
Wise and intelligent; brilliant of mind
Quick-witted, sharp, keen; intelligent and quick to react
Keen-eared, sharp of hearing; perceptive to sounds and subtleties

浪.note_tr: This kanji primarily uses the on'yomi ろう and appears in compound words. It often refers to turbulent waves but can also convey meanings of recklessness or wandering.

examples.meaning_tr: Ronin; a masterless samurai; also a student taking a year off to prepare for university entrance exams

亜.note_tr: This kanji is almost always used with the onyomi reading (あ) in modern Japanese, functioning as a prefix in scientific and technical terminology meaning 'sub-' or 'quasi-'. The kunyomi reading (つ.ぐ) meaning 'follow' or 'rank second' is archaic and essentially unused in contemporary Japanese.

覧.note_tr: This kanji typically uses the on'yomi reading (らん) in compounds. The listed kun'yomi (み.る) is rare and generally not encountered in isolated usage. Examples below emphasize the dominant onyomi patterns.

詐.note_tr: The onyomi さ is used in most compound words (詐欺 'scam', 詐称 'false claim'). The kunyomi いつわる serves as the verb meaning 'to deceive.' Distinguish from 偽 (fake; false), which implies falsehood without necessarily fraudulent intent.

壇.note_tr: 壇 is primarily used in compound words and refers to elevated or ceremonial platforms. The reading だん is more common in everyday vocabulary (花壇, 演壇), while たん appears in more formal or religious contexts (祭壇).

examples.meaning_tr: on the stage, on the platform

勲.note_tr: The onyomi くん dominates modern usage, appearing in compounds like 勲章 (medal, decoration). The kunyomi いさお is archaic and rarely used outside of proper names.

魔.note_tr: 魔 is read as ま (onyomi) in most compounds and rarely appears standalone. This kanji is especially common in anime, manga, and fantasy games, where it frequently describes supernatural and magical phenomena.

酬.note_tr: The onyomi しゅう is most common in compounds like 報酬 (reward/compensation). The kunyomi むくいる appears in literary or formal contexts meaning 'to repay' or 'to be rewarded.'

examples.meaning_tr: to repay; to reward; to be requited
repayment of a debt of gratitude

紫.note_tr: The kunyomi むらさき is used when naming the color itself, as in 紫色 (purple color). The onyomi し appears in compounds and specialized terms such as 紫外線 (ultraviolet) and 紫蘇 (shiso).

examples.meaning_tr: Shiso; perilla (Japanese herb used in cooking)

曙.note_tr: The kun'yomi reading あけぼの is used for the standalone noun, appearing frequently in poetry and literary contexts. The on'yomi reading しょ appears in formal compounds like 曙光 (dawn light).

examples.meaning_tr: Dawn light; the first light of day breaking through the sky
Pale pink; a traditional Japanese color name resembling the sky at dawn

紋.note_tr: 紋 is pronounced only as もん (mon) and appears almost exclusively in compounds. This kanji is essential for understanding Japanese cultural context, family crests (家紋) appear frequently in historical texts, manga, and anime, especially in stories dealing with samurai or feudal Japan.

examples.meaning_tr: kimono or garment decorated with a family crest

卸.note_tr: Most commonly used with the kunyomi readings おろす and おろし in modern Japanese, particularly in commercial and trading contexts. The onyomi しゃ is rarely encountered in contemporary usage. Do not confuse with 下ろす (to lower), which uses a different kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: To unload; to lower; to sell wholesale

meanings_tr: to exert oneself; to make efforts
to be roused; to be stirred up
奮.note_tr: On'yomi ふん is predominant in modern Japanese, especially in compounds like 奮闘 (strenuous effort) and 奮起 (to be roused), both common in anime and manga. Kun'yomi ふる.う (to wield) is less frequently used today.

examples.meaning_tr: to be stirred up; to be roused to action
to make a spurt; to exert oneself; to splurge
to wield; to brandish; to exert
to exert oneself; to make efforts

欄.note_tr: The on'yomi らん is standard in modern Japanese compounds (記入欄, 投書欄, コメント欄). The kun'yomi てすり (handrail) is rarely used with this kanji; 手すり or 手摺 is the typical spelling.

examples.meaning_tr: Entry blank; space on a form or document to fill in information
Readers' column; newspaper section for letters and comments from readers
Comments section; area for comments on websites or social media
Manga column; manga section in a newspaper or magazine
Journalist's column; newspaper section written by reporters
Outside the column; margin or space beyond a column

meanings_tr: To deviate, stray, veer off course
逸.note_tr: The on'yomi いつ appears in compound (two-kanji) words like 逸話, 秀逸, 逸脱, and 逸品. The kun'yomi それる (intransitive, "to swerve off") and そらす (transitive, "to divert/avert") form a common pair, as in 話が逸れる ("the topic strays") vs 目を逸らす ("to avert one's eyes"). はぐれる ("to get separated from a group," e.g. 人混みではぐれる) shares the same kanji but is a rarer reading and is usually written in kana rather than with 逸.

examples.meaning_tr: deviation, digression (from a rule or topic)
to stray, veer off, go off course (e.g. a ball or a topic)
to avert one's eyes, to look away

涯.note_tr: 涯 uses がい (gai) in formal, literary words like 天涯 (horizon), and はて (hate) in common adjectival phrases like 涯しない (endless). The core meaning revolves around boundaries, edges, and the limits of space or abstract concepts.

examples.meaning_tr: the ends of the earth; distant horizon
the end of the world; the edge of existence

拓.note_tr: Use kunyomi ひら.く for the verb 拓く (to pioneer or develop). Onyomi たく appears in compounds like 開拓 (land reclamation). Unlike the common 開く (to simply open something), this kanji emphasizes breaking new ground or pioneering new territory.

examples.meaning_tr: to open; to pioneer; to develop
to pioneer a path; to open new ground; to forge ahead

眼.note_tr: 眼 is the formal or medical-focused variant of everyday 目 (me/eye); the on'yomi がん dominates in modern compounds and medical terminology, while the kunyomi is rare, appearing in literary expressions like 眼差し (manazashi, gaze). Distinguish it from 目 by its specialized register in ophthalmology and written language.

examples.meaning_tr: gaze; look; expression in the eyes

獄.note_tr: 獄 uses only the onyomi reading ごく and is most familiar through the common word 地獄 (hell), which appears throughout anime and manga. Do not confuse with 牢 (ろう), which also means prison but refers to a holding place or cell, whereas 獄 carries a formal or literary tone.

尚.note_tr: The reading なお typically functions as a conjunctive particle meaning 'still' or 'yet'. The on-reading しょう appears primarily in formal compound words where it often conveys respect or elevated regard.

examples.meaning_tr: Book of History; One of the Five Classics

彫.note_tr: ちょう (onyomi) appears in compound nouns like 彫刻 and 彫像, while ほる/ぼり (kunyomi) form action verbs and descriptive expressions. This is a sculptural and artistic kanji, especially common in fine arts contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: To carve; to engrave; to sculpt

穏.note_tr: The kun'yomi reading おだやか is used in everyday contexts to describe something calm or peaceful (e.g., 穏やかな天気 'calm weather'). The on'yomi reading おん appears in formal compound words (e.g., 穏健 'moderate faction'). Do not confuse with 静 (shizuka), which emphasizes silence and stillness rather than inner peacefulness.

顕.note_tr: 顕 primarily uses the onyomi けん in modern Japanese. The kunyomi readings (あきらか for clear, あらわれる for appear) are formal or archaic; 明らか and 現れる are the preferred modern forms for these meanings.

巧.note_tr: The onyomi こう is used in most common compounds like 巧妙 (clever) and 巧者 (skilled person). The kunyomi たくみ appears in the adjective 巧み (skillful), while うまい is rarely used in modern Japanese. Do not confuse with similar-looking kanji 工 (craft/work) or 考 (think).

矛.note_tr: 矛 primarily appears in 矛盾 (contradiction), read むじゅん in modern Japanese. The literal meaning 'spear' (ほこ) surfaces in historical contexts and compounds like 矛先 (point of a spear); 矛盾 itself derives from the paradox of 'spear and shield' being unable to coexist.

examples.meaning_tr: Tip of a spear; target of criticism or attack

垣.note_tr: The kunyomi かき is far more common than the onyomi えん in everyday usage. 垣 typically refers to garden hedges or fences, while the similar kanji 塀 (へい) refers to formal or sturdy walls.

examples.meaning_tr: Living hedge; a hedge made of living plants
Stone wall; stone fortifications (common in castle architecture)
To catch a glimpse of; to peek (between the cracks of a fence)

欺.note_tr: The on-yomi ぎ primarily appears in compound words, especially the very common 詐欺 (fraud/scam). The kun-yomi あざむく serves as the main verb 'to deceive' or 'to trick.' Both readings frequently appear in anime and manga scenes involving deception or trickery.

釣.note_tr: The kunyomi つる (to fish) is the most common form in everyday Japanese, used in the basic verb 釣る. The noun form 釣り means "the activity of fishing." The onyomi ちょう is rare and typically appears only in formal or specialized contexts.

萩.note_tr: The kunyomi (はぎ) is the primary reading used in modern Japanese and dominates most compounds. The plant holds deep cultural significance in Japanese tradition, symbolizing autumn and appearing frequently in poetry and seasonal references. Do not confuse with 茨 (いばら, briar).

examples.meaning_tr: Hagi no Tsuki (famous Sendai confectionery; literally 'bush clover moon')
Hagi ware (traditional Japanese pottery style from Yamaguchi Prefecture)
Bush clover viewing; autumn excursion to appreciate the flowering shrub

粛.note_tr: On'yomi しゅく appears mainly in formal compounds (粛清, 厳粛); kunyomi つつしむ is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese. Most frequently encountered as the adverb 粛々と, meaning "quietly and solemnly."

examples.meaning_tr: Quietly and solemnly; in a grave manner
Purge; elimination; cleanup (political or organizational context)
To be cautious; to refrain; to restrain oneself

栗.note_tr: The reading くり is standard for the chestnut nut and compounds. The onyomi り/りつ rarely appear in everyday Japanese and are found mainly in proper names.

愚.note_tr: The kunyomi 'oroka' (おろか) appears in everyday conversational Japanese as a standalone adjective. The onyomi 'gu' (ぐ) is used in formal written compounds and literary contexts. Unlike 馬鹿 (baka), which is casual and sometimes offensive, 愚 carries a more formal or moral tone.

嘉.note_tr: 嘉 is primarily a formal and literary kanji, most commonly appearing with the onyomi か in compounds, names, and historical contexts. The kunyomi よい (good) and よみ.する (to praise) are archaic and rarely encountered in modern Japanese text. Expect to see this kanji in historical period names and formal contexts related to appreciation or praise.

examples.meaning_tr: Carnival; a spectacular festival or celebration
To accept or approve of favorably

遭.note_tr: The onyomi そう is most common in formal compounds like 遭遇 (encounter) and 遭難 (disaster/shipwreck). The kunyomi あう is less frequently used but appears in expressions like 遭う (to encounter), typically with an unpleasant event.

examples.meaning_tr: To encounter, to undergo, to experience (usually something difficult)

架.note_tr: The kunyomi 架ける (transitive) means to build or construct, while 架かる (intransitive) means to span or be built. The onyomi reading appears in technical compounds like 架線 and 架台; do not confuse with 掛ける (to hang).

examples.meaning_tr: a bridge spans; a bridge is built

鬼.note_tr: 鬼 refers to demons in Japanese folklore, traditionally depicted with horns. The on'yomi (き) appears in compounds like 鬼滅 (demon slaying), while kun'yomi (おに) is used for the demon figure itself. Very common in anime, manga, and traditional storytelling.

庶.note_tr: 庶 primarily appears in compounds using the on'yomi しょ. Most common in modern Japanese through 庶民 (common people/the masses) and 庶務 (general office affairs). The 'illegitimate/bastard' meaning appears in historical narratives, period dramas, and fantasy anime/manga dealing with feudal contexts or nobility.

examples.meaning_tr: common people, the masses, ordinary citizens
general affairs, office administration, clerical work
born out of wedlock, illegitimate birth

稚.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 稚 predominantly appears in formal or literary compounds using the onyomi ち. It emphasizes immaturity or underdevelopment. Compare with 幼 (young, tender); together they form 幼稚 (childish).

examples.meaning_tr: immature, crude, clumsy (in writing or performance)

滋.note_tr: The on'yomi じ is used in most modern words about nutrition and flavor (滋養, 滋味). The on'yomi し appears mainly in the place name 滋賀県 (Shiga Prefecture). No kun'yomi is in common use.

幻.note_tr: The onyomi げん is the productive reading in modern Japanese, especially in compounds. The kunyomi まぼろし is more classical and appears in fixed expressions like 幻のメニュー (phantom menu), common in anime, manga, and casual speech. Often confused with 幽 (yū, ghostly/spectral) in supernatural contexts.

煮.note_tr: Use the kunyomi reading に in most everyday contexts; the onyomi しゃ is rare. This kanji refers to cooking in water or liquid (simmering), distinct from 焼く (grilling) or 炒める (stir-frying).

examples.meaning_tr: To boil; to cook in water
To be boiled; to be cooked
Simmered radish (a classic Japanese side dish)

姫.note_tr: The kunyomi reading ひめ is by far the most common in modern Japanese and refers to 'princess'. The onyomi き is rarely used in contemporary texts. This kanji frequently appears in proper nouns, especially Himeji (姫路), a historic city known for its castle.

誓.note_tr: The kunyomi ちか.う is used for the verb form (誓う = to vow/swear). The onyomi せい appears mainly in compound words like 宣誓 (oath) and 誓約 (pledge/contract). This kanji often appears in formal, serious, or emotional contexts, common in anime/manga during oath or promise scenes.

examples.meaning_tr: to vow; to swear; to pledge
a vow; a pledge; a commitment
pledge; vow; promise (often in contracts or formal agreements)

把.note_tr: Primarily read as は (ha) in most compounds, such as 把握. When used as a counter for bundles or groups, the pronunciation shifts to ぱ (pa), as in 一把 (one handful). The onyomi わ is rarely found in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to grasp; to grip; to understand; to comprehend
a handful; a bunch; a bundle
to hold; to grip; to maintain a hold on

践.note_tr: The onyomi reading せん is far more common in modern Japanese, appearing primarily in the compound 実践 (practice). The kunyomi ふ.む means to step on or tread upon, rarely used in everyday Japanese. Focus on 実践 and related compounds for recognition.

examples.meaning_tr: to step on; to tread on

呈.note_tr: Used primarily in formal and written contexts. The reading てい is the only reading for this kanji. Can be confused with 提 (carry/lead) or 定 (fixed/determined), which share the same reading but have entirely different meanings.

examples.reading: しょうじょうをていする
examples.meaning_tr: to display symptoms, to show signs
to express an opinion, to present a viewpoint
to present a work (of art or music)

meanings_tr: To shun, to neglect, to avoid
疎.note_tr: The kunyomi うと.い and うと.む appear in everyday adjectives and verbs expressing distance or rejection; onyomi そ dominates formal compounds and literary contexts. The similar kanji 粗 (rough) shares the そ reading, distinguish by context: 疎 emphasizes separation or scarceness, 粗 emphasizes crude quality.

examples.meaning_tr: To shun, to avoid, to alienate

meanings_tr: lie on one's back, face upward
仰.note_tr: This kanji has multiple readings with distinct uses: おっしゃる (honorific 'to say') is extremely common in anime and formal speech; あお.ぐ (to look up at) expresses admiration; ぎょう appears in compounds like 仰天 (astonishment). Context determines which reading applies.

examples.meaning_tr: to look up at, admire, respect
lying on one's back, supine, face-up position

剛.note_tr: 剛 has only the onyomi reading ごう (gō); no kunyomi. It primarily appears in compounds expressing physical or moral strength. Common in anime and manga for character descriptions emphasizing toughness or determination.

疾.note_tr: The onyomi しつ appears frequently in medical and speed-related compounds. The kunyomi はや.い is less common in modern Japanese; 早い is the standard word for 'fast/quick.' Pay attention to context to distinguish between disease and speed meanings.

examples.meaning_tr: rapid speed, swift pace, high velocity

征.note_tr: 征 appears almost exclusively in compounds using the onyomi reading せい. It is heavily featured in military, historical, and strategy game contexts (RPGs, tactical games), making it particularly useful for anime, manga, and game enthusiasts. Do not confuse with 攻 (attack/strike); 征 emphasizes subjugation and dominance, while 攻 focuses on the aggressive action itself.

examples.meaning_tr: Expedition, long-distance campaign or exploratory journey
Going to war, military deployment or expedition

砕.note_tr: The kunyomi くだ.く is transitive (to break something apart), while くだ.ける is intransitive (to break or shatter). The onyomi さい commonly appears in technical compounds like 砕石 (crushed stone) and 粉砕 (pulverization).

examples.meaning_tr: To break, to smash, to crush
To break apart, to shatter, to crumble
To scatter and shatter into pieces

謡.note_tr: The onyomi reading よう appears primarily in Noh chanting contexts (謡曲), while kunyomi readings うたう and うたい refer to singing more broadly. Do not confuse with 歌 (うた), which is the more common character for everyday songs and singing.

嫁.note_tr: The reading よめ (yome) is most common and refers to a bride or daughter-in-law; the reading とつぐ (toutugu) is used for the verb "to marry" and applies primarily to women. This kanji appears frequently in anime and manga, particularly in family drama contexts involving relationships with mothers-in-law (姑).

examples.meaning_tr: Bride's entrance into new home after marriage (cultural custom)

謙.note_tr: The on-reading けん appears in common compound words like 謙虚 (humility) and 謙遜 (modesty), while the kun-reading へりくだる functions as a standalone verb. Both convey humble and respectful attitudes valued in Japanese culture and frequently depicted in anime/manga character interactions.

后.note_tr: This character primarily means 'empress' or 'queen' and is most common in formal titles like 皇后 (こうごう) for imperial consorts. The archaic meanings 'after' and 'behind' are rarely encountered in modern Japanese.

嘆.note_tr: The kunyomi なげ.く is used for the verb form 嘆く, common in emotional or narrative contexts (anime/manga dialogue). The onyomi たん appears in formal compounds like 嘆願 (petition) and 嘆息 (literary sigh). The kunyomi adjective なげ.かわしい means "deplorable" or "pitiable."

菌.note_tr: Only onyomi pronunciation (kin) is used. Primarily appears in compounds referring to microorganisms in medical, biological, and food contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Lactic acid bacteria (in yogurt, fermented foods)

鎌.note_tr: Kunyomi かま refers to the farm tool (sickle). Onyomi readings appear mainly in place names and historical terms such as Kamakura (鎌倉). The 'trick' meaning is archaic or specialized and rarely seen in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Kamakura (famous city and historical period in Japan)
Kamakura period (1185–1333 CE in Japanese history)

巣.note_tr: Kunyomi す is used in most everyday words (e.g., 鳥の巣 "bird's nest"). The onyomi そう rarely appears in modern Japanese. The form すくう (from the given kunyomi す.くう) means "to build or make a nest."

examples.meaning_tr: staying indoors; sheltering in place (nesting at home)

頻.note_tr: The onyomi reading ひん is used in most modern compound words (e.g., 頻繁, 頻度). The kunyomi しきりに is less common and appears in more formal or literary contexts, expressing an earnest or persistent quality.

examples.meaning_tr: Frequency; the number of times something occurs
Frequently appearing or occurring (especially common on exams)

琴.note_tr: The kunyomi こと refers specifically to the traditional koto. The onyomi きん is used in compounds and metaphorical expressions (琴線 = heartstrings). The onyomi ごん is rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Heartstrings; sensitive emotional nerve (frequently used metaphorically in anime and manga)
Sound of a koto; melodious stringed instrument sound

班.note_tr: This kanji is read primarily as はん with no common kunyomi. It appears frequently in school and workplace contexts to denote small groups or squads organized for specific tasks or purposes.

棚.note_tr: The kunyomi たな is used for the standalone word "shelf"; the suffix form -だな is standard in compounds (e.g., 本棚 bookshelf, 食器棚 dish cabinet). The onyomi ほう is rarely used in modern everyday Japanese.

潔.note_tr: The onyomi けつ dominates compounds (潔白 'innocence', 潔癖 'fastidiousness', common in anime for character traits). The kunyomi いさぎよい is used in adjective and adverbial forms expressing honest or graceful withdrawal. Not typically confused with similar kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: fastidiousness, obsessive attention to cleanliness (often used to describe character traits in anime)

examples.reading: けっぱくをしゅちょうする

酷.note_tr: The kunyomi ひどい is much more common in everyday conversation and writing (e.g., 「ひどい天気」means "terrible weather"). The onyomi こく appears mainly in formal or literary compounds like 「酷評」(harsh criticism) and 「酷暑」(severe heat).

examples.meaning_tr: To go through something terrible; to have a rough experience

meanings_tr: To lead, to command, to superintend
宰.note_tr: The on'yomi さい is the only reading used in compounds. This kanji appears almost exclusively in formal or historical government contexts, with 宰相 (prime minister) as the dominant modern usage.

examples.meaning_tr: To lead, to command, to superintend

廊.note_tr: 廊 is read exclusively as ろう. The most common compound is 廊下 (ろうか), often featured in school settings in anime and manga.

寂.note_tr: The kunyomi readings (especially さびしい) dominate in everyday speech, anime, and songs, expressing loneliness or sadness. The onyomi readings (じゃく, せき) mainly appear in formal compounds like 静寂 (silence).

examples.meaning_tr: Lonely, lonesome; feeling sad or isolated
Loneliness (noun); the feeling of being alone
To become desolate; to fall into disrepair or abandonment
Looking lonely, forlorn; appearing sad or melancholic

辰.note_tr: The on'yomi readings しん and じん appear mainly in technical compounds; the kun'yomi たつ appears primarily in 辰年. Historically, this character marked the 7–9am time slot in traditional Japanese horology.

霞.note_tr: The kunyomi readings かすみ and かす.む are standard in modern Japanese and appear in everyday contexts, while the onyomi readings か and げ are rarely used. This kanji is frequently found in poetic and literary descriptions of misty landscapes, making it common in nature imagery, classical literature, and atmospheric scenes in anime and manga.

examples.meaning_tr: to become hazy; to grow dim

伏.note_tr: The kunyomi 伏せる is common in everyday Japanese meaning 'to hide' or 'to cover.' The onyomi ふく appears in storytelling terms like 伏線 (foreshadowing), which is important for anime and manga fans. Avoid confusing 伏 (to hide/cover) with 服 (fuku = clothing); both are pronounced the same but have completely different meanings.

examples.meaning_tr: to hide; to cover; to lay face down
censored character; masked text; redacted character
to lie down; to be prone; to prostrate

碁.note_tr: This kanji refers specifically to Go (囲碁), the classic East Asian board game played with black and white stones. Always read as ご (onyomi); no kunyomi exists. Common in compounds related to the game itself.

examples.meaning_tr: Go salon; Go club (venue where people play Go)

俗.note_tr: 俗 is used exclusively with the onyomi reading ぞく. The kanji primarily appears in compound words (compounds with other characters), often describing either negative, vulgar qualities (e.g., 低俗 "vulgar") or traditional customs and folklore (e.g., 風俗 "customs," 民俗 "folk traditions"). Common in anime and manga for slang references.

examples.meaning_tr: Customs, manners, social practices, way of life
Folk customs, folklore, traditional ways of a people
Popular belief, urban legend, folk theory

漠.note_tr: This kanji appears only with the onyomi reading ばく. Most commonly encountered in 砂漠 (desert). When used in other compounds like 漠然と, it conveys a sense of 'vague' or 'hazy'.

邪.note_tr: The onyomi じゃ dominates modern Japanese, appearing in many compounds, most famously in 邪魔 (a very common word). The kunyomi よこしま, meaning wicked or crooked, is archaic and rarely encountered in contemporary usage.

examples.meaning_tr: Obstacle, hindrance, nuisance; to get in someone's way
Wicked or unfair method; foul play
Evil or wicked intention; malicious thought
Evil intent, malicious spirit, dark aura

晶.note_tr: This kanji appears almost exclusively in compound words using the onyomi reading しょう. It describes crystalline structures, transparency, or luminosity. No kunyomi is commonly used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Liquid crystal (used in LCD displays and screens)

墨.note_tr: Use kunyomi (すみ) for the basic noun 'ink' and traditional art-related compounds like 墨絵. The onyomi (ぼく) appears mainly in formal and technical compounds such as 墨汁 (liquid ink).

鎮.note_tr: The kunyomi shizumeru (鎮める) means to actively calm or suppress something, while shizumaru (鎮まる) means to become calm or settle down naturally. The onyomi chin (ちん) appears frequently in formal compounds related to military, firefighting, and medical terminology.

examples.meaning_tr: to be enshrined, to be stationed (honorific, often used for deities in shrines)

洞.note_tr: Onyomi 'dō' is mainly used in compounds like 洞窟 (cave) and 洞察 (insight). Kunyomi 'hora' specifically refers to a cave or cavern, frequently appearing in adventure stories and fantasy contexts.

meanings_tr: To fulfill, to carry out, to perform
履.note_tr: The kunyomi は.く ('to wear') is everyday usage for footwear and lower-body garments. The onyomi り appears in formal written compounds like 履歴 (history, record) and 履修 (enrollment in a course).

examples.meaning_tr: taking a course, enrollment in a class

劣.note_tr: The kunyomi おとる is used in the standalone verb 劣る (to be inferior). The onyomi れつ appears in compound words like 優劣 (superiority and inferiority) and 劣悪 (poor quality). This kanji is commonly used in comparisons and discussions about quality or capability.

examples.meaning_tr: to be inferior, to be worse

那.note_tr: 那 is rarely used in modern Japanese outside of proper nouns, particularly place names (especially in the Okinawa region). Do not confuse with 何 (なに/なん), which is the standard modern word for "what."

examples.meaning_tr: Naha, the capital city of Okinawa Prefecture
Nasu, a region in Tochigi Prefecture known for hot springs and nature
Nachi, a location in Wakayama famous for waterfalls and historical temples

殴.note_tr: The kun'yomi 殴る (to hit) is far more common than the on'yomi form. This kanji implies forceful or aggressive hitting, distinguishing it from similar verbs like 叩く (tap) or 打つ (hit more generally).

examples.meaning_tr: to be beaten, to be hit

娠.note_tr: This kanji is almost exclusively encountered in medical and formal contexts as part of the compound 妊娠. The onyomi しん combines with 妊 (にん, to be pregnant) to form this standard medical term for pregnancy.

examples.reading: にんしんとうにょうびょう

奉.note_tr: The ほう onyomi is used in formal compounds like 奉仕 (volunteer service). The classical kunyomi たてまつる appears in literature and anime dialogue. This kanji often marks shrine/temple offerings, formal service, or ceremonial presentation contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: dedication offering (as to a shrine or temple)

憂.note_tr: The on'yomi ゆう primarily appears in compounds like 憂鬱 (melancholy/depression), the most common modern usage. The kunyomi うれ.える and うれ.い are classical or literary forms expressing worry and sorrow, commonly encountered in traditional literature and poetry.

examples.meaning_tr: To worry; to grieve; to be troubled by

朴.note_tr: Onyomi ぼく is predominant in Sino-Japanese compounds. Kunyomi ほお/ほう is less common; ほおば (朴葉, magnolia leaf) is the most frequent kunyomi usage in everyday Japanese, appearing especially in food and traditional contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: sincere and unpretentious; candid but simple
magnolia leaf (used in Japanese cuisine and wrapping)
nettle tree; a deciduous East Asian tree (Celtis sinensis)

meanings_tr: Restaurant (especially upscale or traditional Japanese restaurant)
亭.note_tr: The onyomi てい is standard in modern Japanese; ちん is archaic. The kanji most commonly appears in restaurant names and formal dining contexts (料亭 'upscale restaurant', 茶亭 'tea house').

examples.meaning_tr: Master of a house; husband (archaic term)

淳.note_tr: This kanji is primarily used in Japanese given names and formal writing contexts. The onyomi reading じゅん is by far the most common; the kunyomi reading あつい is extremely rare and almost never appears in modern Japanese. You'll encounter this kanji frequently in anime and manga character names.

examples.meaning_tr: Junichi; a very common Japanese male given name
Jumpei; a common Japanese male given name
simplicity and sincerity; honesty and straightforwardness
pure and profound; deeply sincere and generous

怪.note_tr: The on'yomi かい appears in compound nouns like 怪獣 (kaiju) and 怪物 (monster), especially common in anime and fantasy content, ideal for your interests. The kun'yomi forms あやしい and あやしむ function as an adjective and verb meaning suspicious or strange. The reading け is rare in modern Japanese.

鳩.note_tr: The kunyomi はと is the primary reading in modern usage. This kanji frequently appears in animal-related vocabulary and cultural references, especially in phrases about peace or nature.

酔.note_tr: Most common as the verb 酔う (to get drunk) or in compounds like 酔い止め (motion sickness medication). The onyomi すい is rarely used in modern everyday Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to get drunk; to become intoxicated

惜.note_tr: The adjective 惜しい (pity/regret) is the most common form, widely used in everyday speech and media. The verb 惜しむ (to spare/grudge) typically takes an object and is often negated for emphasis (惜しまない), while the onyomi reading mainly appears in literary compounds like 惜別.

examples.meaning_tr: to spare / to grudge / to be stingy with
not to spare time / to dedicate time willingly (common in sports/training contexts)
to value one's life / to be cautious about one's life

穫.note_tr: This kanji uses only the on-yomi かく (kaku) and appears almost exclusively in the compound 収穫 (harvest). It has no native Japanese (kunyomi) reading and is rarely encountered independently in modern usage.

佳.note_tr: 佳 is an on'yomi-only kanji (か) used primarily in formal, literary, and artistic contexts, especially common in anime/manga discussions (佳作 for masterpiece) and culinary terms (佳肴 for delicacies). This N1-level kanji rarely appears in everyday beginner conversation.

潤.note_tr: The kunyomi readings (うるおう, うるむ) chiefly mean 'moist' or 'lubricated'; the onyomi じゅん appears in formal or technical compounds like 潤沢 (abundant) and 潤滑 (lubrication). The 'profit/benefit' sense is literary and less common in everyday speech.

examples.meaning_tr: to become moist, to be moistened

悼.note_tr: The kunyomi いたむ appears in the verb form 悼む (to mourn). The onyomi とう is used in formal compounds like 哀悼 (condolence) and 悼念 (lamentation), commonly found in news articles and formal eulogies. This kanji carries a solemn tone and is primarily used in serious or respectful contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: to mourn; to grieve over; to lament

乏.note_tr: This kanji most commonly appears as 乏しい (とぼしい), meaning "scarce" or "lacking." It is frequently paired with the particle に to indicate what is in short supply (e.g., 水に乏しい means "lacking in water").

examples.reading: じょうほうにとぼしい
しょくりょうにとぼしい

該.note_tr: 該 (gai) appears almost exclusively in compounds; only onyomi (gai) is used. Most common in formal, technical, and academic writing. The compound 該当 (gai-tō, meaning applicable/relevant) is by far the most frequently seen.

examples.meaning_tr: to apply to; to be applicable to

meanings_tr: Assume a new post, take up a position
赴.note_tr: 赴 uses two main readings: ふ (onyomi) appears primarily in formal administrative contexts like 赴任 (taking a new post), while おもむく (kunyomi) appears in literary or narrative texts meaning 'to go toward' or 'to proceed.' The kanji is relatively formal and less common in everyday conversation.

examples.meaning_tr: to take a new post, to assume an office
place of assignment, new post location

桑.note_tr: Kunyomi くわ refers to the mulberry tree itself, used in agricultural and rural contexts. Onyomi そう mainly appears in compounds like 桑園 (mulberry orchard).

桂.note_tr: The onyomi けい appears in food compounds like 肉桂 (cinnamon spice) and in shogi terminology (桂馬, knight piece), while the kunyomi かつら emphasizes the tree itself. Modern usage focuses primarily on the cinnamon/spice context.

髄.note_tr: The onyomi reading ずい (zui) is standard in all compounds; no kunyomi is common. 髄 appears frequently in medical contexts (bone marrow, cerebrospinal fluid) but also means the essence or innermost nature of something in abstract usage.

examples.meaning_tr: to one's very core; to the marrow (idiom)

虎.note_tr: Kunyomi とら is used for the tiger animal itself; onyomi こ appears primarily in set expressions like 虎視眈々. Tiger imagery is significant in Japanese martial arts terminology and cultural symbolism.

meanings_tr: Obon; the traditional Japanese summer festival
Basin; a low area surrounded by mountains
盆.note_tr: Read as ぼん. Most commonly encountered in the context of Obon (お盆), the traditional August family gathering festival. The geographical meaning 'basin' appears in terms like 盆地 (basin-shaped valley). Also found in everyday words such as 盆栽 (bonsai) and 洗面盆 (wash basin).

examples.meaning_tr: Obon; the traditional summer festival when families gather together in August
Bon dance; a traditional folk dance performed at Obon festivals
Bonsai; miniature ornamental trees grown in shallow trays
Basin; a geographical valley surrounded by mountains on all sides
Wash basin; a bowl or sink used for washing hands and face

晋.note_tr: 晋 is rare in modern Japanese, appearing mainly in formal contexts and personal names. The onyomi (しん) is used in 晋級, common in gaming and sports for rank advancement. The kunyomi (すす.む) is largely obsolete in modern usage; use 進む instead for 'to advance'."

examples.meaning_tr: Promotion, level-up, advancement in rank (common in games, sports, competitions)
A male given name (popular in anime and manga)

穂.note_tr: This kanji mainly uses the kun'yomi ほ in everyday words, typically in agricultural or nature contexts. The on'yomi すい is uncommon in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Tip of grain spike; brush point

壮.note_tr: Primarily read as そう in nearly all modern compounds; the kunyomi さかん is very rarely used. Emphasizes grandeur and vigor, distinguishing 壮 from the simpler 大 (big).

堤.note_tr: Onyomi てい is used primarily in modern compound words like 堤防 (teibou), while kunyomi つつみ appears in more traditional or literary contexts. This kanji specifically describes structures built to contain or control water, particularly riverbank embankments.

飢.note_tr: The kunyomi うえる is used for the everyday verb "to starve/go hungry"; the onyomi き typically appears in compounds such as 飢饉 (famine). Related but more severe: 餓 (to starve to death).

傍.note_tr: The onyomi ぼう is used in formal compounds like 傍観 (observation from the sidelines) and 傍観者 (bystander), expressing detachment or neutrality. The kunyomi かたわら means 'beside' and often indicates simultaneity or proximity in literary or narrative contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Observation from the sidelines; standing back without involvement

疫.note_tr: The reading えき is standard for modern words like 疫病, 疫学, and 防疫. The reading やく appears rarely, mainly in classical or folkloric terms like 疫神.

examples.meaning_tr: Plague deity; god of disease (in Japanese folklore)

累.note_tr: This kanji is almost always read as the on'yomi るい and appears primarily in compound words. The 'trouble' meaning derives from the metaphor of troubles piling up or accumulating. Rarely used with kunyomi in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: implication; involvement in trouble with others
to reach; trouble affects someone; consequences reach

痴.note_tr: This kanji predominantly uses the on-yomi reading ち in modern compounds, typically carrying derogatory or negative connotations. The kun-yomi readings are rare in contemporary Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Groper; sexual harasser on public transportation

搬.note_tr: This kanji uses only the onyomi はん. It appears in many compounds related to moving goods or cargo. Similar to 運 (to transport), but 搬 emphasizes the physical action of carrying or moving heavy items from one place to another.

examples.meaning_tr: transport; transportation; conveyance (often used for emergency evacuation or goods delivery)
to bring in; to move in (furniture, equipment, or goods into a location)
to carry out; to remove; to take out (goods or items from a place)
transportation; conveyance; carrying and moving cargo or goods

晃.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji's primary modern usage is in the adjectival noun 晃々 (こうこう), meaning 'shining' or 'glittering,' commonly found in anime and manga descriptions. It also frequently appears in male character names (e.g., Kōichi, Kōtarō). The kunyomi reading あきらか is archaic; modern Japanese uses 明らか instead for 'clear' or 'obvious.'

examples.meaning_tr: Shining, brightly (adverbial form; used as '晃々と輝く' to shine brightly)
Shining, glittering (adjectival form; as in '晃々とした瞳' meaning shining eyes)
Luminous, bright, shining (variant/classical form of 晃々)

癒.note_tr: Most commonly used with the transitive reading いやす (to soothe/comfort). The noun 癒し appears very frequently in modern Japanese. Distinguished from 治す (to medically treat), which focuses on curing rather than providing emotional comfort.

examples.meaning_tr: to heal, to soothe, to comfort
to be healed, to be comforted, to feel soothed
one's heart is comforted, one feels emotionally healed

桐.note_tr: Kunyomi きり is most common in everyday contexts. Onyomi とう appears in specialized terms like 桐油 (tung oil). The paulownia is culturally significant in Japan, valued for its lightweight wood and appearing prominently in traditional family crests and fine craftsmanship.

examples.meaning_tr: Storage box made of paulownia wood (traditional Japanese craft)
Lightweight wooden sandal made from paulownia

寸.note_tr: This kanji is primarily used in the onyomi reading すん, especially in technical and measurement contexts (e.g., 寸法). It commonly expresses concepts related to smallness or brevity in compounds.

examples.meaning_tr: One sun, a traditional unit of length (about 3 centimeters)
Stopping just short of, pulling one's punch (martial arts term)
Issun Boshi, a character from Japanese folklore; literally 'one-sun monk'

郭.note_tr: This kanji represents walls and enclosed spaces. The kunyomi くるわ is used for the enclosure or rampart itself, while the onyomi かく appears in compound words describing fortified structures (城郭) and spatial boundaries (外郭). Common in historical and fantasy contexts.

尿.note_tr: The onyomi reading にょう is the only standard reading used in modern Japanese. The kunyomi readings (ゆばり, いばり, しと) are archaic and not encountered in contemporary usage. This kanji appears almost exclusively in medical and scientific contexts, particularly in healthcare and chemistry.

examples.meaning_tr: Urea; a compound found in urine

凶.note_tr: 凶 is read きょう (on'yomi only) with no common kun'yomi. It typically appears in compounds and is used to describe something as unfortunate, evil, or dangerous. Commonly seen in anime and manga when describing villains or ominous situations.

吐.note_tr: The kunyomi 吐く (はく) expresses physical actions like spitting, vomiting, or exhaling, while the onyomi 吐 (と) typically appears in literary compounds such as 吐露 (confess). This character frequently appears in anime and manga to convey disgust or illness.

examples.meaning_tr: To spit, to vomit, to exhale
To spit out, to expel forcefully
To confess, to reveal one's true feelings

宴.note_tr: The on'yomi (えん) is more commonly used in modern contexts, particularly in compound words like 宴会 (enkai). The kun'yomi (うたげ) is more classical or literary. This kanji typically refers to formal or ceremonial social gatherings, often involving food and drink.

examples.meaning_tr: Banquet; party (especially a social gathering with drinks and food)
Banquet seat; place at a party

meanings_tr: Falcon (used broadly for birds of prey in some contexts)
鷹.note_tr: The kunyomi たか is by far the most common reading, used both alone (鷹 = hawk) and in compounds like 大鷹 or 若鷹. The onyomi おう appears in the word 鷹揚 (dignified, easygoing). The other onyomi よう is rarely used in everyday vocabulary. Don't confuse 鷹 (hawk, has 鳥-related radical 隹) with the visually similar 応 or 広, which share the top part but have unrelated meanings.

examples.meaning_tr: dignified and calm, magnanimous (lit. 'soaring like a hawk')

賓.note_tr: 賓 is a formal, literary kanji used primarily in compound words to denote guests or distinguished visitors. Always read as ひん (hin). Commonly found in ceremonial or formal contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: guest, visitor (someone who comes as a guest to an event)

虜.note_tr: The reading とりこ is most common in modern usage (especially in 恋の虜), while りょ appears in formal compounds. The kanji conveys a literary or archaic tone.

examples.meaning_tr: To be captivated by; to fall under the spell of; to become a captive
Captive to love; in love; head over heels

陶.note_tr: The onyomi (とう) dominates modern usage in pottery and ceramics terms. The kunyomi (すえ) is archaic and rarely used in contemporary Japanese.

鐘.note_tr: The kunyomi かね is used in standalone words (鐘, time bell) and basic contexts. The onyomi しょう appears in Sino-Japanese compounds like 鐘楼 (bell tower) and 警鐘 (alarm bell). A different kanji, 鈴, refers to smaller bells or chimes.

examples.meaning_tr: Time bell; the historic bell of the Edo period

憾.note_tr: The on-reading かん is far more common in practice, especially in the formal term 遺憾 (いかん). The kun-reading うら.む is attested but rarely appears in modern Japanese; the kanji 恨 is the standard character for "to resent" or "to harbor resentment."

examples.meaning_tr: to feel regret; to regret; to think it a pity
unfortunately; regrettably; much to one's regret
expression of regret; words of regret

猪.note_tr: The kunyomi いのしし refers specifically to wild boar, distinct from 豚 (domestic pig). The onyomi ちょ appears primarily in compounds and idioms like 猪突猛進 (reckless charge).

紘.note_tr: The onyomi reading こう is standard in formal or literary compounds. The kunyomi readings (つな, おおづな, つなぐ) are archaic and rarely appear in modern Japanese; modern writers prefer 綱 (つな) or 縄 (なわ) for rope. This character frequently appears in Japanese personal names, especially given names.

examples.meaning_tr: Broad dharma; universal law (Buddhist philosophical term)

磁.note_tr: Always uses the onyomi じ; no kunyomi. The homophones 磁気 (magnetism) and 磁器 (porcelain) are context-dependent, context and compound word help distinguish them.

弥.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 弥 is most commonly encountered in the month name 弥生 (やよい – March) and the Yayoi historical period. The adverbial meaning "increasingly" is archaic or literary, appearing mainly in formal or ceremonial contexts. The kanji typically uses kun'yomi (や) for historical and calendar words, and onyomi (み) for Buddhist terms.

examples.meaning_tr: March (the third month of the year); also refers to the Yayoi period, an important era in early Japanese history (roughly 300 BCE–300 CE)
Yayoi period – a foundational era in Japanese history marked by the introduction of wet-rice agriculture and new technologies from the continent
Maitreya Bodhisattva – an important Buddhist deity; commonly depicted in anime, manga, traditional art, and temples as a compassionate future Buddha
Lasting prosperity, eternal glory – used in ceremonial blessings and formal toasts (archaic/formal style); conveys hopes for enduring success and flourishing
A traditional Japanese male given name; historically famous from Sakuma Yosuke's retainer in the 15th century (appears in historical fiction and anime)

昆.note_tr: This kanji primarily uses the onyomi こん and is rarely found in isolation. It most commonly appears in 昆虫 (insect) and 昆布 (kelp), both everyday vocabulary words. The archaic meanings "descendants" and "elder brother" are rarely used in modern Japanese.

粗.note_tr: The kunyomi form (あらい) functions as an i-adjective describing coarse or rough texture, surface, behavior, or manner. The onyomi (そ) appears primarily in compounds like 粗末 (rough treatment) and 粗悪 (poor quality). Avoid confusing with 荒 (wild, desolate), which emphasizes wilderness and abandonment rather than crudeness.

examples.meaning_tr: Coarse; rough (used to describe texture, surface, behavior, or manner)
Crude; simple; rough treatment (often implies poor or careless treatment)
Poor quality; crude; inferior (describes low-quality products or materials)
Coarse salt (culinary ingredient used in cooking)
Rough-hewn; crudely shaped (describes roughly carved or shaped objects in art and craftsmanship)

訂.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 訂 is almost always read using the onyomi てい (tei) in compounds. The kunyomi ただす is rarely used in contemporary texts.

芽.note_tr: The kunyomi め is far more common in everyday vocabulary, appearing in words like 新芽 (new sprout) and 芽が出る (to sprout). The onyomi が typically appears in formal or compound terms like 発芽 (germination). Do not confuse 芽 with the visually similar kanji 目 (eye/mark); while both can share the reading め in certain words, 芽 specifically refers to plant buds or sprouts.

examples.meaning_tr: To sprout; to emerge; to come forth

庄.note_tr: This kanji primarily appears in historical Japanese contexts referring to feudal landholding units and village administration. The reading しょう is most common and appears in 庄園 (manor/estate) and 庄屋 (village headman).

傘.note_tr: The kunyomi reading かさ is standard for everyday use. Note the rendaku (sound changes) in compounds like 日傘 (ひがさ) and 雨傘 (あまがさ) where かさ becomes がさ.

敦.note_tr: This kanji is rare in modern Japanese and appears mainly in literary contexts, historical references, and proper nouns. The onyomi readings are far more productive than the kunyomi; the reading atsui is less common than the synonymous 厚い. Expect to encounter 敦煌 (Dunhuang) in history or travel contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Dunhuang (ancient city in northwestern China; important historical and Silk Road reference)
earnest and kind-hearted; sincere and thick-hearted

meanings_tr: counter for riders or mounted soldiers
騎.note_tr: 騎 uses only the on'yomi reading き and appears almost exclusively in compounds. This kanji is common in historical, fantasy, and sports contexts, expect to see it frequently in anime, manga, games, and historical fiction.

寧.note_tr: The kunyomi むしろ (rather, preferably) is the most frequently encountered usage in modern Japanese, appearing in both formal speech and written contexts. The onyomi ねい appears primarily in classical or literary compounds expressing peace and quietness. This is an advanced N1 kanji with limited everyday usage.

循.note_tr: This kanji primarily appears in compound words with the on'yomi reading じゅん (jun), expressing cyclical or sequential movement. Distinguish it from the similar kanji 順 (order), which emphasizes arrangement rather than cyclical motion.

忍.note_tr: Use the onyomi にん in compounds like 忍者 (ninja) and 忍耐 (patience); use the kunyomi しのぶ as a verb meaning to endure, bear, or conceal. The kanji is especially popular in anime and manga due to its strong association with ninja culture.

examples.meaning_tr: Ninja; a trained martial artist from feudal Japan
To endure; to bear; to conceal
To sneak in; to creep in; to steal into

怠.note_tr: The kunyomi なま.ける (to be lazy, to slack off) is more common in everyday speech and anime/manga. The on'yomi たい appears in formal compound words like 怠慢 (negligence) and 怠惰 (laziness). The kunyomi おこた.る (to neglect) is more formal and rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: To be lazy, to slack off, to avoid work
To be negligent, to neglect, to fail to do

如.note_tr: The kun reading ごと.し forms literary/classical compounds ごとき (like, resembling) and ごとく (as if, following). The on reading にょ appears in Buddhist terminology (如来); じょ is used in comparative expressions (不如, inferior to). The kanji fundamentally expresses similarity or resemblance.

examples.meaning_tr: Tathagata, Buddha; an enlightened being in Buddhism
Like, resembling, such as; used in literary and manga contexts
Inferior to, not as good as; used in comparisons
As if, like, in the manner of; literary/classical form
True nature, the actual state of things

寮.note_tr: This kanji denotes institutional group housing such as student dormitories or company employee housing. It is always read as りょう (ryō) with no kunyomi variant. Unlike 宿 (general inn/accommodation), 寮 specifically refers to organized residential facilities with formal management and shared amenities.

examples.reading: じゅうぎょういんりょう

祐.note_tr: 祐 is primarily found in personal names (especially common in anime and manga character names) rather than in everyday vocabulary. The ゆう reading dominates modern usage; the kunyomi reading たす.ける is rarely used in contemporary Japanese, with 助ける being the standard word for 'to help' instead.

examples.meaning_tr: Yuichi, a very common male name
divine protection; safeguard (formal or classical context)

鵬.note_tr: A rare N1 kanji from Chinese mythology emphasizing vastness and freedom. The onyomi ほう appears in literary compounds and classical references; the kunyomi おおとり is rarely used in modern Japanese. Do not confuse with 鳳 (phoenix), which refers more specifically to a mythical fire-bird. This kanji appears mainly in proper names, classical literature, and fantasy contexts in anime/manga.

examples.meaning_tr: The Great Phoenix; vast heaven (also the name of the legendary sumo wrestler Taihō)
Boundless prospects; vast distance; unlimited potential (from classical Chinese literature)
Wings of the great bird; soaring wings (poetic/classical usage)

鉛.note_tr: The onyomi えん (en) dominates in compounds like 鉛筆 (pencil) and 鉛中毒 (lead poisoning), while the kunyomi なまり (namari) appears mainly in descriptive terms like 鉛色 (lead-colored). This kanji refers to the metal element itself, not the past tense "led." Similar-looking: 沿 (yoi/en, "along") shares the えん reading but has an entirely different meaning, distinguish by context.

珠.note_tr: Pearl is the primary meaning, especially in 真珠. The on'yomi しゅ appears in literary compounds like 珠玉 (precious thing); the kun'yomi たま refers to beads or spheres. Do not confuse 珠 with 玉 (jade, sphere, ball) or 球 (sphere, globe).

凝.note_tr: The onyomi ぎょう appears in most compound words (凝視, 凝固, 凝結), often used metaphorically for intense focus or staring in anime and manga. The kunyomi こ.る emphasizes physical stiffening or freezing.

examples.meaning_tr: To freeze; to stiffen; to become rigid

苗.note_tr: The kunyomi (なえ) is used for seedlings and young plants in everyday contexts. The variant reading (なわ-) appears in traditional agricultural terms like 苗代 (rice seedbed).

examples.meaning_tr: Rice seedbed; nursery where rice seedlings are grown

獣.note_tr: The onyomi じゅう is standard in compounds (獣医 veterinarian, 獣人 beastman), appearing in writing and formal contexts. The kunyomi けもの is everyday speech for "animal" or "beast"; けだもの is a slightly emphatic or archaic variant emphasizing the savage nature. Often appears in anime/manga titles and fantasy contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: beastman; beast humanoid (common in anime and fantasy games)
animal trail; path made by animals

哀.note_tr: The kunyomi かな.しい and あわ.れ appear in narrative and everyday contexts common in anime and manga. The onyomi あい is reserved for formal or literary compound words (哀愁, 哀悼). Do not confuse with 悲 (hi), which is more frequently used in modern Japanese for the emotion 'sadness'.

examples.meaning_tr: Pathos, melancholy, sense of sadness and beauty

跳.note_tr: は.ねる (ha.neru) means to bounce, while と.ぶ (to.bu) means to jump, the most common readings. The onyomi ちょう appears in formal compounds like 跳躍 (jumping).

匠.note_tr: Kunyomi たくみ is used for the standalone word meaning 'artisan' or 'craftsperson'; onyomi しょう appears in compounds like 名匠 (master craftsman). This kanji emphasizes skill and artistic mastery in craftsmanship.

examples.meaning_tr: Master craftsman; renowned artisan; master of a craft
Masterful technique; the craftsmanship of a skilled artisan

垂.note_tr: Onyomi (すい) appears in formal compounds like 垂直 (vertical), while kunyomi (たれる, たらす) describes the action of hanging or dripping. Common in cooking contexts where sauces drip.

examples.meaning_tr: to drip, to let hang down

蛇.note_tr: Use へび for everyday 'snake.' Onyomi readings じゃ and だ appear mainly in compounds and idioms like 蛇足 (literally 'snake foot', meaning unnecessary addition). This N1 kanji's basic form is quite beginner-friendly.

澄.note_tr: 澄 primarily uses kunyomi readings (す.む for intransitive 'to become/be clear', す.ます for transitive 'to clarify'). The onyomi ちょう is rare in modern usage. Commonly describes water, sky, voice, eyes, and mind becoming or being clear, frequent in anime character descriptions and nature writing.

examples.meaning_tr: to become clear, to clear up
to be completely clear and transparent
one's mind becomes clear or serene

縫.note_tr: The kunyomi ぬ.う is used in everyday verbs like 縫う (to sew). The onyomi ほう appears in more formal technical compounds such as 縫製 (tailoring) and 縫合 (surgical suturing).

僧.note_tr: This kanji uses only the onyomi そう and appears in Buddhist religious contexts. It specifically refers to Buddhist monks or priests (typically male).

examples.meaning_tr: high priest; eminent monk; venerable monk

眺.note_tr: Use ながめる (kunyomi) as the main verb meaning 'to gaze at' or 'to contemplate'; ちょう (onyomi) appears in formal compounds like 眺望. Often describes a contemplative or leisurely looking at scenery, distinct from 見る (simply seeing) and 観る (formally observing).

examples.meaning_tr: To gaze at, to look at, to view
To admire the scenery, to gaze at the landscape
To gaze out at the sea, to look out at the ocean
To look out from a window

亘.note_tr: This kanji primarily uses the kun'yomi reading わたる in modern Japanese. It typically appears with temporal or spatial expressions (like 終日, 全国) to indicate something extends or continues across a period or area. The on'yomi readings are rarely encountered in everyday usage.

examples.meaning_tr: throughout the country; spanning the nation
spanning a year; lasting throughout the year

meanings_tr: to give; to do something for someone
呉.note_tr: The onyomi ご is commonly used in historical and place-name contexts such as 呉国 (Kingdom of Wu). The kunyomi く.れる appears in the common verb くれる, meaning "to give to me/us," though in modern Japanese this verb is almost always written entirely in hiragana rather than using the kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: to give; to do something for someone

凡.note_tr: The onyomi ぼん is most common, especially in anime/manga contexts (凡人 for ordinary character, 非凡 for extraordinary). The onyomi はん appears less frequently (mainly in technical terms like 凡例). Kunyomi およそ means 'approximately' and is useful in everyday speech.

examples.meaning_tr: An ordinary person; an average person
Legend; key (of a diagram, map, or chart)

憩.note_tr: The kunyomi forms (いこう/いこい) appear in both literary and modern Japanese, while the onyomi けい is used mainly in formal or technical compounds. Distinguish from 休 (きゅう/やすむ), which simply means to take a break or rest, without the deeper connotation of peace or repose that 憩 carries.

examples.meaning_tr: To rest; to take a break
A place of rest; a spot to relax
A moment of rest during travel

媛.note_tr: The kun'yomi reading ひめ is the primary modern usage. The on'yomi reading えん appears chiefly in names and classical texts. Similar to 姫 (ひめ), which is more common for "princess" in everyday Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Ehime Prefecture, a prefecture in southwestern Japan
A princess; a lady of noble rank (formal or classical)

溝.note_tr: The kunyomi みぞ is used for the basic word and figurative expressions about "gaps" (e.g., 知識の溝 "knowledge gap"); the onyomi こう appears mainly in technical compound words like 側溝 (roadside ditch) and 排水溝 (drain).

examples.meaning_tr: Roadside ditch; drainage ditch along a road

恭.note_tr: In formal compounds like 恭敬 (respect), the onyomi きょう is used. In narrative and descriptive contexts, the kunyomi form うやうやしい (respectful, deferential) appears frequently in literature and anime, especially when depicting characters showing deference or polite behavior toward superiors.

刈.note_tr: The kunyomi 刈る (かる) is the standard form used as a verb meaning "to cut" or "to mow," especially in gardening and harvesting contexts. The onyomi readings (がい, かい) appear rarely in everyday speech and are found mainly in classical or literary compounds. This kanji is very useful for nature-related vocabulary.

睡.note_tr: The onyomi すい is standard in modern sleep-related compounds. The kunyomi ねむ.る and ねむ.い are rarely used with this kanji; instead, 眠 (ねむ) is more common for everyday sleepiness. Both kanji share similar meanings, learn to distinguish them.

examples.meaning_tr: Sleepiness, drowsiness (literally 'sleep demon', common in anime and manga)

錯.note_tr: The onyomi さく (saku) is standard in modern Japanese; しゃく (shaku) is rarely used. Distinguish from 誤 (go/ayamaru), which means simple factual error, 錯 emphasizes confusion, tanglement, or perceptual mistakes.

伯.note_tr: A formal kanji primarily used in nobility titles like 伯爵 (Count/Earl), commonly seen in fantasy and historical anime. The 'uncle' meaning (father's older brother) in 伯父 is archaic.

笹.note_tr: This is a kokuji (Japanese-created character) with only the kunyomi reading ささ; it has no onyomi. It appears frequently in food contexts (bamboo leaf wrappings) and nature-related words, making it useful for learners interested in food and traditional Japanese settings.

examples.meaning_tr: bamboo leaf rice cake; a Japanese dumpling wrapped in bamboo leaves
small paper boat folded from a bamboo leaf

穀.note_tr: 穀 is typically used in formal, food-related, or historical contexts. The on'yomi reading こく is standard in compounds. Not commonly used as a standalone kanji in everyday speech.

examples.meaning_tr: five grains (rice, wheat, millet, beans, and either barley or sorghum)

陵.note_tr: This kanji appears primarily in historical and formal contexts describing mausoleums and burial sites. The onyomi reading (りょう) dominates in modern compounds, while the kunyomi (みささぎ) traditionally refers to imperial tombs specifically.

霧.note_tr: The kunyomi reading きり is the standard and most common; the onyomi readings (む、ぼう、ぶ) are rarely used independently. Frequently appears in anime and manga for atmospheric descriptions and nature scenes.

魂.note_tr: Use たましい for the standalone concept of soul or spirit; こん primarily appears in compound words. Do not confuse with 霊 (れい), another kanji meaning spirit with different nuances.

examples.meaning_tr: Ghost, spirit of a dead person
To be startled, to be amazed

弊.note_tr: 弊 is primarily used in formal or written contexts, often appearing in humble/modest expressions about one's own company or store (弊社, 弊店). It carries a negative connotation when used independently and is rarely encountered in everyday conversation or anime/manga aimed at beginners.

examples.meaning_tr: our company (humble/formal expression used by a company about itself)
our store (humble/formal expression used by a shop about itself)
bad habit; vice; corruption; evil custom

meanings_tr: queen (especially consort of a king or emperor)
妃.note_tr: The kunyomi きさき is used in classical or standalone contexts. The onyomi ひ appears primarily in compounds and formal contexts. This kanji refers specifically to imperial or royal women of high status, common in historical and fantasy settings.

examples.meaning_tr: queen; queen consort (wife of a king)
Your Imperial Highness; Her Imperial Majesty (formal address)

舶.note_tr: This kanji mainly appears in compounds like 舶来 (imported goods), derived from the concept of foreign goods arriving by ship. Only onyomi reading (はく) is used.

餓.note_tr: The onyomi が appears mainly in compound words like 餓死 (starvation death) and 飢餓 (famine), while the kunyomi うえる forms the verb 餓える (to starve). In anime and manga, 餓鬼 (demon/brat) is a common word to encounter.

examples.meaning_tr: To starve; to be very hungry
Demon; brat (common in anime and manga)

窮.note_tr: On'yomi きゅう is standard in all modern compounds. The alternative きょう and kun'yomi forms are archaic and rarely appear outside classical literature. The core sense spans financial poverty, physical confinement, and desperate situations alike.

examples.meaning_tr: destitution; poverty; being in dire straits

掌.note_tr: Use kunyomi てのひら when referring to the literal body part (palm). Onyomi しょう appears mainly in compounds like 掌握 (to grasp/control) and 掌編 (short story); the metaphorical sense derives from holding something in your palm.

examples.meaning_tr: to grasp; to control; to have a firm grip on (a situation, information, etc.)
in the palm of one's hand; within one's grasp
palm of the hand (medical or formal register)

麗.note_tr: 麗 most commonly appears with onyomi reading れい in compound words like 美麗 (beautiful) and 華麗 (gorgeous). The kunyomi form うるわしい is a poetic/formal adjective; this kanji is more elegant and literary than everyday beauty words like 美しい.

綾.note_tr: The kunyomi あや is far more common in everyday Japanese, especially in words related to patterns, elegance, and the traditional children's game cat's cradle. The onyomi りん is rarely encountered in common usage and appears mainly in specialized or formal contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Wave pattern; rippled or undulating design
Elegance; grace; refinement; pattern or design
Twill weaving (a type of fabric weave creating diagonal patterns)

臭.note_tr: The reading くさい (kun'yomi) is the most common, used as an i-adjective. The reading しゅう (on'yomi) appears in formal compound words like 悪臭 and 体臭. The readings にお.う and におい are less frequently encountered than くさい in modern Japanese.

悦.note_tr: The kunyomi よろこぶ forms the verb 悦ぶ (to be pleased) and noun 悦び (joy), which appear in everyday speech. The onyomi えつ appears mainly in formal or literary compound words like 喜悦 (joy) and 悦楽 (pleasure).

刃.note_tr: The kun'yomi reading は appears in most everyday words. The on'yomi reading じん is used in more formal or literary compounds like 剣刃.

examples.meaning_tr: Blade tip; the sharp point of a blade
Double-edged blade; having two sharp edges
Sword blade; blade of a sword
A sword's blade; the sharp edge of a sword

縛.note_tr: The kunyomi reading しば.る is used for the standalone verb meaning 'to bind' or 'to tie'; the onyomi reading ばく typically appears in compound words like 束縛 (restraint/bondage). Both readings share the core concept of physically or mentally restricting something.

meanings_tr: System of counting days and months
暦.note_tr: Use the kunyomi こよみ when 暦 stands alone, especially in everyday speech about "calendar" or "almanac." The onyomi れき is used in compounds like 暦年 (calendar year) and 太陽暦 (solar calendar). Do not confuse 暦 with 歴 (history/record), a different kanji entirely.

宜.note_tr: The kunyomi よろ.しい／よろ.しく appears in everyday greetings like よろしく and よろしくお願いします, though in modern writing these are usually written in hiragana rather than with the kanji 宜. The onyomi ぎ shows up in more formal, written compounds such as 適宜 and 便宜, meaning "as appropriate" or "convenience."

examples.meaning_tr: kind regards; please treat me well (common greeting)

examples.reading: よろしくおねがいします
examples.meaning_tr: please treat me favorably / nice to meet you (polite set phrase)
good, fine, all right (polite form of 良い)
as appropriate, suitably, at one's discretion

盲.note_tr: The onyomi もう is the standard reading in modern Japanese and appears in most compounds. The kunyomi めくら is less common in contemporary usage but may appear in older texts or as a standalone adjective.

examples.meaning_tr: blindness; also used figuratively to mean being unaware or ignorant of something

粋.note_tr: The kunyomi いき appears mainly in the adjective form 粋な (chic, stylish). The onyomi すい is used in compounds like 粋人 (sophisticated person) and with the negative prefix 不粋 (inelegant). This kanji reflects traditional Japanese aesthetic values, particularly from the Edo period.

examples.meaning_tr: a refined person, a sophisticated individual

辱.note_tr: The on'yomi じょく typically appears in compounds like 屈辱 (humiliation), while the kun'yomi はずかしめる is used for the verb meaning "to shame" or "to embarrass someone." This kanji carries connotations of losing honor or face.

examples.meaning_tr: to shame; to embarrass; to disgrace
to suffer humiliation; to be insulted

毅.note_tr: 毅 emphasizes moral strength and resolute character, not physical strength, contrast this with 強. It appears almost exclusively in compounds using the onyomi readings (き or ぎ); the kun-reading is rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Resolutely; in a firm and determined manner
Resolute and dauntless; showing great moral strength

轄.note_tr: The onyomi かつ is standard in administrative and governance contexts (管轄, 統轄). The kunyomi くさび refers to 'wedge' but is uncommon in modern usage. Expect this N1 kanji mainly in texts about law, government, or organizational structure.

examples.meaning_tr: Jurisdiction; administrative authority over an area
Comprehensive control; overall command of an organization

猿.note_tr: Kunyomi さる is the standard everyday reading used for the animal monkey, particularly common in manga and anime. Onyomi えん is rarely used in modern Japanese and appears mainly in historical or specialized contexts.

meanings_tr: String (especially bowstring or stringed instrument string)
弦.note_tr: The on-reading げん typically appears in compound words like 弦楽器 (stringed instrument), common in formal and technical contexts. The kun-reading つる is the standalone word, used in classical texts and everyday speech when referring to a single string or bowstring.

稔.note_tr: The kunyomi みのる/みのり (to ripen, harvest) is used in everyday and literary contexts describing crops or plants. Onyomi ねん appears in formal compound words like 豊稔 (bumper harvest). Often found in agricultural, seasonal, or classical texts.

examples.meaning_tr: to ripen, to mature, to bear fruit
ears of rice ripen, rice matures

窒.note_tr: This kanji primarily uses the onyomi reading ちつ (or ちっ in geminated compounds). It appears most commonly in 窒素 (nitrogen) and 窒息 (asphyxiation/suffocation), with no standard kunyomi readings in modern usage.

炊.note_tr: This kanji primarily refers to cooking rice in Japanese. Use the on'yomi すい in formal or technical terms like 炊飯器 (rice cooker), and the kun'yomi た.く in the everyday verb 炊く (to cook rice).

examples.meaning_tr: Rice cooked with various ingredients mixed in

洪.note_tr: 洪 is used exclusively with on'yomi (こう); no productive kun'yomi exists. Most commonly found in 洪水 (flood), which appears frequently in news reports and disaster contexts. This kanji is rare outside of formal or classical writing.

meanings_tr: To take in; to intake; to consume
To manage; to oversee; to preside over
To act as; to serve as; to hold an office
Vicarious; on behalf of another; surrogate
摂.note_tr: 摂 primarily appears in onyomi compounds (せつ/しょう) in formal or technical contexts rather than as a standalone verb. The most familiar everyday word is 摂氏 (Celsius), commonly seen in weather reports and temperature contexts. The character typically conveys meanings of both 'taking in' and 'managing or overseeing.'"

examples.meaning_tr: Celsius; Centigrade (the temperature scale used in most countries)
Intake; consumption; the act of ingesting (especially food, nutrients, or calories)
Regent; a person who rules or governs on behalf of a monarch or superior (historical term)

meanings_tr: to tire of / to get bored
飽.note_tr: The kunyomi 飽きる is most common in everyday speech and media, expressing boredom or weariness with something. The onyomi 飽和 is used in technical contexts such as color saturation or market saturation.

examples.meaning_tr: to become tired of / to get bored
got bored / got tired of (past tense)
fed up with / sick and tired of

冗.note_tr: This kanji appears only with the onyomi reading じょう; there is no kunyomi. It is commonly used in formal and technical contexts to express redundancy and verbosity, as well as in the very common everyday word 冗談 (joke).

桃.note_tr: The kunyomi もも is the everyday word for the peach fruit and is most common at beginner level. The onyomi とう appears in compounds and formal contexts like 白桃 (white peach) or 桃園 (peach orchard).

examples.meaning_tr: Momotarō (Peach Boy, famous Japanese folk tale)

狩.note_tr: The kunyomi readings (かり, かる) are used in everyday words like 狩人 (hunter) and 狩り (hunting), while the onyomi (しゅ) appears in formal compounds like 狩猟. Don't confuse 狩 with similar-sounding 刈る (to cut/reap), which uses different kanji.

朱.note_tr: The onyomi (しゅ) dominates modern usage, appearing in all common compounds; the kunyomi (あけ) is rarely seen in contemporary words. Historically, 朱 refers to the red pigment cinnabar and is found in traditional art, official seals, and formal documents.

examples.meaning_tr: Red ink paste (used with name seals and stamps)
Red pen or red brush (for marking/writing in red)
Written or marked in red ink

渦.note_tr: The kunyomi うず is used in most everyday words and nouns. The onyomi か appears mainly in formal or literary compounds like 渦中 (in the midst of turmoil). Beginners should focus on the うず reading first, as it appears in much more common vocabulary.

examples.meaning_tr: In the midst of; at the center of (turmoil, conflict, etc.)

紳.note_tr: The kanji 紳 has only the onyomi reading しん with no kunyomi. It primarily appears in formal or respectful contexts, most commonly in 紳士 (gentleman). You'll encounter this kanji mainly in formal literature, historical texts, anime/manga with period settings, and when discussing refined or dignified individuals.

枢.note_tr: The onyomi reading すう is most common in modern compounds. The kunyomi からくり relates to mechanisms and tricks, reflecting the rotating pivot concept of the kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: Axis; pivot point; the Axis powers (WWII)
Privy Council (an advisory body to the government)

碑.note_tr: The onyomi reading ひ is used in virtually all modern compounds. The kunyomi いしぶみ is archaic and rarely appears in contemporary writing. This kanji frequently appears in historical and travel contexts, especially in compounds like 記念碑 (commemorative monument) and 戦争記念碑 (war memorial).

鍛.note_tr: The kunyomi 鍛える (kitaeru) is used for training or building up skills, body, or character. The onyomi たん appears mainly in technical terms like 鍛造 (tanzo, forging).

examples.meaning_tr: To train, to strengthen, to forge (one's character or skills)
To train or build one's body; to get in shape
To train or strengthen one's mind or spirit
Forging; the metalworking process of shaping metal through heating and hammering

刀.note_tr: When 刀 stands alone, use kunyomi かたな. In compound words, use onyomi とう. The reading そり is less common and refers to curved blades.
