examples.meaning_tr: Brave and spirited (used adjectivally); dauntless and courageous

漸.note_tr: The kunyomi ようやく is by far the most common reading, usually written as 漸く or even just in kana (ようやく) meaning "finally" or "at last, barely." The onyomi ぜん appears mainly in formal/written compounds about gradual change (漸次, 漸進, 漸増, 漸減). Be careful not to confuse 漸 with the similar-looking kanji 暫 (ざん, "temporary," as in 暫定 ざんてい); the two are easy to mix up by shape but have unrelated meanings.

蚊.note_tr: Almost always uses the kunyomi 'ka' in modern Japanese. The onyomi 'bun' is extremely rare in contemporary usage, so focus on learning the 'ka' reading as a beginner.

meanings_tr: A plant of the mallow family
A traditional symbol of summer in classical Japanese poetry
葵.note_tr: The kunyomi reading あおい is the primary and most common reading for this kanji. Although あおい can also mean "blue" when written as 青い, this kanji specifically denotes the hollyhock flower, which is deeply significant in Japanese cultural and historical contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Aoi Festival; one of Kyoto's three major traditional festivals, celebrated annually on May 15th
Hollyhock; a flowering plant with showy blooms in the mallow family, also commonly used as a Japanese given name
Asarum sieboldii; a woodland plant with heart-shaped leaves belonging to the wild ginger family

厄.note_tr: 厄 reads only as やく (onyomi) with no kunyomi. It appears mainly in traditional or formal contexts like 厄年 (unlucky year, age 25/42 for men, 19/33 for women in Japanese culture) and 厄介 (troublesome/annoying). The kanji often carries cultural or spiritual significance rather than everyday usage.

examples.meaning_tr: Unlucky year; age believed to be prone to misfortune (25, 42 for men; 19, 33 for women)
Charm or talisman to ward off bad luck
Ritual purification; ceremony to dispel misfortune

藻.note_tr: The onyomi そう is more common in compounds like 海藻 (seaweed) and 藻類 (algae). The kunyomi も is less frequently used but appears in standalone or simpler contexts. Though an N1 kanji, 藻 frequently appears in food and nature-related contexts, making it useful despite the advanced level.

禄.note_tr: The onyomi reading ろく dominates modern Japanese, appearing in compound words like 俸禄 (official salary) and the formal phrase 禄寿 (prosperity and longevity). The kunyomi readings are archaic and rarely encountered in contemporary usage.

examples.meaning_tr: To receive a salary or hold an official position

孟.note_tr: 孟 appears most frequently in historical and literary contexts. The もう reading dominates modern usage, especially in 孟子 (Mencius, the ancient Chinese sage-philosopher). Classical seasonal compounds (孟春, 孟夏, etc.) meaning the first month of each season appear in poetry and historical texts. The kunyomi かしら is rarely used in contemporary Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Mencius; an ancient Chinese philosopher and sage, famous in East Asian philosophy and history
early spring; the first month of spring (classical/poetic term)
early summer; the first month of summer (classical/poetic term)
early autumn; the first month of autumn (classical/poetic term)
early winter; the first month of winter (classical/poetic term)

嫡.note_tr: 嫡 uses the onyomi reading ちゃく in nearly all modern contexts, describing legitimate family lines, heirs, or a main wife, common in historical anime and manga. The alternative reading てき is rare and appears mainly in specialized academic texts.

meanings_tr: Virtuous, enlightened (archaic; from legendary sage-king Yao)
尭.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji appears almost exclusively in historical and classical texts referring to the legendary Chinese sage-king Yao (尭帝). The onyomi ぎょう dominates actual usage; the kunyomi たか.い is virtually never encountered in modern Japanese, since 高 is the standard kanji for 'high'.

examples.meaning_tr: Yao and Shun; legendary wise rulers of ancient China
Emperor Yao; legendary virtuous ruler of China
Sage Yao; exemplar of wisdom and virtue
Virtue or benevolence of Yao; moral exemplar

嚇.note_tr: The kunyomi おど.す is the primary reading in modern Japanese, appearing in everyday verbs meaning "to threaten" or "to intimidate." The onyomi かく appears in formal compound words like 嚇迫. Note: the kanji 脅 is more commonly used for these meanings in contemporary Japanese, though 嚇 is also valid.

meanings_tr: Sign of the Snake (Serpent) in the Chinese zodiac
the hours of 9-11am in the old Japanese time system
the sixth sign of the twelve zodiac signs
巳.note_tr: This kanji almost always appears in zodiac or old-calendar contexts, read as み in words like 巳年 (Year of the Snake); the onyomi し shows up in classical/compound terms like 上巳. Don't confuse it with the visually similar 己 (self, おのれ/こ) or 已 (already, い); all three look alike but have completely different meanings.

examples.meaning_tr: Year of the Snake (in the Chinese zodiac)
Day of the Snake (a day in the traditional calendar cycle)
the hour of the Snake, roughly 9-11am in the old time system
the Double Third festival (an old seasonal festival, related to today's Doll's Festival)

凸.note_tr: The onyomi とつ (totsu) appears primarily in technical or formal contexts, especially in 凸版 (relief printing) and 凸レンズ (convex lens). The kunyomi でこ (deko) is most common in the everyday word 凸凹 (でこぼこ, bumpy/uneven), which you may encounter in manga or casual conversation.

暢.note_tr: The onyomi ちょう appears regularly in formal or literary compounds, with 流暢 being particularly common in language studies. The kunyomi のび.る is rarely used in modern Japanese. Not to be confused with 伸 (shin), which is the standard kanji for physical stretching or extension.

examples.meaning_tr: Fluent; smooth and natural-sounding (especially of language ability)
Unobstructed; free-flowing (of passage, traffic, or communication)
Eloquent; fluent and expressive in speech or writing

韻.note_tr: 韻 is always pronounced いん (on'yomi) with no kun'yomi. It primarily appears in literary, poetic, and musical contexts, especially in words describing rhyming patterns and elegant language."

examples.meaning_tr: to rhyme; to create rhyming words (common in rap and music)
rhyming; rhyme scheme in poetry or music
end rhyme; rhyme at the end of lines
alliteration; repetition of initial sounds in words

霜.note_tr: The kun'yomi (しも) is used in everyday and traditional contexts describing frost phenomena, while the on'yomi (そう) appears mainly in formal compounds. This kanji typically refers to frost formed on the ground or other surfaces during cold nights.

examples.meaning_tr: Frost forms; frost falls on the ground
Frost pillars; thin needle-like ice formations
Marbled beef; highly graded beef with frost-like fat patterns

硝.note_tr: This kanji uses only the onyomi reading しょう (no kunyomi). It appears primarily in chemistry and historical contexts, forming compounds for nitrates and saltpeter, materials historically important for gunpowder and fireworks production.

勅.note_tr: This N1 kanji is primarily used in historical and formal contexts. The onyomi ちょく (choku) dominates modern usage, appearing in compounds describing imperial authority and government decrees. You'll encounter it frequently in historical anime and manga set in feudal or imperial Japan. The kunyomi readings are rare in contemporary Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Imperial intention; the will of the emperor

芹.note_tr: The reading せり is used in everyday contexts when referring to the vegetable itself, while きん appears mainly in compound words. This is food and nature-related vocabulary commonly used in Japanese cooking.

杏.note_tr: The kunyomi あんず (anzu) is the common everyday reading for apricot fruit and tree. The onyomi きょう appears mainly in compounds like 杏仁 (apricot kernel), a popular ingredient in Asian desserts and traditional medicine.

examples.meaning_tr: Almond tofu (Chinese dessert with apricot kernel)

棺.note_tr: This kanji almost always appears in funeral-related compounds using the onyomi かん; it is rarely used alone as a standalone word. Be careful not to confuse it with the visually similar kanji 官 (かん, "official"), which has a completely different meaning.

examples.meaning_tr: coffin (the everyday word for a coffin box)
the coffin leaving the house/hall for the funeral procession
placing the body into the coffin (part of funeral rites)

儒.note_tr: The kanji 儒 uses only the on'yomi じゅ (ju) in modern Japanese; there is no kun'yomi. It appears almost exclusively in academic and historical contexts related to Confucian philosophy and East Asian intellectual history, making it primarily an N1/advanced vocabulary item.

examples.meaning_tr: Confucianism (as a religion or teaching system)
a Confucian scholar; a follower of Confucianism
the Confucian school; Confucianism as a philosophical tradition

鳳.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 鳳 almost always appears in the compound 鳳凰 (ほうおう, phoenix). The onyomi ほう is standard; ふう is archaic or rarely used in contemporary language. This kanji enriches anime, manga, and historical contexts with mythological significance.

examples.meaning_tr: Phoenix; legendary pair of birds (male and female together)
Flame tree; Royal Poinciana (ornamental tropical tree)
Horainji Temple; a historic temple in Aichi Prefecture, Japan

馨.note_tr: This elegant, literary kanji primarily means "fragrant" or "fragrance." Use kunyomi かおり for the noun form "fragrance," while onyomi けい appears in formal compounds and traditional names. Often found in poetry, literature, and descriptions of aromas.

examples.meaning_tr: to be fragrant, to emit fragrance

慧.note_tr: This advanced N1 kanji appears most commonly in the compound 慧眼 (keen eye; penetrating insight), using the けい reading. The kunyomi さとい is less frequent in modern Japanese. The え reading is found mainly in Buddhist terminology such as 慧根 (spiritual wisdom).

examples.meaning_tr: keen eye; discerning perception; penetrating insight; astute observation
spiritual wisdom; spiritual capacity; aptitude for enlightenment

愁.note_tr: The onyomi しゅう appears in formal compounds; the kunyomi うれい/うれ.える is used in simpler or standalone expressions. This kanji is primarily found in literary, poetic, or formal contexts to express emotional pain or sorrow.

examples.meaning_tr: Autumn melancholy; the sadness felt during autumn

楼.note_tr: 楼 primarily uses the on-reading ろう when naming types of buildings and structures; the kun-reading たかどの is rare in modern Japanese. Distinguish from 塔 (tower/pagoda), which refers to standalone structures, 楼 typically describes tall residential or commercial buildings with multiple stories.

彬.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji appears primarily in formal and literary Japanese, and is frequently used in personal names. The onyomi ひん is standard in compounds like 彬彬; the onyomi ふん is archaic. The kunyomi forms (うるわしい 'beautiful' and あきらか 'clear') are obsolete in modern usage.

examples.meaning_tr: Refined and cultured; elegant manner or bearing
Elegant and refined in appearance or style
In a refined and elegant manner; with grace and sophistication

匡.note_tr: The on'yomi きょう is most common in documented compounds like 匡正 (correction) and 匡救 (rescue). The kun'yomi すく.う appears mainly in classical or formal Japanese expressions with meanings of 'to help' or 'to save.' The on'yomi おう is rarely used in modern vocabulary.

examples.meaning_tr: Refutation of erroneous theories; correction of false teachings
To save a nation; to restore a country to order
To assist one's ruler; to help one's lord

眉.note_tr: Use kun'yomi (まゆ) for the word 眉 itself and in expressions like 眉をひそめる; use on'yomi び in compounds like 眉毛 (eyebrow hair); and use on'yomi み in words like 眉間 (space between eyebrows). This kanji frequently appears in manga and anime.

examples.meaning_tr: to frown, to furrow one's brows

欽.note_tr: The kanji 欽 predominantly uses the きん reading in modern Japanese, appearing in formal and literary contexts to express deep respect or admiration for someone. The kunyomi つつし.む is rarely encountered in contemporary usage. Do not confuse with similar-meaning kanji like 敬 (respect) and 尊 (honor), which are far more common but carry different nuances.

examples.meaning_tr: Admiration; deep affection and respect for a worthy person
Respectful reverence; formal honor shown toward someone of high standing
Looking up to; admiration and respect for someone worthy of admiration
Authorized; officially established or designated by authority (as in 欽定聖書, King James Version)

薪.note_tr: The kunyomi reading たきぎ appears in formal or traditional contexts, while まき dominates modern everyday use (e.g., 薪割り, 薪ストーブ). Contains the wood/plant radical (木部), so do not confuse with related kanji such as 材 (materials).

褐.note_tr: 褐 is read as かつ (katsu) in compounds. The most essential term is 褐色 (brown color), which appears frequently in descriptive and scientific writing though rarely in casual everyday speech.

賜.note_tr: This N1 kanji almost exclusively uses the onyomi 賜 (し) in modern Japanese; the kunyomi forms (たまわる, たまう) are archaic and rarely appear today. 賜 implies a formal or hierarchical act of giving (from superior to subordinate), unlike casual verbs like 与える (ataeru). Most commonly seen in sports contexts and formal/historical writing.

examples.meaning_tr: An awarded cup or trophy, especially common in sports competitions and anime tournaments
A gift, a precious blessing; something granted or bestowed to you
Imperial grace or favor; a reward granted by a ruler
A divine gift; a blessing bestowed by heaven or fate
To humbly receive something as a gift or honor from a superior

嵯.note_tr: Rare kanji used almost exclusively in proper nouns and geographical names. Reading さ is standard and widely used in 嵯峨 (Saga); reading し is an alternate form rarely encountered in practice. Most learners first meet this character through Kyoto place names and anime/manga set in historical Kyoto.

examples.meaning_tr: Saga; a steep, mountainous district near Kyoto, Japan, known for cultural heritage and temples
Sagano; an area in Kyoto famous for bamboo groves, scenic landscapes, and natural beauty
Sagano bamboo grove; a renowned scenic nature spot in Kyoto often featured in anime and travel

綜.note_tr: The onyomi そう appears almost exclusively in compound words, most commonly 綜合 (comprehensive/synthesis). The kunyomi readings おさ.める and す.べる are archaic or literary and rarely used in modern Japanese.

繕.note_tr: The kunyomi つくろう is used for modern everyday verbs meaning to repair or mend; the onyomi ぜん rarely appears in common words. Look for つくろう in compound verbs (e.g., 服を繕う, to mend clothes) and idiomatic expressions (e.g., 嘘を繕う, to cover up a lie).

examples.meaning_tr: To mend, to repair, to darn
To mend clothes, to repair clothes
To groom oneself, to tidy up one's appearance
To cover up a lie, to gloss over

栓.note_tr: This kanji uses only the onyomi reading せん in modern Japanese. It typically appears in compound words referring to closures, stoppers, and valves. 栓抜き (bottle opener) is one of the most common everyday compounds.

examples.meaning_tr: To pull out a plug or cork

翠.note_tr: The two kunyomi readings have distinct uses: かわせみ refers specifically to the kingfisher bird, while みどり means "green." The onyomi すい appears mainly in compound words. As an N1 kanji, this character is found primarily in literary, formal, and artistic contexts, perfect for nature descriptions in manga and literature.

鮎.note_tr: The kunyomi reading あゆ (ayu) refers to sweetfish, a small freshwater fish popular in Japanese cuisine and recreational fishing. The onyomi readings でん and ねん are archaic and rarely appear in modern Japanese text.

榛.note_tr: The kunyomi reading はしばみ is the standard reading in modern Japanese for this tree and its nuts. The onyomi readings しん and はん are rarely encountered; this kanji appears primarily in nature and food vocabulary.

凹.note_tr: The kanji 凹 most commonly appears in 凹凸 (おうとつ, unevenness) using onyomi, and as the verb 凹む (へこむ, to dent or feel discouraged) using kunyomi. Remember that 凸 is the opposite kanji (convex), and they frequently appear together as 凹凸.

examples.meaning_tr: Unevenness; irregularity; bumpy or uneven surface
To become dented or indented; to feel discouraged or down
To dent or indent something; to discourage someone
Dented; indented; feeling discouraged or downhearted

艶.note_tr: The reading つや describes the lustrous or glossy appearance of a surface. When describing elegant or sophisticated beauty, especially in fashion or appearance, use あでやか. The on'yomi えん appears mainly in formal literary compounds like 艶麗.

惣.note_tr: This formal kanji primarily appears in 惣菜 (sōzai, prepared food). The onyomi そう is standard throughout; note that 総 and 惣 are often interchangeable in modern usage.

examples.meaning_tr: prepared food, deli food, side dish
eldest son, head of household, clan leader

蔦.note_tr: The kunyomi つた is the standard reading in modern Japanese; the onyomi ちょう rarely appears in contemporary texts. This kanji is primarily used in literary, nature, and botanical contexts. Note the distinction from 蔓 (つる): 蔦 specifically means ivy or climbing vines, while 蔓 refers more broadly to any vining or creeping growth.

examples.meaning_tr: Ivy in autumn foliage; autumn ivy

錬.note_tr: The onyomi れん appears in almost all common words (錬金術, 鍛錬, 精錬), while the kunyomi ね.る is rarely used on its own in everyday vocabulary. Be careful not to confuse 錬 (metal radical 金, meaning 'to temper/refine metal') with the very similar-sounding 練 (silk radical 糸, meaning 'to practice/knead', as in 練習 renshuu); they share the れん/ねる readings but have different meanings and radicals.

examples.meaning_tr: alchemy (famous from anime/games like Fullmetal Alchemist)
synthesis/tempering; forming through training (also an anime term for 'transmutation')

隼.note_tr: The kunyomi reading はやぶさ refers to the bird (falcon), while onyomi しゅん appears in technical compounds like 隼級 (falcon-class warship designation). This kanji became internationally famous through the Japanese Hayabusa space probe.

examples.meaning_tr: Hayabusa; an ancient Japanese ethnic people

渚.note_tr: The kunyomi なぎさ is the only practical reading for this literary kanji, used for beach and shore in poetic, descriptive contexts. Unlike the more common 浜 (hama, beach) or 磯 (iso, rocky shore), 渚 carries a more lyrical quality and frequently appears in poetry, place names, and anime/manga titles (notably as a female given name).

衷.note_tr: 衷 is read as ちゅう in formal and literary contexts, expressing sincerity and deep genuine emotion. It appears frequently in anime and manga for emotional depth. No kunyomi.

examples.meaning_tr: from the bottom of one's heart; sincerely

meanings_tr: One by one; item by item
逐.note_tr: This N1 kanji primarily appears in formal compounds conveying 'one by one' (逐一, 逐次) or 'pursuit' (追逐). Avoid confusing it with 追 (to chase, more common in everyday conversation) or 続 (to continue).

examples.meaning_tr: One by one; item by item

斥.note_tr: The onyomi (せき) dominates in modern Japanese compounds like 排斥 (exclusion) and 斥力 (repulsive force). The kunyomi しりぞ.ける, meaning "to push away or drive back," appears primarily as a standalone verb and is less common in compounds but maintains the core sense of rejection and repulsion. No common kanji confusion.

examples.meaning_tr: to reject; to repel; to drive away

稀.note_tr: The onyomi き is used in formal compounds (稀少, 稀有), while the kunyomi まれ is used in colloquial expressions and the standalone adjective form. In chemistry, 稀 means 'dilute,' especially in compounds like 稀酸 (dilute acid).

芙.note_tr: The kanji 芙 is primarily used in the compound 芙蓉 (ふよう), meaning hibiscus or lotus flower. It appears most commonly in poetry, literature, and historical place names, often symbolizing beauty and purity in classical Japanese contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Hibiscus City (historical name for Chongqing, China)

詔.note_tr: The onyomi reading しょう is used in formal compounds and appears mainly in historical texts, official documents, and historical anime/manga. The kunyomi みことのり is rarely used in modern Japanese.

meanings_tr: the fifth month of the lunar calendar
satsuki azalea (a type of flowering shrub)
皐.note_tr: This rare kanji appears almost exclusively in 皐月 (さつき), meaning the 5th lunar month or the satsuki azalea flower. Although こう is listed as the onyomi, modern Japanese uses only the kunyomi さつき; the archaic meanings like "marsh" or "shore" appear mainly in classical texts and poetry.

examples.meaning_tr: Satsuki; the fifth month of the lunar calendar; the satsuki azalea flower
early summer rain; rain falling in May
May memorial; a memorial service held in the fifth lunar month
satsuki club; an association of satsuki azalea enthusiasts and growers

雛.note_tr: The onyomi readings (すう, す, じゅ) are extremely rare and barely appear in everyday vocabulary; almost every common word uses the kunyomi ひな. Note the visual similarity to 難 (nan): both characters share the bird radical 隹 on the right side, but the left-side elements are different, so don't confuse them.

examples.meaning_tr: Doll's Festival (Hinamatsuri, Japan's Girls' Day celebration on March 3rd)
hina dolls displayed for the Doll's Festival

惟.note_tr: This is a formal, literary kanji used primarily in classical texts and philosophical writing. The reading ゆい appears most commonly in the compound 惟一 (only, sole). The reading い is rare in modern Japanese except in academic terms like 思惟 (thought). This kanji is not used in everyday casual speech.

examples.meaning_tr: only, sole, the one and only, unique
I alone am supreme (famous Buddhist phrase expressing self-supremacy)

佑.note_tr: 佑 appears primarily in formal/literary contexts and personal names. It is less common in everyday modern Japanese compared to similar characters like 助 or 祐. The kunyomi reading たす.ける is archaic; the onyomi ゆう appears mainly in compounds and names. Learners most frequently encounter this character in anime and manga character names.

examples.meaning_tr: given name (help + assist); very common in anime and manga
given name (big/great + help); frequently seen in manga
given name (healthy/strong + help); common character name
given name (peace/wellness + help); seen in anime/manga

耀.note_tr: The kun'yomi かがやく is the main verbal form and is more commonly used in everyday contexts. The on'yomi よう appears primarily in formal compounds and classical idioms. This is a literary kanji frequently encountered in anime titles, manga, and poetic expressions.

examples.meaning_tr: to shine; to sparkle; to gleam
the eyes sparkle (often seen in anime descriptions)
to display one's power or might; an idiom meaning to show off one's strength

黛.note_tr: This classical kanji primarily appears in the modern color term 黛色 (indigo), though it originally referred to blackened eyebrows as a beauty practice in classical Japan. The kunyomi まゆずみ preserves this original meaning.

examples.meaning_tr: Indigo; a traditional dark blue color

渥.note_tr: An exceptionally rare N1 kanji found mainly in formal or literary contexts. The onyomi reading あく (aku) appears in the compound 恩渥 (favor, benevolence). The kunyomi readings are seldom used in modern Japanese and are more common in classical texts or personal names.

examples.meaning_tr: Favor, grace, or benevolence shown to someone; royal favor
A peninsula in Aichi Prefecture; also used as a surname

meanings_tr: To yearn for; to long for
To admire; to look up to
憧.note_tr: The kunyomi form is standard in modern Japanese: 憧れる (verb) means to admire or yearn for, and 憧れ (noun) means yearning or admiration. The formal noun 憧憬 (しょうけい) uses the onyomi and appears mainly in literary contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: To yearn for; to admire; to look up to
An admired person; someone you look up to; an idol

宵.note_tr: Use kunyomi よい for most words, this kanji describes the early evening and twilight hours. Common in anime/manga and traditional contexts; it refers to an earlier time than 夜 (night). The onyomi しょう is rarely used in beginner materials.

examples.meaning_tr: crescent moon; moon in early evening

妄.note_tr: Most common with the もう reading, especially in 妄想 (delusion/fantasy). The ぼう reading typically appears in more formal or literary contexts like 妄動 (reckless action). Distinguish from 忘 (forget).

examples.meaning_tr: reckless words, wild talk, absurd remarks
reckless action, hasty move, precipitous behavior
blind faith, unfounded belief, false conviction
vain thought, delusional thinking, idle fancy

惇.note_tr: A rare N1 kanji found mainly in formal, classical, or literary writing and personal names. The じゅん reading predominates in compounds; the kunyomi あつい is very uncommon with this particular character in modern Japanese.

脩.note_tr: A rare N1 kanji appearing primarily in formal, literary contexts, mostly with the on'yomi reading しゅう. The original meaning of dried meat is archaic; modern usage emphasizes repair and cultivation senses similar to 修.

甫.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji appears mainly in proper names and classical texts. The onyomi (ほ, ふ) is standard in traditional names; the kunyomi (はじめて) is literary/archaic. Learners typically encounter it in character names from historical anime, period dramas, or older literature.

examples.meaning_tr: A traditional Japanese name or name component, meaning 'beginning' or 'just starting'
Archaic/classical term meaning 'barely' or 'scarcely' (rare in modern usage)
Classical negative form meaning 'not yet' or 'not until' (archaic poetry and old texts)
Classical compound meaning 'very beginning' or 'first moment' (found in historical literature)

酌.note_tr: Use kunyomi く.む (くむ) when referring to the action of pouring or drawing liquids; use onyomi しゃく in compounds like 酌人 (bartender) or formal contexts like 酌量 (consideration). This kanji appears often in historical or formal writing about hospitality and sake service, common in anime set in traditional Japan or with bar scenes.

examples.meaning_tr: To pour or draw; to scoop up (especially sake or water)
A bartender or person who pours sake
To offer or present sake as a gesture of hospitality
Consideration; allowance; to take circumstances into account
A drinking companion; one who shares drinks with another

蚕.note_tr: Kunyomi かいこ refers to the silkworm insect itself. Onyomi さん is primarily used in compounds related to silk production and sericulture (養蚕 'sericulture,' 蚕糸 'raw silk'). Reading てん is less common, appearing mainly in 天蚕.

嬉.note_tr: The reading うれしい is by far the most common, used in daily speech and anime/manga to express the speaker's happiness. The onyomi き and the alternative kunyomi たのしむ are rare with this kanji.

蒼.note_tr: The kunyomi あおい functions as a standalone adjective meaning 'blue' or 'pale.' The onyomi そう appears primarily in literary or formal compounds like 蒼天 (sky) and 蒼穹 (azure sky). Distinguish from 青 (common modern 'blue'), 蒼 carries a more archaic or poetic connotation, often appearing in anime/manga dialogue and nature descriptions.

examples.meaning_tr: pale, pallid (especially a character's shocked face)

暉.note_tr: This kanji is rare in everyday vocabulary and shows up mainly in personal names (like 大暉 or 陽暉) and in literary/poetic compounds. The everyday word for "to shine" is normally written with the similar-looking kanji 輝く (かがやく), so be careful not to mix up 暉 and 輝.

examples.meaning_tr: Light, shine (used as a standalone male given name)
"Great shine"; a popular Japanese male given name
"Sunlight/shine"; a common Japanese male given name
Afterglow; the lingering light of the setting sun (literary word)
Warm spring sunlight (literary/poetic, often symbolizing a parent's love)

頒.note_tr: In modern Japanese this kanji appears almost exclusively in the compound 頒布 (はんぷ, "distribution"), read with onyomi はん; the kunyomi わかつ is rare and mostly literary; for everyday "to divide/share," 分かつ (using 分) is far more common. Fun fact for anime/manga fans: 頒布 is the standard word used at doujinshi events like Comiket, where fan-made works are "distributed" (頒布する) rather than "sold."

examples.meaning_tr: distribution, dissemination (e.g. of goods, information, or doujinshi at fan events)
distribution price (the price at which something is distributed, often used for doujinshi/fan works)
subscription club / distribution society (e.g. a monthly sake or goods subscription)

只.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 只 is almost always read with its kun'yomi ただ (as in ただいま or ただ働き); the on'yomi し barely appears in everyday vocabulary. Don't confuse it with 唯 (also read ただ, meaning "only/sole"); 只 leans more toward "free of charge" or "merely," while 唯 stresses exclusivity ("the one and only").

examples.meaning_tr: "I'm home!" (greeting); also means "right now, at present"
to be no ordinary person (someone impressive/suspicious)
to be no small matter; something serious is going on

肢.note_tr: 肢 uses only onyomi し and appears in formal medical contexts, like in the compounds 下肢 (lower limb) and 上肢 (upper limb). Unlike the everyday word 足 (foot/leg), 肢 is a formal register term.

examples.meaning_tr: all four limbs; the four extremities

檀.note_tr: The onyomi だん is used in most compound words, particularly in Buddhist temple contexts (檀家, 檀林) and when referring to sandalwood products. The kunyomi まゆみ specifically refers to the spindle tree. Not to be confused with 壇, which means platform or stage.

examples.meaning_tr: Parishioner; member of a Buddhist temple parish
Sandalwood incense; fragrant incense made from sandalwood wood
Spindle tree; a type of ornamental deciduous tree
Buddhist monastery; temple school or Buddhist educational institution

凱.note_tr: 凱 predominantly uses the onyomi reading (especially がい) in modern compounds like 凱旋 (triumphal return). The kunyomi readings are archaic or poetic. Common in historical, military, anime, and sports contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Triumphal arch (e.g., Arc de Triomphe in Paris)

彗.note_tr: The onyomi reading すい is the most common in modern Japanese and appears in 彗星 (comet), which is the primary modern usage of this N1 kanji. The kunyomi ほうき ('broom') reflects the historical association with a comet's sweeping tail. This kanji is almost exclusively encountered in astronomy and science fiction contexts.

謄.note_tr: 謄 is read almost exclusively as とう (onyomi). The most common word is 謄本 (certified copy or official transcript), frequently appearing in administrative and legal documents.

examples.meaning_tr: property register extract; real estate transcript
family register transcript; certified family record

梓.note_tr: The kunyomi reading 'あずさ' dominates modern Japanese usage, especially in place names and tree references. The onyomi 'し' is archaic, appearing mainly in historical terms related to woodblock printing and carving. This N1 kanji surfaces most often in geographical contexts, historical texts, and artistic traditions.

examples.meaning_tr: Azusa River; a major river in Nagano Prefecture, Japan (common in travel and geography contexts)
Catalpa tree; also a popular female given name in anime and manga
A traditional bow made from catalpa wood; appears in historical arts and games
A woodblock printer or artisan who carves printing blocks (uses the onyomi 'し')

meanings_tr: Second sign of the Chinese zodiac
The hour from 1 to 3 AM in traditional Japanese timekeeping
丑.note_tr: The kun'yomi うし is used in zodiac and timekeeping terms. In anime and manga, time expressions like 丑の刻 and 丑三つ時 frequently appear in supernatural or horror scenes to create an eerie atmosphere.

examples.meaning_tr: The Hour of the Ox (1–3 AM)

meanings_tr: To succeed to (a position or throne)
嗣.note_tr: 嗣 is used primarily in formal and literary contexts, particularly for succession to important positions such as the imperial throne. The on'yomi reading し is standard in compounds. This kanji frequently appears in historical anime, manga, and formal Japanese texts. Do not confuse with 継 (つぐ), which means to continue or carry on in a general sense; 嗣 specifically denotes direct succession or heirship to an important position or title.

examples.meaning_tr: Heir; son designated to inherit (usually the eldest son)
Crown prince; heir apparent to the throne
Imperial heir; the designated successor to the emperor
Successor; heir; one who comes after another

叶.note_tr: The kunyomi readings かなう (intransitive: to come true) and かなえる (transitive: to grant/fulfill) are far more common in modern Japanese than the onyomi きょう. This kanji frequently appears in anime and manga when characters discuss their dreams (夢) or wishes (願い) coming true, かなえる is used with a direct object (what you fulfill), while かなう is used intransitively (what comes true).

汐.note_tr: The kunyomi しお is used for the literal meanings of tide and salt water in most contexts. The onyomi せき appears primarily in the formal compound 潮汐 (ちょうせき, tides). Often confused with 潮 which also means tide or salt water but is more commonly used in modern Japanese.

絢.note_tr: This N1 kanji uses only the onyomi reading (ken); no kunyomi exists. It appears primarily in formal or literary contexts describing brilliant patterns, splendid displays, or luxurious designs. Most commonly found in compounds like 絢爛. Frequently appears in anime, manga, and period literature.

朔.note_tr: The kunyomi ついたち is primarily used for 朔日 (first day of the month), especially in historical and traditional contexts. The onyomi さく appears mainly in compound words related to astronomy and geography, common in historical texts and literary works.

examples.meaning_tr: New moon and full moon (lunar phases)

伽.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji is primarily encountered in Buddhist terminology. The reading が is predominant in modern usage (伽藍, monastery), while きゃ appears in 伽羅 (aloe wood incense used in Buddhist rituals). Other readings and traditional meanings rarely occur in contemporary Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Aloe wood; fragrant incense wood used in Buddhist temples

畝.note_tr: The kunyomi うね is the primary reading used in agricultural contexts to describe ridges or furrows between crop rows. This kanji appears most frequently in farming and gardening vocabulary and aligns well with your interest in food and nature.

examples.meaning_tr: Ridging; furrowing; making furrows for planting

抄.note_tr: 抄 uses only the onyomi reading しょう (no kunyomi). This kanji appears primarily in formal, academic, and literary contexts, most often meaning 'summary' or 'excerpt.' Common in manga/anime subtitles when discussing summaries (抄録) or translated excerpts (抄訳).

爽.note_tr: The kunyomi さわやか is the most common form in modern Japanese, used to describe refreshing or fresh qualities of people, scenes, or sensations. Onyomi そう appears mainly in formal compounds like 爽快, conveying exhilaration or invigoration.

examples.meaning_tr: Sense of exhilaration or refreshment (common in game and sports reviews)
Bright and cheerful, clear in mind

黎.note_tr: Usually appears in 黎明 (dawn/daybreak). The kunyomi reading is rare in modern Japanese; onyomi rei/ri dominates compound formation.

惰.note_tr: This kanji is rarely used independently and primarily appears in compounds using the on'yomi だ (da). It frequently pairs with 怠 (meaning neglect) to form 怠惰 (indolence). The key distinction: 怠 emphasizes negligence, while 惰 emphasizes unwillingness or reluctance to act.

examples.meaning_tr: Indolence, laziness; a state of being unwilling to work or exert effort
Inertia; unwillingness to change; doing something purely out of habit
Oversleeping, sleeping in; lying in bed lazily

蛮.note_tr: Use ばん (onyomi) in most modern compounds; the kunyomi えびす is rarely seen in contemporary Japanese. This kanji typically describes uncivilized, violent, or reckless behavior.

examples.meaning_tr: Barbarism; savagery; uncivilized behavior or person
Brute force; raw strength without skill (often used in sports and action contexts)
Barbarian tribe; savage people (common in history and anime)
Barbaric act; savage behavior; outrage or atrocity

meanings_tr: Cold, chilly, or bracing (especially of weather)
冴.note_tr: The primary reading is さ.える (kunyomi); onyomi readings ご and こ are rare in modern Japanese. 冴 emphasizes mental clarity or skill with a refined quality, distinguishing it from 冷 (cold), which refers to physical temperature only.

examples.meaning_tr: to be clear, sharp, alert, or skilled; (of weather) to be bracing cold
clear, sharp, brilliant, or excellent (commonly used in manga to describe appearance or technique)
dull, plain, mediocre, or unattractive (opposite of 冴えた)
eyes become sharp or alert; unable to sleep with one's mind racing

旺.note_tr: The onyomi おう is the most commonly used reading in modern Japanese, appearing in 旺盛 to express vigor and energy. The kunyomi forms for 'beautiful' and 'prosperous' are rarely encountered in contemporary usage, but the kanji overall conveys a sense of thriving abundance and brightness.

萌.note_tr: 萌える (moeru, kunyomi) is the most common form meaning 'to sprout' or 'to bloom'; in modern anime/manga culture, 萌え (moe) refers to cute character aesthetics. The onyomi ほう appears in formal compounds like 萌芽 (houga, 'bud/sprout') and 萌生 (housei, 'germination').

examples.meaning_tr: To sprout; to bloom; (modern) moe – cute character appeal

偲.note_tr: The kunyomi しの.ぶ is the primary reading used in modern Japanese, appearing mainly in formal or literary contexts, especially when remembering the deceased or recalling the past. The onyomi readings (さい, し) are rarely encountered in contemporary usage.

examples.meaning_tr: To remember with emotion; to recollect
To remember and honor the deceased

meanings_tr: One (formal, official version used in documents and financial contexts)
壱.note_tr: 壱 is the formal kanji for 'one,' designed to prevent document forgery and commonly seen on currency or in official papers. The onyomi いち is used in formal contexts (e.g., 壱万円 on banknotes), while the kunyomi ひとつ or ひとり appears in traditional or counted contexts; in modern casual Japanese, the simpler 一 is far more common, so expect 壱 mainly in historical manga, old documents, and official writing.

瑠.note_tr: This JLPT N1 kanji is primarily used in compounds, especially 瑠璃 (lapis lazuli), a color name frequently seen in anime, manga, and traditional Japanese art. The る reading is standard; りゅう is rare and appears mainly in Buddhist terminology.

examples.meaning_tr: Lapis lazuli; also a type of deep blue used in traditional and modern art
Lapis lazuli blue; a deep blue color
Lapis Lazuli Light; the Buddhist Buddha of healing and medicine

允.note_tr: 允 is a formal kanji rarely used in modern Japanese, appearing mainly in literary or legal contexts. The on'yomi いん is found in compounds such as 允許 (いんきょ) and 允可 (いんか), both meaning "permission" or "approval," though these are archaic or literary forms. Modern Japanese typically uses simpler alternatives like 許可 or 認可. Other readings are seldom encountered in contemporary texts.

侯.note_tr: This kanji is read exclusively as こう (onyomi) in modern Japanese. It appears primarily in the compound 侯爵 (marquis) and is used mainly in historical, formal, and fantasy contexts when discussing feudal nobility or European aristocracy.

examples.meaning_tr: Marquis; a rank of nobility (feudal rank below duke, above count)
Various feudal lords; daimyo; regional nobles
Marchioness; the wife or widow of a marquis

examples.reading: こうしゃくれいじょう
examples.meaning_tr: Marquis's daughter; a nobleman's young daughter (common in historical anime/manga)

蒔.note_tr: The kunyomi ま.く (maku) is the standard modern reading meaning "to sow seeds" or "to scatter," while the onyomi readings し and じ are rarely used in contemporary Japanese. Don't confuse with 植える (ueru, "to plant"), which is written with a different kanji.

鯉.note_tr: Use こい (kunyomi) for the fish itself and everyday contexts. This reading appears prominently in 鯉のぼり (koinobori), Japan's iconic colorful carp-shaped wind-sock decoration flown on Children's Day (May 5). The onyomi り is used in compounds with other kanji.

examples.meaning_tr: koinobori; colorful carp-shaped wind socks displayed on Children's Day (May 5)
carp dishes; cuisine prepared with carp

弧.note_tr: 弧 uses only the onyomi reading こ with no kunyomi form. It primarily appears in technical and descriptive contexts, particularly in geometry, architecture, and nature descriptions.

遥.note_tr: The kunyomi reading はるか is more poetic and literary, often found in romantic or nostalgic contexts, while the onyomi よう appears in formal compounds. Not to be confused with 遠 (far, common), which is more frequent in everyday language.

examples.meaning_tr: From far away, a long way
A long time ago, ancient times

舜.note_tr: This is an extremely rare kanji in modern Japanese, primarily known as the name of 舜 (Shun), the legendary Chinese sage emperor and successor to Emperor Yao. He appears frequently in classical literature as a symbol of virtuous, exemplary rule. The botanical meanings are highly specialized or archaic and unlikely to appear in contemporary texts. This kanji is most commonly encountered as a proper name in historical literature, classical texts, or anime and manga with East Asian historical themes.

examples.meaning_tr: Shun; the legendary Chinese sage emperor
Emperor Shun; the ancient exemplary ruler
Yao and Shun; legendary sage emperors symbolizing good government

meanings_tr: Sparkle or brilliance of a jewel
瑛.note_tr: 瑛 appears most frequently in personal names, where it conveys imagery of crystalline purity and brightness. It has only onyomi (えい) with no kunyomi. The kanji rarely appears in everyday compounds.

附.note_tr: The on'yomi ふ (fu) is standard in formal compound words like 附属 (affiliated school). The kun'yomi つ.ける and つ.く are rarely used with this kanji; modern Japanese typically uses the simpler 付 instead. 附 is considered archaic or formal in contemporary writing.

examples.meaning_tr: Affiliated with, attached to, subsidiary (common in school names: 大学附属高校 = university-affiliated high school)
Appendix, supplement (often found at the end of manga volumes and books)
Postscript, additional note (used in formal documents and manga footnotes)
Addition, increment (technical term: 附加価値 = added value)

彪.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji appears mainly in anime/manga character names and classical texts. The onyomi ひょう forms 彪悍 (fierce, bold), while the kunyomi あや (stripe, pattern) is rare in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: tiger stripes, striped like a tiger

meanings_tr: Fourth sign of the Chinese zodiac
卯.note_tr: The reading う is most common in zodiac and calendar contexts (卯月 for April, 卯年 for Year of the Rabbit). The Sino-Japanese reading ぼう appears in classical time-telling terms like 卯刻. The kanji is one of the twelve celestial branches (十二支) used in traditional East Asian timekeeping and astrology.

examples.meaning_tr: April (literally 'Month of the Hare'), commonly used in formal writing and traditional contexts
Year of the Rabbit, used when discussing the zodiac cycle
Deutzia (a flowering shrub that blooms in spring), appears in poetry and nature discussions
Hour of the Hare (5-7 AM), the traditional time period in classical Japanese timekeeping

但.note_tr: The kunyomi reading ただし is overwhelmingly more common in modern Japanese than the onyomi たん. ただし functions primarily as a conjunction meaning 'however' or 'but,' used in both spoken and written contexts. The compound 但し書き (conditions; provisions) appears frequently in legal documents, agreements, and formal notices.

examples.word: 安いです。但し品質が良いです
examples.reading: やすいです。ただしひんしつがよいです
examples.meaning_tr: It's inexpensive. However, the quality is good

examples.word: 参加費は無料ですが、但し事前登録が必要です
examples.reading: さんかひはむりょうですが、ただしじぜんとうろくがひつようです
examples.meaning_tr: Participation is free, but advance registration is required

examples.word: 確かにそう見えます、但し現実は違うかもしれません
examples.reading: たしかにそうみえます、ただしげんじつはちがうかもしれません
examples.meaning_tr: It certainly looks that way, but reality might be different

綺.note_tr: The kanji 綺 is most frequently encountered in the common word 綺麗 (きれい), meaning beautiful or clean. The on'yomi き dominates modern usage; the kun'yomi あや rarely appears in everyday Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: love of cleanliness, tidy person, neat freak

芋.note_tr: The kunyomi reading いも dominates in everyday Japanese, especially in food and nature contexts. The onyomi う is rare in common words. This kanji frequently appears in food-related compounds.

meanings_tr: Madder (a plant used for red dye)
茜.note_tr: This kanji is primarily used with the kunyomi reading (あかね) in modern Japanese; the onyomi (せん) is rarely encountered. It frequently appears in color names and poetic descriptions of sunsets and nature, making it especially common in anime and manga.

examples.meaning_tr: Madder red; a warm reddish color reminiscent of sunset
Crimson clouds; reddening clouds at sunset (poetic, often used in anime/manga)
Madder plant; also used as a girl's given name

凌.note_tr: The kun-reading しのぐ is used for the verb form (凌ぐ) meaning "to endure/brave through/surpass," while the on-reading りょう appears in Sino-Japanese compounds like 凌駕 and 凌辱. Be careful not to confuse this kanji with the similar-looking 陵 (also read りょう), which means "hill, mausoleum" and has a completely different meaning.

examples.meaning_tr: to endure, brave through, stave off; also: to surpass
to take shelter from the rain, to keep the rain out
to tide over an emergency, to get through a crisis
to surpass, to outstrip, to outdo

皓.note_tr: The onyomi こう appears mainly in literary and formal vocabulary, particularly in expressions like 皓月 (bright moon). The kunyomi しろい and ひかる relate to whiteness and radiance respectively. Do not confuse this kanji with 白 (the common kanji for white), while 白い is the everyday standard, 皓い is a more classical and literary variant. This N1-level kanji is frequent in poetry, classical literature, and formal descriptions.

examples.meaning_tr: bright moon; luminous moon; full moon
white; clear (literary form of 白い)

洸.note_tr: This kanji is predominantly used in Japanese personal names, especially male given names, where it conveys meanings of brightness and sparkle. Only the onyomi reading こう (kou) is available; no kunyomi exists.

毬.note_tr: The kunyomi まり is most common, referring to a ball or sphere. The reading いが appears primarily in 毬栗 (iga-kuri, the spiky husk of chestnuts). The onyomi きゅう is rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: marimo (spherical algae, famous in Japanese culture)

婆.note_tr: This N1 kanji appears frequently in literature and historical texts. The kunyomi ばあさん (grandmother) is more common in modern everyday speech and anime/manga than the onyomi form 老婆, which is formal and literary.

examples.meaning_tr: demon hag, ogre woman (in folklore and anime)

緋.note_tr: In modern Japanese, primarily uses the onyomi reading (ひ) in compounds. 緋 specifically describes a vibrant scarlet/crimson hue, often seen in anime, manga, and traditional contexts.

鯛.note_tr: The kunyomi reading たい is the primary and most commonly used reading for this kanji. The listed onyomi ちょう is rarely encountered in modern Japanese. 鯛 is especially famous in Japanese food culture, particularly in taiyaki (鯛焼き), a beloved snack that frequently appears in anime and manga.

examples.meaning_tr: taiyaki; a popular Japanese snack of red bean paste pastry shaped like a sea bream
sea bream; a valued Japanese food fish
Japanese red seabream; a premium food fish prized for sushi and sashimi
salt-grilled sea bream; a classic Japanese grilled fish dish

怜.note_tr: This N1 kanji is uncommon in modern everyday Japanese and appears more frequently in literary or classical contexts and personal names. The most common compound is 怜悧 (shrewd, clever) using the れい reading; it appears frequently in anime and manga character names, which makes it relevant to your interests.

examples.meaning_tr: A male given name (using りょう reading)
A female given name (using れい reading); common in anime
A female given name (using れい reading)

邑.note_tr: The onyomi ゆう is more common in compounds and classical texts; the kunyomi むら is rarely used in modern Japanese. This kanji frequently appears in historical and fantasy anime/manga, as well as in formal and literary contexts.

倣.note_tr: The kunyomi 倣う (ならう) is the most common form, meaning 'to imitate' or 'to follow someone's example.' The onyomi ほう appears mainly in formal compounds like 模倣 (imitation) and 習倣 (custom). Distinguish from 習う (to study), which emphasizes learning through instruction.

examples.meaning_tr: to imitate; to follow; to copy
to emulate one's predecessors; to follow in the footsteps of past masters

碧.note_tr: The reading へき is standard in compounds; ひゃく is very rare in modern usage. 碧 is more formal and literary than 青 (blue), appearing often in poetic, nature-related, and anime/manga contexts where vivid blue description is needed.

啄.note_tr: This kanji represents the pecking action of birds. The kunyomi readings (つつく, ついばむ) are far more commonly used than the onyomi readings in modern Japanese. The kanji appears frequently in nature-related vocabulary, particularly in words for woodpecker.

examples.meaning_tr: To peck at; to pick up with the beak

穣.note_tr: 穣 appears most commonly as part of 豊穣 (ほうじょう, "abundant harvest"), which uses the on'yomi じょう. The kun'yomi readings (わら, ゆたか) are historically documented but rarely appear in modern Japanese compounds; most contemporary usage relies on the on'yomi.

examples.meaning_tr: bountiful harvest of five grains, prosperous crops (common cultural phrase)
year of good harvest, prosperous year

酉.note_tr: 酉 primarily appears in zodiac contexts (酉年), traditional festivals (especially 酉の市), and historical timekeeping. The kunyomi とり emphasizes the rooster/bird meaning, while onyomi ゆう is used in formal astrological compounds; do not confuse with 鶏, the modern kanji for chicken.

examples.meaning_tr: Tori Festival, a famous festival held every November at Inari shrines, especially in Tokyo, where visitors buy decorative bamboo rakes for good luck and prosperity in the coming year
Year of the Rooster, the 10th year in the 12-year zodiac cycle; people born in this year are said to have specific personality traits according to tradition
Hour of the Rooster, in traditional Japanese timekeeping, the time from 5 PM to 7 PM; commonly referenced in historical and period drama contexts

悌.note_tr: A formal, classical kanji appearing primarily in literary and philosophical contexts. Frequently paired with 孝 (filial piety toward parents) in the compound 孝悌, representing key Confucian virtues of family respect. Reading: てい (tei). Uncommon in modern everyday Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Filial obedience; respectful deference to one's parents and elders
Filial piety and brotherly respect; core Confucian virtue of family loyalty
Respectful heart; the spirit of reverence toward one's elders

倹.note_tr: The onyomi けん is used mainly in compounds like 倹約 (frugality, economy). The kunyomi つましい functions as an adjective meaning 'frugal' or 'humble,' though it appears less frequently in modern usage.

examples.meaning_tr: Living simply and frugally, simplicity and thrift

柚.note_tr: The kunyomi reading ゆず is the standard pronunciation; onyomi readings are rare in modern vocabulary. Yuzu is an important ingredient in Japanese cuisine and appears in cultural practices, especially cooking and winter solstice bathing traditions.

examples.meaning_tr: Yuzu, citron (a yellow citrus fruit used in Japanese cooking and cosmetics)
Yuzu tea (a sweet beverage made with yuzu, often served hot or cold)
Yuzu pepper (a Japanese condiment made from yuzu zest, salt, and chili pepper)
Yuzu bath (a traditional Japanese bathing practice with whole yuzu fruits, especially on winter solstice)
Yuzu peel or rind (the fragrant outer skin of yuzu used to flavor dishes)

繭.note_tr: The kunyomi まゆ is the primary reading used in most words and contexts, while the onyomi けん appears mainly in compounds like 蚕繭 (silkworm cocoon). This kanji is closely associated with silk production, sericulture, and the life cycle of silkworms.

examples.meaning_tr: cocoon ball; ornamental spheres made from cocoons, often displayed in New Year decorations
from cocoon to butterfly; the transformation from chrysalis to butterfly

meanings_tr: one-tenth of a go (traditional unit of volume)
勺.note_tr: 勺 is read only as しゃく (onyomi) with no kunyomi. It appears rarely in modern Japanese outside of historical texts or traditional measurement contexts. The most common modern usage is in the compound 一勺 (one ladle or one-tenth of a go).

examples.meaning_tr: one ladle; one-tenth of a go (traditional volume measure)

meanings_tr: Monme (a traditional Japanese unit of weight)
匁.note_tr: This is a kokuji (a kanji character created in Japan, not derived from Chinese). It uses only the kun'yomi reading もんめ (monme) and refers to a traditional weight measurement. You'll encounter it primarily in historical texts, period dramas, traditional recipes, and antique contexts, especially in shows and manga set in the Edo period.

斤.note_tr: 斤 uses only the onyomi reading きん. It functions primarily as a measurement unit for weight (catty) or as a counter for bread and food items, appearing frequently in compound expressions for quantities.

examples.meaning_tr: Half a catty; half a loaf of bread
One catty; one loaf of bread (used as a counter for bread)

且.note_tr: The kunyomi かつ in 且つ is the most common reading in modern Japanese, appearing mainly in formal or written contexts to connect two words or clauses meaning "and" or "both...and". The onyomi readings are rarely used in contemporary usage.

examples.reading: あたらしくかつふるい
おおきくかつちいさい

meanings_tr: Third heavenly stem; one of the ten traditional East Asian calendar stems
丙.note_tr: 丙 is primarily used in the traditional ten heavenly stems system and zodiac calendar, where the kunyomi ひのえ combines with zodiac animals (e.g., 丙午 = Fire Horse year). The onyomi へい appears in classification and ranking contexts like 丙種 (third class/grade).

examples.meaning_tr: Fire Horse year; the year of the Fire Horse (historically significant in Japanese culture)
Third class; third grade; third rank
Third class license (such as for certain vehicle licenses in Japan)
Fire Monkey year; the year of the Fire Monkey
Fire Dog year; the year of the Fire Dog
Fire Rat year; the year of the Fire Rat

旦.note_tr: The onyomi 'dan' (だん) is most important and appears in 旦那 (husband/master), very common in anime and manga contexts. The 'tan' (たん) reading appears in 元旦 (New Year's Day). Other readings are archaic or literary in modern usage.

丞.note_tr: 丞 is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese except in historical and classical contexts. It appears primarily with its onyomi (じょう or しょう) in compounds like 丞相 (chancellor/prime minister), which you may encounter in historical fantasy anime and manga, especially adaptations of historical novels set in ancient China. The kunyomi are virtually never seen in practice. This is an N1 kanji but appears infrequently outside of period literature.

examples.meaning_tr: chancellor; prime minister (a historical administrative position, especially in Chinese contexts)
district official; subprefectural aide (historical administrative title)
county official; county magistrate's assistant (historical post)

meanings_tr: Hour of the Pig (9 PM to 11 PM)
Twelfth sign of the Chinese zodiac
亥.note_tr: The kunyomi い is by far the most common in modern Japanese, appearing prominently in 亥年 (Year of the Pig) when discussing zodiac years and birth years. The onyomi がい appears mainly in historical or traditional contexts, such as 亥刻 (the hour of the Pig, used in classical timekeeping). The onyomi かい has minimal modern usage.

examples.meaning_tr: Year of the Pig (occurs once every 12 years in the zodiac cycle; people born in this year are said to be born in the year of the pig)
The hour of the Pig (9 PM to 11 PM in the traditional Japanese time system, often appearing in historical fiction and period dramas)
The month of the Pig (the eleventh lunar month in the traditional calendar, roughly November)

亦.note_tr: This kanji is rare in modern Japanese; it mainly survives as a literary/classical stand-in for また (also, again) in Confucian-style quotations and a few fixed phrases. The on'yomi えき・やく are almost never used outside proper nouns (e.g. institution names inspired by the Analects). Don't confuse it with 赤 (red) or 変 (change); 亦 has a distinct "亠+ハ+ハ" shape.

examples.meaning_tr: also; too (literary form of また)
"Is this not a joy?"; famous line from the Analects of Confucius
that too is amusing/interesting (a fixed literary phrase)

伎.note_tr: 伎 is a formal kanji found mainly in compounds about performing arts, using the ぎ reading. The kunyomi わざ is rare/archaic. Do not confuse with 技 (ぎじゅつ/わざ, 'technology/skill'), which is far more common in everyday Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Performing arts; artistic techniques and skills

凪.note_tr: 凪 is a kokuji (created in Japan, not from Chinese). The primary reading is なぎ (nagi), used for calm or stillness, especially of seas and wind. The reading なぐ (nagu) combines to form the verb 凪ぐ, meaning 'to become calm' or 'to subside.' This kanji appears frequently in literary and classical contexts, and has nautical/weather terminology.

examples.meaning_tr: calm, stillness (of the sea or wind)
slack water (nautical term: cessation of tidal current)
summer calm, the still weather of summer

吏.note_tr: This N1 character appears primarily in formal and historical contexts, always using the onyomi reading り (ri). It refers to government officials and appears mainly in compound words rather than standalone. Related characters like 史 (history) should not be confused.

弐.note_tr: 弐 is the formal "daiji" variant of 二 (two), used in contracts, checks, receipts, and legal documents to prevent numbers from being altered or forged. In real-world vocabulary it is almost always read with the onyomi に; the kunyomi ふた.つ/そえ exist in dictionaries but are essentially never used in actual compound words.

examples.meaning_tr: two (formal numeral, used instead of 二 in official documents)
two thousand yen (formal notation, e.g. on a receipt)
"the sum of twenty thousand yen" (standard contract/receipt phrasing)

伶.note_tr: This is a classical kanji rarely used in modern Japanese. The れい (rei) reading is most common in everyday contexts, while りょう (ryō) appears in older or formal compounds. It originally referred to court musicians and performers in ancient China, and later took on the meaning "clever" or "witty" in certain compounds.

冶.note_tr: The onyomi や is the standard reading in modern Japanese; the kunyomi い.る is virtually unused. This kanji appears almost exclusively in metallurgy and metalworking terminology, making it specialized technical vocabulary rather than everyday use.

examples.meaning_tr: Metallurgy; the science and technology of working with metals
Metalworker; someone who smelts or forges metal
Smelting furnace; forge for heating and refining metal
Casting; the process of shaping metal by pouring molten metal into a mold

汰.note_tr: 汰 is predominantly used in the compound 淘汰 (touta), meaning "natural selection" or "elimination by filtering." It takes the onyomi た in this common usage. The kunyomi readings provided are archaic or rarely appear in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: to be eliminated; to be weeded out

玖.note_tr: This kanji is exceptionally rare in modern Japanese, appearing almost exclusively in proper names, place names, and occasionally in classical literature. The standard character for 'nine' is 九. The onyomi readings (きゅう and く) are encountered primarily in names rather than everyday words.

examples.meaning_tr: Kusu (a town in Ōita Prefecture, Japan)
Kusu District (an administrative region in Ōita Prefecture)
Nine (formal or classical usage; rarely seen in contemporary Japanese)

侃.note_tr: Primarily used in set phrases like the idiom 侃侃諤諤. The onyomi かん is the standard reading; the kunyomi つよ.い is archaic and rarely appears in modern Japanese.

meanings_tr: Urge someone to eat, encourage eating
侑.note_tr: This kanji is primarily used in personal names with the onyomi reading ゆう. The kunyomi readings (encourage and help) are rarely used in modern Japanese. Since you enjoy anime and manga, you'll frequently encounter 侑 in character names in those media.

昂.note_tr: The onyomi こう is used in formal compounds like 昂揚 (high spirits) and 昂然 (proudly). The kunyomi たかぶる means to become excited or spirited, often found in manga and creative contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Elevation of spirits; high morale; boosting enthusiasm
To become excited; to swell with pride; to be spirited
To be in high spirits; to feel elated; to be full of vim and vigor

茄.note_tr: This character most commonly appears in 茄子 (なす, eggplant), the standard Japanese word for the vegetable. While the on'yomi reading か exists, it is rarely used in everyday Japanese; beginners will primarily encounter this kanji through food-related vocabulary and cooking contexts.

茉.note_tr: This is an uncommon kanji used mainly in Japanese female given names with the ま reading. It also appears in compounds referring to jasmine flowers, such as 茉莉 and 茉莉茶 (jasmine tea), where the まつ reading is typically employed.

meanings_tr: To guide, to lead, to direct
To edify, to enlighten, to instruct
迪.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji is primarily used in names and classical or literary texts. The kunyomi reading みちびく carries the core meaning of guiding or leading someone along a path. The onyomi てき most commonly appears in the compound 啓迪 (enlightenment, edification). In everyday modern Japanese, the more frequently used character 導 (with どう reading) conveys the 'to guide' sense; 迪 is mainly encountered in academic study or proper names.

examples.meaning_tr: to guide, to lead, to direct

采.note_tr: This rare JLPT N1 kanji primarily uses the onyomi reading (さい) in modern Japanese. The more common counterpart 採 has largely replaced 采 in everyday usage. You'll encounter 采 mainly in historical texts, formal/literary contexts, and in anime/manga that reference classical Japanese or Chinese history, especially relevant to your interest in Anime & Manga and History.

examples.meaning_tr: Command; baton; exercise of judgment or discretion (commonly used in sports, games, and military contexts in anime/manga)
Gathering; collection; compilation (especially of folklore, materials, or data; relevant to your interest in Nature and History)
Court attendant or musician (historical term from Chinese court tradition, appearing frequently in historical anime and period dramas)

勁.note_tr: 勁 emphasizes vigorous or muscular strength and is quite rare in modern Japanese, the kanji 強 (strong) is far more common. The onyomi けい is used in formal or literary contexts, while the kunyomi つよい is rarely seen in contemporary usage.

examples.meaning_tr: formidable enemy; worthy rival (common in anime, games, sports)

哉.note_tr: This classical Japanese particle (N1 grammar) primarily appears in formal, poetic, and literary contexts. It expresses surprise, emotion, or emphasis in exclamatory and rhetorical questions. The kunyomi かな is far more common than さい or や in actual usage. You will encounter this character frequently in anime and manga with historical settings, classical literature references, and formal or archaic speech patterns.

meanings_tr: The God of Literature (Kuixing in Chinese tradition)
奎.note_tr: This classical kanji is rarely used in modern Japanese, appearing mainly in literary contexts, references to Kuixing (the god of literature and scholarly success in Chinese astrology), or proper names. The onyomi けい is standard; the reading き is less common in contemporary usage.

examples.meaning_tr: Kuixing; the god of literature and scholarly success in Chinese astrology and tradition
Star; the character itself, found in personal and place names and classical literature
Star; alternate onyomi reading, primarily encountered in classical texts and historical documents

宥.note_tr: The kunyomi reading なだめる (to soothe, calm) is the most practical for modern Japanese and appears in everyday contexts. The onyomi ゆう is primarily used in formal compounds like 宥恕 (ゆうじょ, 'forgiveness'); note that 許す is the more standard kanji when writing 'to forgive.'

examples.meaning_tr: to soothe, to calm, to pacify
to soothe a child, to calm a child down
to appease anger, to calm someone's anger
to soothe the other person, to pacify someone

昴.note_tr: The kunyomi すばる is most common, referring to the Pleiades constellation (and origins of the Subaru brand). The onyomi ぼう appears mainly in formal astronomy and astrology contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: Pleiades mansion (one of 28 lunar mansions in traditional East Asian astronomy)

柊.note_tr: The kunyomi reading ひいらぎ is the standard way to refer to holly in modern Japanese. The onyomi readings しゅ and しゅう rarely appear in contemporary usage. This plant holds cultural significance in Japan, particularly in Setsubun traditions where holly and sardines are displayed to ward off evil spirits.

examples.meaning_tr: Sardine head and holly decoration (used during Setsubun)

柾.note_tr: This is a kokuji (Japanese-created character) used primarily in woodworking and botanical contexts. The reading masame (まさめ) is most common for the wood grain pattern, while masaki (まさき) refers to the spindle tree plant. Rarely encountered outside specialized fields.

examples.meaning_tr: Straight wood grain; the vertical grain pattern in lumber, highly prized in traditional Japanese carpentry and furniture making
Spindle tree; a small ornamental shrub with red-orange seed capsules, used in Japanese gardens and traditional art
Straight-grain lumber; wood specifically selected to display the vertical grain pattern for high-quality traditional crafts and construction

洵.note_tr: This is a rare JLPT N1 kanji, primarily found in classical and literary Japanese. The onyomi reading じゅん is most frequently used in modern contexts, especially in the adverbial form 洵に (じゅんに) meaning "truly" or "indeed." The alternate readings (しゅん, の.ぶ, まこと.に) are archaic or rarely encountered in contemporary usage.

耶.note_tr: 耶 is a classical/archaic kanji rarely seen in modern Japanese. It primarily appears in historical texts, classical literature, and period-setting anime/manga. The onyomi readings や and じゃ function as interrogative particles marking questions; the kunyomi か is less frequently encountered. Pay attention when reading classical texts or historical narratives.

examples.meaning_tr: How is it? What is the matter? (classical interrogative)
Is it or is it not? (classical philosophical questioning)
Is it so? Is that true? (classical affirmation question)

胤.note_tr: This rare kanji primarily uses the いん (on'yomi) reading in formal, historical, and literary contexts, including period anime and historical fantasy manga. The kunyomi たね is essentially obsolete in modern Japanese. 胤 most commonly appears in compounds describing royal, noble, or hereditary bloodlines and succession. You'll encounter it mainly in history-related texts and feudal-setting stories.

examples.meaning_tr: Imperial lineage or descent; the royal line
Legitimate heir or direct descendant of a noble house
Blood lineage; kinship by blood descent

衿.note_tr: 衿 primarily refers to the collar of traditional garments, especially kimono. The kun'yomi reading えり is overwhelmingly common in modern usage; onyomi readings are rare and mostly literary. Appears frequently in period anime and manga set in historical Japan.

examples.meaning_tr: collar opening; collar adjustment (adjusting a kimono's neckline)
white nape area (the exposed nape of the neck visible with kimono)

倖.note_tr: This kanji is less common than the similar kanji 幸 (sachi/shiawase). The kunyomi readings さいわい and しあわせ are productive and commonly seen in phrases expressing luck or happiness; the onyomi こう appears mainly in given names and formal compounds.

恕.note_tr: This kanji appears primarily in formal or literary contexts. The onyomi (じょ) is more frequently encountered in compounds like 寛恕 and 恕度, while the kunyomi ゆる.す is less common than its synonym 許す (ゆるす). Both readings emphasize compassion and forbearance rather than mere permission.

examples.meaning_tr: to forgive; to excuse; to tolerate
to forgive a sin; to pardon a transgression

meanings_tr: Late (especially of the evening or sunset)
晏.note_tr: The onyomi あん is primarily used in classical, formal, and Buddhist contexts. This is a rare kanji that appears mainly in classical texts, poetry, and formal compounds rather than in modern everyday Japanese. The kunyomi おそ.い relates to the "late" or "slow" meaning but is less frequently encountered.

examples.meaning_tr: Imperial carriage; a procession for an imperial dignitary
Peacefully; calmly; in a tranquil manner
Sitting peacefully; peaceful meditation (Zen Buddhist context)
Yan Zi, a renowned statesman and diplomat from ancient China

晟.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji appears mainly in formal, literary, and specialized contexts or personal names. The kunyomi あきらか is typically rendered as 明らか or in hiragana; both onyomi readings appear primarily in formal compounds.

examples.meaning_tr: obviously, clearly, evidently, in an obvious manner
bright and clear, luminous, pure and brilliant

meanings_tr: I, me (imperial first-person pronoun; majestic plural used by emperors)
Imperial we (formal archaic usage in official contexts and edicts)
朕.note_tr: 朕 is a formal archaic pronoun used exclusively by emperors in official edicts, classical texts, and historical fiction. In modern Japanese, it appears mainly in period anime, manga, and classical literature. Always read as ちん. Unlike everyday pronouns such as 私 (watashi) or 僕 (boku), 朕 carries strong imperial and formal connotations.

examples.meaning_tr: I, me (majestic or imperial first-person pronoun)
methinks, I presume (classical expression of imperial opinion)
I (with subject particle); used in imperial contexts like 朕が治める (I rule)
my, of mine (possessive); used in phrases like 朕の天下 (my realm)

栞.note_tr: The kunyomi reading しおり is the standard for everyday use in both physical books (paper bookmarks) and digital contexts (bookmark feature). The onyomi かん rarely appears in modern Japanese.

紗.note_tr: In modern Japanese, 紗 uses the onyomi reading しゃ in compounds, while さ and the kunyomi うすぎぬ are archaic. The kanji appears mainly in textile vocabulary and can be confused with 沙 (sand) based on visual similarity, differentiate by radical: 紗 uses 糸 (thread), 沙 uses 氵 (water).

examples.meaning_tr: Gauze curtain; sheer curtain used in theater or traditional spaces
A type of rough-textured fabric; linen-like cloth used in traditional garments

耗.note_tr: Most commonly used in the compound 消耗 (shōmō, using the もう reading) meaning wear and tear. The こう reading is rarer and typically found in formal or technical language.

examples.reading: たいりょくのしょうもう

莉.note_tr: 莉 is primarily a name character (人名用漢字), typically read り (ri) in female given names and rarely appearing in common vocabulary. The jasmine connotation makes it popular in anime and manga character names.

meanings_tr: Rush grass; igusa (used for tatami mats)
莞.note_tr: The on'yomi かん appears in 莞爾, a literary term meaning 'smiling' or 'with a smile.' The kun'yomi い is used in 莞草 (igusa), the rush plant traditionally used to make tatami mat covers. This N1 kanji is uncommon in everyday use.

examples.meaning_tr: A smile; smiling; with a smile
With a smile; smiling (while doing something)
Igusa; rush grass used to make tatami mat covers
To show a smile; to smile

崚.note_tr: This is a specialized N1 kanji appearing primarily in geographical texts, maps, and descriptions of mountain terrain. Always pronounced りょう (ryō) with no common kunyomi reading. Useful when reading about hiking destinations, mountain ranges, natural landscapes, or adventure-themed manga and novels, content aligned with your interest in nature and travel.

examples.meaning_tr: rocky promontory; a coastal cape with steep, jagged cliffs
ridge line; mountain escarpment; a sharp, continuous mountain ridge
dangerous rocky cliffs; treacherous mountain terrain

捷.note_tr: The onyomi reading しょう is the primary reading in modern compounds like 捷径. The meaning "victory" appears in formal contexts (捷報), while the kunyomi はや.い and alternate reading そう are less common in contemporary use.

捺.note_tr: Most common in modern Japanese is the onyomi だつ, particularly in 捺印 (stamping an official seal), which frequently appears in business and legal contexts. The kunyomi readings (さ.す and お.す) are rarely used in contemporary Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: sealing; stamping of an official seal
to press; to stamp; to print
to affix an official registered seal

晨.note_tr: 晨 is a formal, literary kanji for morning, primarily used with the onyomi しん in modern Japanese. Though kunyomi readings exist (あした, とき, あさ), they are rarely used in contemporary writing; for everyday "morning," the simpler kanji 朝 is preferred.

examples.meaning_tr: Morning star (Venus; also used metaphorically for a herald)

梢.note_tr: こずえ is the primary reading for treetops, commonly found in nature writing and poetry; しょう is used in poetic compounds like 梢風. The second kunyomi くすのき (camphor tree) is archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese.

梧.note_tr: This rare N1 kanji is primarily found in the compound 梧桐 (ごとう). The onyomi ご is used in compounds, while the kunyomi あおぎり refers to the tree itself in classical or botanical contexts. The parasol tree holds cultural significance in East Asian literature and traditional Japanese aesthetics.

examples.meaning_tr: Grayish-green color used in traditional Japanese aesthetics

眸.note_tr: 眸 is almost exclusively used in its kunyomi reading ひとみ and appears primarily in literary, poetic, or manga contexts. The onyomi readings ぼう and む are rarely encountered in modern Japanese. You'll see this kanji mainly in emotional or descriptive passages common in anime and manga.

examples.meaning_tr: to widen one's eyes in surprise; to stare intently
to be reflected in one's eyes; to catch one's eye
to have bright, shining eyes (eager or excited expression)
the depths of one's eyes; the look in someone's eyes

meanings_tr: A wind instrument used in traditional East Asian court music
笙.note_tr: Only the reading しょう is used in modern Japanese (the kunyomi ふえ is archaic). This specialized kanji refers to a reed mouth organ in traditional East Asian court music (gagaku).

examples.meaning_tr: The sheng; a traditional reed instrument

紬.note_tr: つむぎ (kunyomi) is the primary reading, referring to pongee, a traditional silk fabric used in Japanese kimonos. The verb form つむ.ぐ (to spin/weave) and onyomi ちゅう are archaic and rarely used in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Pongee; a lightweight silk fabric with a distinctive nubby texture
Ōshima pongee; a famous traditional textile from Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan
Summer pongee; a lightweight pongee worn during warm months

絃.note_tr: 絃 is a literary or archaic variant of the more common modern kanji 弦 (both mean "string"). The onyomi げん is typically used in compounds like 絃楽器 (string instrument), while the kunyomi いと describes the physical string itself.

菖.note_tr: This kanji most commonly appears in the compound 菖蒲 (iris), particularly in seasonal and garden contexts. It is culturally significant in May traditions, such as iris baths (菖蒲湯) during the Tango no Sekku festival (May 5th).

examples.meaning_tr: iris bath; traditional bath with iris leaves

菫.note_tr: The kunyomi すみれ is the primary and virtually exclusive reading used in modern Japanese, appearing in nature contexts, poetry, and botanical texts. The onyomi きん is extremely rare and seldom appears in practical use. This is a specialized kanji, perfect for your interest in nature.

examples.meaning_tr: White violet (a type of violet flower)

袈.note_tr: This kanji appears almost exclusively in the compound 袈裟 (けさ), using the け reading, which refers to the ceremonial vestment worn by Buddhist monks. The kanji is extremely rare outside of this context in modern Japanese.

examples.meaning_tr: Buddhist vestment; the ceremonial robe worn by Buddhist monks
diagonal wearing method; carrying something diagonally across the chest
diagonal sword slash (a sword technique named after the diagonal pattern of a Buddhist robe)

椋.note_tr: This advanced JLPT N1 kanji rarely appears in modern Japanese except in the compound 椋鳥 (grey starling), which uses the kunyomi reading. The onyomi りょう is uncommon and found mainly in proper names and literary contexts. Given your interest in nature, you may encounter this in nature-themed anime, manga, or classical literature.

examples.meaning_tr: Grey starling - a small migratory songbird native to East Asia
Kunyomi reading; refers to the deciduous tree in botanical or classical texts
Onyomi reading; used in proper names and rare literary compounds

琳.note_tr: This is a very rare kanji (JLPT N1) used predominantly in proper names, especially in anime and manga. The on'yomi りん is the only reading; there is no kun'yomi. The primary dictionary compound is 琳琅 (precious jade or beautiful stones). Beyond these few literary/poetic uses, you'll encounter this kanji mainly in Japanese given names and fictional character names.

examples.meaning_tr: Beautiful jade; precious stones; something valuable and precious
A dazzling display; an abundance of beautiful or precious things arranged together

痘.note_tr: This on'yomi-only kanji appears primarily in medical and historical contexts, particularly in terms related to vaccination and smallpox. No kunyomi exists for this character. Useful for history and medical texts.

竣.note_tr: This kanji primarily uses the onyomi reading しゅん and appears almost exclusively in formal or technical contexts, rarely in everyday conversation. The most common usage is in compounds like 竣工 (completion of construction), frequently seen in technology, architecture, and real estate contexts.

examples.meaning_tr: completion of construction; finished work on a project
completion ceremony; opening ceremony after construction
completion of construction work; finished building project

脹.note_tr: The onyomi ちょう appears mainly in formal or medical compounds like 脹張 (expansion) and 脹脈 (varicose vein). The kunyomi readings (ふく.らむ, ふく.れる, は.れる) describe everyday physical swelling in creative writing and speech. Note: 膨 is the more common kanji variant in modern Japanese for these same readings.

examples.meaning_tr: expansion; dilation; increase in volume or size
to expand; to swell up; to balloon; to puff out
to swell; to puff up; to become bloated; to bulge

塑.note_tr: The onyomi そ is the standard reading, appearing mainly in compound words related to sculpting, molding, or material properties. Unlike 捏 (kneading), 塑 suggests artistic or formal shaping, relevant to your interest in art and anime.

meanings_tr: be bulky; take up space; be cumbersome
swell; grow or increase in volume
mount up; accumulate (in quantity or cost)
